correctAnswer: B. Axial CT scans in single slices, while helical CT scans continuously in a spiral.
explanationHtml:
The key difference is that axial CT acquires images one slice at a time, whereas helical CT continuously collects data in a spiral path as the patient moves through the scanner.

Axial and Helical CT: Axial CT (Computed Tomography) and Helical CT(also known as Spiral CT) are two different scanning techniques used in medical imaging to obtain cross-sectional images of the body.

Axial CT

Helical CT

Definition

  • Axial CT scans acquire images in discrete slices or cross-sections of the body. The scanner rotates around the patient, capturing one slice at a time.
  • Helical CT scans acquire images continuously in a spiral pattern as the patient moves through the scanner.
  • This allows for a continuous data stream and overlapping slices.

Data Acquisition

  • The table holding the patient moves in small increments between scans.
  • After each slice is acquired, the table stops to allow for the next slice to be taken.
  • The scanner rotates around the patient while the table moves through the gantry simultaneously, resulting in a spiral path of data collection.

Scan Time

  • Generally longer due to the stepwise approach, as the table must move and stop for each slice.
  • Much faster than axial CT, as the entire area can be scanned in a single breath-hold, which is beneficial for patients who may have difficulty remaining still.

Image Quality

  • Typically provides high-resolution images, making it ideal for detailed examinations, especially of the brain and other structures.
  • Provides good quality images and can be processed for 3D reconstructions, making it useful for dynamic studies and quick imaging.

Advantages

  • High-resolution images, ideal for detailed examinations.
  • Faster scans, less motion artifact, and the ability to reconstruct images in multiple planes.

Disadvantages

  • Longer scan times and may be less effective for dynamic imaging.
  • May require higher radiation doses depending on parameters and can have slightly lower image resolution compared to axial scans.

  • Axial CT uses contrast agents, while helical CT does not.(Option A): Both axial and helical CT can use contrast agents, depending on the clinical requirements.
  • Helical CT requires more radiation than axial CT.(Option C): Helical CT does not inherently require more radiation than axial CT; radiation exposure can depend on various factors, including scan parameters.

Axial CT produces 3D images, while helical CT produces 2D images.(Option D): Both axial and helical CT can be processed to create 3D images.



Reference:

David Sutton Textbook of Radiology edition 8, page 254, 255, 256 & 257

Therapeutic applications of USG- High-intensity focused ultrasonography (HIFU)

Mechanism

(Option B)

correctAnswer: A. Aliasing; mitigate by increasing the pulse repetition frequency (PRF).
explanationHtml:
• Aliasing is the most common artifact seen in spectral and color Doppler ultrasound, especially when high blood flow velocities are being measured, such as in the carotid arteries.

  • It occurs when the velocity of blood flow exceeds the Nyquist limit (which is half the PRF), causing the displayed waveform to wrap around, leading to overestimation or misinterpretation of velocity.

  • Aliasing appears as a sudden shift or wrap-around of the spectral waveform or color scale reversal (e.g., red to blue).

To mitigate aliasing:

  • Increase PRF (not decrease).

  • Use a lower frequency transducer.

  • Adjust the baseline downward.

  • Use continuous wave Doppler if feasible.

So, the mitigation option in the question is incorrect — you should increase PRF, not decrease it.

Corrected Answer:

Aliasing; mitigate by increasing the pulse repetition frequency (PRF).

Ruling Out Incorrect Options:

  • Blooming (Option B):
    Incorrect, because blooming causes overestimation of vessel diameter or area due to excessive gain; it doesn’t affect velocity. Increasing wall filter doesn't mitigate blooming.

  • Direction Ambiguity (Option C):
    Incorrect, this occurs with transcranial or abdominal Doppler using large sample volumes; not typical in carotid studies.

  • Twinkle Artifact (Option D):
    Incorrect, seen in color Doppler near calcifications or stones, not relevant to velocity overestimation in carotids.

Summary Table:

Artifact Appearance Best Solution
Aliasing Wrap-around waveform or reversed color Increase PRF, lower frequency, shift baseline
Blooming Overfilled color/velocity extending beyond vessel wall Reduce gain, optimize wall filters
Direction Ambiguity Flow appears in both directions Use angle correction, reduce sample volume
Twinkle Artifact Color speckling behind calcified area Lower color gain or change angle


Reference:

David Sutton textbook of Radiology & Imaging Edition 8, Volume I, Page 209-221

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

CECT is preferred for evaluating lung nodules because the contrast enhances the visibility of the nodule and its characteristics, which helps in differentiating between benign and malignant lesions. It also allows for better assessment of surrounding structures and lymph nodes.


Non-Contrast Computed Tomography (NCCT) and Contrast-Enhanced Computed Tomography (CECT)

Non-Contrast Computed Tomography (NCCT)

Contrast-Enhanced Computed Tomography (CECT)

NCCT refers to CT imaging performed without the use of intravenous contrast agents.

[[figure-1]]

CECT involves the administration of an intravenous contrast agent to enhance the visibility of vascular structures and improve differentiation of tissues in the body.

[[figure-2]]

Indications:

  • Bone Injuries: Fractures, especially of the spine and long bones. (Option A ruled out)
  • Kidney Stones: Evaluation of renal calculi (stones) and urinary tract obstruction. (Option C ruled out)
  • Head Trauma: Detecting hemorrhage or skull fractures. (Option D ruled out)
  • Acute Abdomen: Initial evaluation of acute abdominal pain (appendicitis, diverticulitis).

Indications:

  • Tumor Detection: Identifying and characterizing masses or tumors in various organs.
  • Pulmonary Diseases: Assessing lung pathology (pneumonia, lung nodules). (Option B)
  • Vascular Assessment: Evaluating blood vessels for stenosis, thrombosis, or aneurysms.
  • Infection: Assessing abscesses or inflammatory conditions where contrast can delineate structures.
  • Staging of Cancer: Determining the extent of malignancies by evaluating lymph nodes and distant metastases.
  • Assessment of Organ Perfusion: Evaluating blood flow in organs.

Advantages:

  • No Allergic Reactions: Eliminates the risk of allergic reactions to contrast agents.
  • No Need for Renal Function Assessment: Suitable for patients with renal impairment who cannot tolerate contrast.
  • Faster: Typically quicker to perform than CECT, as no time is needed for contrast administration.
  • Cost-effective: Generally less expensive than CECT.

Advantages:

  • Enhanced Visualization: Improves the contrast between different tissues, making it easier to identify abnormalities.
  • Better Soft Tissue Detail: Provides superior detail of soft tissue structures compared to NCCT.
  • Vascular Imaging: Excellent for visualizing blood vessels and detecting vascular pathologies.

Limitations:

  • Limited Diagnostic Capability: May not provide enough detail for soft tissue structures or vascular assessments.
  • Less Sensitivity: Lower sensitivity for detecting certain conditions, such as tumors or vascular abnormalities, compared to CECT.

Limitations:

  • Risk of Allergic Reactions: Possible allergic reactions to contrast agents, ranging from mild to severe (anaphylaxis).
  • Renal Impairment: Requires caution in patients with pre-existing kidney disease, as contrast can further compromise renal function (risk of Contrast-Induced Nephropathy).
  • Increased Radiation Exposure: Slightly higher radiation exposure compared to NCCT due to additional imaging phases.


Reference:

www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9672504/

High-Resolution CT (HRCT):

Definition

Specialized imaging technique that provides highly detailed cross-sectional images of the body's internal structures, primarily the lungs

Technique
  • Thin Collimation: Uses thin slices (usually 1 mm or less) to improve image resolution.
  • High Spatial Resolution: Optimized scanning protocols to enhance the detail of structures.

  • Tumor Evaluation: Assessing lung nodules and tumors. (For Pancoast tumor MRI is preferred)

Key Imaging Features
  • Reticular Patterns: Suggestive of fibrosis and interstitial lung disease.
  • Ground-Glass Opacities: Indicate inflammation or partial consolidation.
  • Nodules and Masses: Detailed visualization of pulmonary nodules.

Advantages
  • High Sensitivity and Specificity: Superior ability to detect and characterize lung pathologies compared to standard CT or X-rays.
  • Detailed Assessment: Provides detailed anatomical information, aiding in accurate diagnosis and treatment planning.
  • 3D Reconstruction: Data can be processed to create 3D images for better anatomical visualization.

Limitations

  • Cost: Generally more expensive than standard imaging modalities.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
High window level and wide window width are ideal for visualizing dense structures like bone because it allows for better differentiation of highly dense tissues.


In CT imaging, the window refers to the range of Hounsfield units (HU) that are displayed on the CT image, allowing radiologists to better visualize specific tissues or structures by adjusting the image contrast. The window settings include two key components:

Window Width (WW) Window Level (WL)
  • This defines the range of Hounsfield units that will be displayed. It controls the contrast of the image.
  • A narrow window width is used for better contrast of soft tissues.
  • A wide window width is used for imaging high-contrast structures like bone.
  • This determines the central Hounsfield value of the window range and adjusts the brightness of the image.
  • A higher window level is used to visualize dense tissues like bones.
  • A lower window level is used for soft tissues.


Types of CT Windows:

  • Bone window: High window level and wide window width to clearly view bones and other dense structures.
  • Lung window: Narrow window width and lower window level for optimal visualization of lung parenchyma and air spaces.
  • Soft tissue window: Lower window level and narrower width to focus on soft tissue structures like muscles, organs, and the brain.

Low window level and narrow window width (Option A) are more suitable for soft tissues where contrast needs to be enhanced, not for dense structures like bone.


Low window level and wide window width (Option C) would reduce brightness, making it harder to see dense structures like bones.


High window level and narrow window width (Option D): While a high window level is appropriate for bones, a narrow window width would reduce the ability to distinguish different densities within the bone itself.



Reference:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
The scenario is of tension pneumocephalus - air trapped under pressure in the intracranial space, compressing the brain structures and showing the classic Mount Fuji sign in CT. The black area here is air.


In CT imaging, black areas usually correspond to low-density substances like air or fluid, which do not absorb much X-ray radiation.


Imaging principles of CT scan:

  • CT uses filtered x-ray beams and a computer to create cross-sectional images of the body.
  • CT slices reveal specific anatomy levels, with slice thickness chosen to minimise scatter radiation and superimposition using collimators.
  • CT data are divided into pixels, forming a matrix, each representing different image details.
  • Structures in CT images are depicted in varying shades of grey based on x-ray beam attenuation principles.
  • The linear attenuation coefficient quantifies photon interaction with matter and varies with density, atomic number, and energy.
  • Higher density and atomic number lead to more significant attenuation, affecting image contrast.
  • CT images reflect these coefficients, showing denser materials as white and less dense ones as black.
  • Contrast agents, like iodine, temporarily modify structure density differences for better visualization.


Imaging principles of X-Ray:

X-ray Appearance Cause Examples
Black X-rays pass through less dense tissues and reach the cassette with more energy Air or gas, e.g., lungs, bowel gas
White X-rays are mostly absorbed by very dense tissues, so little reaches the cassette Bone, metal, calcified areas
Gray X-rays pass through intermediate-density tissues Soft tissues, muscles, fat, organs


Dense structures like bone (Option A): Appear white or light gray because they absorb more X-rays.

Introduction
  • Discovered by W.C. Roentgen on 8 November 1895 (International Day of Radiology).

Production
  • By sudden deceleration of fast-moving electron beam (Option A)

Working principle
  • The Cathode (filament) is an electron source that produces the electron beam and the Anode is a tungsten target for the electron beam.
  • The electron beam travels from the cathode (negatively charged) to the anode (positively charged) (Option D)
  • Thermionic emission occurs at the Cathode.
  • Blocking of the electron beam is done at the Anode, where 99% of heat dissipation is by Radiation (Option C) and the remaining 1% escapes through the window onto a film called X-rays.

Components

The Cathode
  • Made up of Tungsten (atomic no.- 74) & Thorium.

The Anode

  • Made up of Lead (Pb).

Focusing cup
  • Made up of Nickel.

[[figure-2]]

Bremsstrahlung radiation (produced by the interaction of electron with nucleus) :

  • Electromagnetic radiation produced by the deceleration of a charged particle when deflected by another charged particle.
  • When an electron beam (negatively charged) travels towards the anode, the nucleus (positively charged) gets deflected and travels in a different direction.
  • Bremsstrahlung radiation depends upon the angle of deflection.

[[figure-3]]

Characteristic radiation: Phenomenon similar to Bremsstrahlung radiation, but depends upon the atomic number of the element, produced by interaction of electron with the orbital shell.

  • On ultrasonography, the appearance of tissues depends on their acoustic properties, particularly the presence or absence of internal interfaces that can reflect sound waves.
  • Bile is a homogeneous fluid with uniform acoustic density. Because there are no internal interfaces within bile to reflect ultrasound waves, it does not produce echoes. MRI primarily works by aligning the hydrogen nuclei in the body's tissues with a strong magnetic field and then detecting the signals produced as these nuclei return to their equilibrium state (relaxation).


Radiofrequency (RF) pulses excite hydrogen protons, and the emitted signals are captured and processed to generate detailed images of internal structures.


MRI:

  • Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is a noninvasive diagnostic technique that uses non-ionizing electromagnetic radiation, making it safer than CT scans, which involve ionizing radiation. (Option D)
  • Principle: MRI operates on the principle of Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR), utilizing a superconducting magnet to produce a strong magnetic field.
  • Mechanism:
    • MRI primarily works by aligning the hydrogen nuclei in the body's tissues with a strong magnetic field and then detecting the signals produced as these nuclei return to their equilibrium state (relaxation).
    • Radiofrequency (RF) pulses excite hydrogen protons, and the emitted signals are captured and processed to generate detailed images of internal structures.
  • Scan duration: Scans typically last from 10 minutes for simpler studies to about an hour for more complex examinations.
  • Noise: The process is noisy due to the rapid switching of gradient coils; hence, patients are provided hearing protection.
  • Specialized Techniques: Advanced methods such as MR angiography (MRA), venography, perfusion imaging, spectroscopy, tractography, and functional MRI (fMRI) are used for specific, detailed evaluations.


Evaluate changes in magnetic field strength around tissues (Option A): MRI focuses on the behavior of hydrogen nuclei rather than changes in magnetic field strength around tissues.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Piezoelectric Principle

  • Ultrasonography is based on the piezoelectric effect
    • Certain crystals generate ultrasound waves when an electric current is applied
    • The same crystals generate electrical signals when deformed by returning echoes
  • This property allows the same transducer to act as both:
    • Transmitter
    • Receiver

Lead Zirconate (PZT)

  • Lead zirconate, combined with lead titanate, forms PZT (Lead Zirconate Titanate)
  • PZT is the most commonly used material in modern ultrasound transducers due to:
    • High piezoelectric efficiency
    • Greater sensitivity to returning echoes
    • Wide bandwidth → improved axial resolution
    • Better mechanical strength and durability
    • Superior signal-to-noise ratio
  • These properties make PZT ideal for real-time, high-resolution imaging

Sodium fluoride (Option A): Does not possess piezoelectric properties and therefore cannot be used to generate or receive ultrasound waves.

Lead zirconate (Option B): Used only in combination with lead titanate as PZT; alone it is not a standard ultrasound transducer material.

Sodium zirconate (Option D): Has no effective piezoelectric application in medical ultrasonography and is not used in transducers.



Reference:

Christensen’s Physics of Diagnostic Radiology, 4th Edition, Page 329.

  • The same crystals act as receivers by converting returning echoes into electrical signals.
  • This dual property allows both transmission and reception of ultrasound waves.
  • Image formation in all ultrasound modes depends on this principle.

MRI (Option A): Uses nuclear magnetic resonance and strong magnetic fields, so it does not involve piezoelectricity or sound wave generation.

MR spectroscopy (Option C): An MRI-based technique for metabolic analysis that does not use ultrasound or crystals.

X-ray (Option D): Uses ionising radiation to create images and does not depend on piezoelectric effects.

explanationHtml:
• X-ray → Radiolucent / Opaque:
    • Radiolucent structures allow X-rays to pass through, appearing dark on the image (e.g., air, fat).
    • Opaque structures do not allow X-rays to pass, appearing white (e.g., bones, metal).
  • CT (Computed Tomography) → Hypodense / Hyperdense:
    • Hypodense areas appear darker on a CT scan, indicating less density (e.g., fluid).
    • Hyperdense areas appear brighter, indicating higher density (e.g., bone, calcifications).
  • MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging) → Hypointense / Hyperintense:
    • Hypointense signals are darker, indicating less hydrogen density (e.g., certain tumors, cysts).
    • Hyperintense signals are brighter, indicating higher hydrogen density (e.g., fluid, edema).
  • USG (Ultrasound) → Hypoechoic / Hyperechoic:
    • Hypoechoic areas appear darker on ultrasound due to fewer echoes returning (e.g., fluid-filled structures).
    • Hyperechoic areas appear brighter due to more echoes (e.g., solid masses, calcifications).


Reference:

Fred A. Mettler, Jr. Essentials of Radiology, 4th Edition, Page 1-6

explanationHtml:
In the single wall puncture technique, the needle is advanced just enough to puncture the front wall of the artery without going through the back wall. While this technique reduces the risk of hematoma and pseudoaneurysm compared to the double-wall (through-and-through) puncture, it does not reduce the risk of arterial dissection. In fact, manipulating the needle tip within the arterial lumen (especially if not carefully aligned) can potentially increase the risk of dissection.

  • Decreases the number of attempts needed.
  • Decreased risk of arterial dissection.
  • It can strike the bony landmark located behind the vessels (such as the femoral head).

The risk of arterial dissection may increase due to guidewire buckling if it is only partially within the lumen.

  • A Faraday cage is a conductive enclosure that shields its inner space from electromagnetic interference.
  • In MRI environments, this enclosure is typically constructed using wooden panels wrapped in copper wires, which provide effective radiofrequency (RF) shielding. This shielding helps minimize interference, which leads to imaging artifacts and ensures clearer and more accurate MRI results.
  • In the MRI facility, the cage is often visible through the special window glass separating the control room from the scanner area, further emphasizing its role in maintaining optimal imaging conditions.

[[figure-2]]

Helmholtz coils (Option B) are a pair of circular coils arranged parallel to one another and function as Z gradient coils in MRI scanners.

[[figure-3]]

Shim coils (Option C) are used to correct minor spatial discrepancies in the main static magnetic field and ensure optimal spatial uniformity, improving MRI image quality by reducing artifacts.

explanationHtml:
• Most cochlear implants are absolute contraindications for MRI due to their metallic components, which can be affected by the strong magnetic fields and may cause image artifacts that compromise scan quality. However, some newer cochlear implants are classified as relative contraindications and may be used in specific conditional circumstances.
  • Risks of MRI are mainly due to
    • The static magnetic field causes high-velocity pull of metals due to the Ferromagnetic nature.

Explanation:

Titanium internal fixation devices are the most MRI-compatible orthopaedic implants because titanium is non-ferromagnetic, produces minimal image artefact, and has excellent biocompatibility.

explanationHtml:
• Susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) is an advanced MRI technique that enhances the visibility of tissues based on magnetic susceptibility differences.
  • It is highly sensitive for detecting microbleeds (common in hypertension), iron deposits (seen in neurodegenerative diseases and hemorrhagic lesions), and calcifications.
  • Black dots on SWI indicate areas of Microbleeds/Iron deposition/Calcification.
  • CSF appears dark, not bright.

[[figure-1]]

Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) (Option B) is primarily used to assess the diffusion of water molecules and is not specifically designed to visualise iron deposition. It is preferred in acute infarcts, brain abscesses, and brain tumours.

[[figure-2]]

Functional MRI (fMRI) (Option C) focuses on detecting brain activity rather than structural changes like iron deposition. Clinically, it is commonly used for pre-surgical planning in brain tumour and Arteriovenous Malformation (AVM) surgeries, as well as for localising language centres and determining hemispheric dominance before epilepsy surgery.

[[figure-3]]

MR Spectroscopy (Option D) provides metabolic information but does not directly assess iron accumulation. Key metabolites include N-acetyl aspartate (NAA) as a marker of neuronal integrity, choline (Cho) associated with membrane turnover and elevated in tumors, creatine (Cr) for energy metabolism, lactate indicative of hypoxia or ischemia, and myo-inositol, reflecting glial activity.

[[figure-4]]

Diffusion-Weighted Imaging (DWI)

  • Measures the diffusion (Brownian motion) of water molecules within tissues and is highly sensitive to changes in cellular density.
  • Areas of restricted diffusion appear hyperintense (bright) on DWI.
  • Common causes of restricted diffusion include:
    • Acute ischemic infarction (earliest MRI sequence to become positive)
    • Brain abscess
    • Epidermoid cyst
    • Hypercellular tumors (e.g., primary CNS lymphoma, medulloblastoma)
  • Acute ischemic stroke typically appears bright on DWI and dark on the apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) map, confirming true restricted diffusion.

FLAIR (Fluid-Attenuated Inversion Recovery)

  • FLAIR is a T2-weighted inversion recovery sequence that suppresses the signal from cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), making adjacent pathological lesions more conspicuous.
  • It is particularly useful for detecting:
    • Periventricular and juxtacortical lesions in multiple sclerosis
    • Cerebral edema
    • Gliosis
    • Acute and subacute infarcts
    • Subarachnoid hemorrhage (particularly after the initial hours)
  • Because CSF is suppressed, lesions adjacent to the ventricles and cortical sulci are visualised more clearly than on conventional T2-weighted images.

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, Volume 2, 7th Edition, Page 1376

c) T1-Weighted MRI
4) d) T2-Weighted MRI

correctAnswer: B. T1 involves energy exchange; T2 involves loss of phase coherence.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

T1-weighted MRI involves energy exchange between spins and the environment, while T2-weighted MRI involves loss of phase coherence among spins.


T1 & T2 Weighted MRI:

Parameter

T1-Weighted MRI

T2-Weighted MRI

Definition

It is time for longitudinal magnetisation to recover to its equilibrium after excitation.

It is time for transverse magnetisation to decay.

Mechanism

Involves energy exchange between spins and surrounding environment (spin-lattice interaction)

Involves loss of phase coherence among spins (spin-spin interaction)

Tissue Assessment

Useful for assessing fat content in tissues (e.g., brain white matter)

Useful for assessing water content in tissues (e.g., cerebrospinal fluid)

Tissue Appearance

Darker for longer T1, brighter for shorter T1

Brighter for longer T2, darker for shorter T2

Bright Area Significance

Bright areas indicate tissues with shorter T1 times (e.g., fat-rich tissues)

Bright areas indicate tissues with longer T2 times (e.g., fluid-rich tissues)

Time Range

Microseconds to seconds

Typically shorter than T1


T1 measures transverse decay; T2 measures longitudinal recovery (Option A): T1 relaxation measures longitudinal recovery — how quickly the net magnetization returns to align with the main magnetic field (along the z-axis). T2 relaxation measures transverse decay — how quickly the spins dephase in the transverse plane (xy-plane).


T1 relaxation is typically shorter in duration than T2 (Option C): T1 relaxation times are typically longer than T2. For most tissues, it takes longer for longitudinal magnetization to recover than it does for transverse magnetization to decay.


Longer T1 appears Brighter & Longer T2 appears Darker (Option D): In T1-weighted images, tissues with short T1 times appear brighter, while those with long T1 appear darker. In T2-weighted images, tissues with long T2 times appear brighter because their signal decays more slowly, maintaining more signal during image acquisition.

  1. Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, Volume 2, 7th Edition, Page 1375

question: Which statements correctly describe the differences between T1 and T2 relaxation in MRI?

correctAnswer: A. Protons align uniformly, get excited, and relax, emitting radiation.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Protons align uniformly in a magnetic field, which then gets excited by Radiofrequency pulses and emits radiation while relaxing. This radiation is detected and used to create MRI Images.

MRI Image Acquisition Process (Four Stages):

  • Resting State: In this initial phase, protons in the body are randomly aligned and moving, resulting in no net magnetisation.
  • Magnetisation: An external magnetic field is applied, causing the protons to align uniformly, creating a net magnetisation vector along the longitudinal axis.
  • Excitation:
    • An RF(Radio Frequency) coil is activated, sending an RF pulse that excites the protons, moving them to a higher energy state.
    • This excitation causes the protons to transition from longitudinal magnetisation to transverse magnetisation.
  • Relaxation:
    • Once the RF coil is switched off, protons return to their lower energy state (longitudinal magnetisation).
    • As they relax, the difference in energy states emits radiation, which is detected to create the MRI images.

[[figure-1]]

question: A 50-year-old female patient with a history of breast cancer is scheduled for a follow-up PET scan. During the consultation, she expresses concern about the long-term effects of radiation exposure. Which of the following statements regarding the stochastic effects of radiation exposure is correct?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Gastrointestinal (GI) syndrome is a form of Acute Radiation Syndrome (ARS) that typically occurs after whole-body exposure to 5-20 Gy of ionising radiation.

  • It results from destruction of the rapidly dividing intestinal crypt stem cells, leading to loss of the intestinal mucosal barrier, severe nausea, vomiting, profuse diarrhea, dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, bacterial translocation, and sepsis.
  • Without aggressive supportive care, death usually occurs within 1-2 weeks.
  • Acute Radiation Syndrome (ARS) refers to the constellation of symptoms that develops after whole-body or significant partial-body exposure to high doses of ionising radiation (generally >1 Gy) over a short period.
  • LD50/60 (Lethal Dose 50/60) is the radiation dose expected to cause death in 50% of exposed individuals within 60 days without medical intervention and is approximately 4.5 Gy.

Clinical Phases of Acute Radiation Syndrome

Phase Time Post-Exposure Features
Prodromal phase 0-2 days Nausea, vomiting, anorexia, fatigue, fever, headache, and early skin erythema (typically with doses >2 Gy)
Latent phase 2-20 days (duration decreases with increasing dose) Temporary clinical improvement despite persistent lymphopenia and bone marrow suppression
Manifest illness phase Timing depends on absorbed dose and syndrome

Hematopoietic syndrome: 1-8 Gy (death over weeks to months if untreated);

Gastrointestinal syndrome: 5-20 Gy (death usually within 1=2 weeks);

Neurovascular syndrome: >20 Gy, with severe disease and death typically within 24-48 hours at very high doses
Final phase Recovery or death Outcome depends on absorbed dose, dose rate, extent of body exposure, and supportive treatment

1–5 Gy (Option A): Whole-body doses of 1–5 Gy primarily produce the hematopoietic (bone marrow) syndrome, characterised by lymphopenia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, and an increased risk of infection and bleeding. Severe gastrointestinal syndrome is uncommon at these doses.

20–30 Gy (Option C): Whole-body doses of 20-30 Gy are associated with the neurovascular (cerebrovascular) syndrome, in addition to severe gastrointestinal injury. Patients rapidly develop confusion, ataxia, seizures, coma, and usually die within 24-48 hours.

>30 Gy (Option D): Radiation doses >30 Gy cause overwhelming neurovascular syndrome with immediate, catastrophic damage to the central nervous system and cardiovascular system, leading to death within 24-48 hours, often before gastrointestinal manifestations become clinically significant.

correctAnswer: B. Continuous fluoroscopy instead of Pulsed fluoroscopy
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Continuous fluoroscopy results in higher radiation exposure compared to pulsed fluoroscopy, which does not align with the ALARA Principle.

ALARA (As Low As Reasonably Achievable)

  • Principle: It serves as a guiding framework for minimising radiation exposure during diagnostic and interventional procedures. Its core application is to reduce radiation exposure while maintaining the quality of medical procedures.
  • Strategies for reducing radiation exposure:
    • Increase distance (Option A ruled out): According to the inverse square law, radiation exposure decreases significantly with increased distance from the source.
    • Use shielding (Option C ruled out): Employ physical barriers to block radiation, such as personal protective equipment (PPE) like lead aprons and thyroid collars, along with architectural shielding in facilities (e.g., concrete walls in X-ray rooms).

Reduce time (Option D): Minimizing the duration of exposure during procedures is crucial, as shorter exposure times directly reduce the risk for both patients and healthcare workers.

Barium contrast study is contraindicated in Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) exacerbation (acute inflammation) as it poses a risk of perforation, where barium can leak into the abdominal cavity, leading to peritonitis and severe complications.

explanationHtml:
The most commonly used photosensitive material in conventional X-ray film is Silver bromide.

Radiographic film is the photographic receptor that converts the attenuated X-ray beam into a visible image. It is 150-300 μm thick and consists of three main layers:

  1. Base:
    A thick, translucent polyester layer that provides mechanical support and dimensional stability, maintaining film shape without distortion.
  2. Emulsion:
    The most critical layer for image formation is measuring 3-5 μm thick. It contains silver halide crystals suspended in gelatin, primarily silver bromide (90-99%) with silver iodide (1-10%), forming silver iodo-bromide. The emulsion is usually coated on both sides of the base (double-emulsion film); however, single-emulsion films are used in applications like mammography to reduce parallax.
  3. Supercoat (Overcoat):
    A thin gelatin layer that protects the emulsion from physical damage, pressure, and contamination, while providing a suitable surface.

Additionally, a subbing (adhesive) layer lies between the base and emulsion to ensure firm attachment and maintain integrity during film processing.

[[figure-1]]

Silver nitrate (Option A): Silver nitrate is used in photographic processing, but is not the photosensitive component of X-ray film.

Silver fluoride (Option C): Silver fluoride is not used in the manufacture of radiographic films.

Silver chloride (Option D): Silver chloride is used mainly in photographic paper and is less sensitive to X-rays than silver bromide.



Reference:

1. Christensen's Physics of Diagnostic Radiology, 4th Edition, Page 138.

question: Which of the following is the most commonly used photosensitive material in conventional X-ray film?

correctAnswer: C. When the electron beam decelerates near the nucleus of atoms in the anode
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • X-rays are produced when high-speed electrons from the cathode are suddenly decelerated on interaction with the anode target.
  • Deceleration of electrons in the electric field of the nucleus produces Bremsstrahlung radiation, which forms the major component of diagnostic X-rays.
  • A smaller fraction of X-rays is also produced by characteristic radiation due to inner-shell electron interactions.

[[figure-1]]

Electron beam strikes the cathode (Option A): The cathode emits electrons by thermionic emission and does not produce X-rays.

Electron beam interacts with the electromagnetic field (Option B): X-ray production requires interaction with the anode target, not free electromagnetic fields.

Electron beam directly strikes the nucleus (Option D): Direct nuclear collision does not occur; X-rays are produced due to deceleration in the nuclear electric field.



Reference:

Christensen's Physics of Diagnostic Radiology, 4th Edition, Page 34.

Explanation:

  • Spiral (helical) CT scanning requires continuous rotation of the X-ray tube and detector system around the patient while the patient table moves steadily through the gantry. The key technological innovation that made this possible is slip ring technology.

[[figure-1]]

  • In early (conventional) CT scanners, the X-ray tube and detectors were connected by electrical cables.
  • These cables limited rotation to about 360°, after which the gantry had to reverse direction (“step-and-shoot” scanning).
  • Slip ring technology replaces these cables with sliding electrical contacts (slip rings and brushes) that allow an uninterrupted power supply to the rotating X-ray tube, continuous transmission of data from detectors to the computer and continuous 360° rotation in one direction without rewinding.
  • This continuous rotation is essential for helical acquisition, where data are collected in a spiral path as the patient moves through the scanner.

[[figure-2]]

Multi-detector arrays (Option A): These enable multislice CT (faster scanning and thinner slices), but spiral CT was possible before multidetector systems and does not depend on them.

Patient couch movement (Option C): Table movement is necessary for spiral geometry, but by itself it cannot produce helical scanning without continuous gantry rotation.

Gantry design (Option D): Gantry design supports rotation, but the ability to rotate continuously without cable limitation specifically comes from slip ring technology.

[[figure-3]]

Christensen's Physics of Diagnostic Radiology, 4th Edition, Page 293.
question: What is the fundamental technological innovation behind spiral CT scanning?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Cardiac CT image quality is highly dependent on minimising cardiac motion, as motion leads to blurring and artefacts. The phase of the cardiac cycle with the least coronary artery motion is mid-diastole, also referred to as the diastasis phase.
    • During mid-diastole, ventricular filling is largely complete and myocardial motion is minimal.
    • Coronary arteries, especially the right coronary artery, show the lowest velocity and displacement in this phase.
    • This period provides a longer, more stable temporal window for image acquisition, improving spatial resolution.
  • ECG-gated cardiac CT synchronises image acquisition to a specific phase of the cardiac cycle.
    • Most protocols target ~70-80% of the R-R interval, which corresponds to mid-diastole in patients with stable, low heart rates.

Early diastole (Option A): Early diastole is associated with rapid ventricular relaxation and motion.

Mid systole (Option B): It is characterised by active myocardial contraction and significant motion.

Early systole (Option D): Early systole involves isovolumetric contraction, which produces motion artefacts.



Reference:

David Sutton’s Textbook of Radiology and Imaging, 7th Edition, Page 271.

Explanation:

  • In acute radiation syndrome (ARS), different organ systems are affected at varying radiation dose levels.
  • The hematopoietic (bone marrow) syndrome occurs at a lower radiation dose (≥2 Gy), while gastrointestinal (GI) syndrome occurs at a higher dose (≥6 Gy).

Acute Radiation Syndrome (ARS)

ARS occurs due to high doses of ionizing radiation and is classified into three main syndromes:

Syndrome

Radiation Dose (Gy)

Clinical Features

Hematopoietic Syndrome

>2 Gy

Pancytopenia, infections, bleeding, anemia

Gastrointestinal Syndrome

>6 Gy

Nausea, vomiting, dehydration, diarrhea, shock

Cardiovascular/CNS Syndrome

>30 Gy

Hypotension, seizures, coma, cardiovascular collapse

Doses greater than 2 Gy cause hematopoietic syndrome with pancytopenia (Option B): Correct because bone marrow suppression occurs at doses above 2 Gy.

Doses greater than 6 Gy cause GI syndrome with dehydration (Option C): Correct because GI symptoms appear at higher doses (>6 Gy), leading to severe dehydration.

Doses greater than 20-30 Gy cause cardiovascular syndrome (Option D): Correct because cardiovascular and CNS symptoms occur at doses exceeding 30 Gy, leading to rapid fatality.

Explanation:

  • FDG-PET scans use a radiolabeled form of glucose, known as Fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG), to assess glucose metabolism.

Fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron-emission tomography (PET-FDG)

  • Uptake of 18F-FDG (Analogue of endogenous glucose) in large quantities by cancer cells as compared to normal cells

Application:

  • Quantification of tumor metabolic activity
  • Diagnosis (lung cancer) and Staging of cancer
  • Assessing distant metastasis
    • More sensitive in primary lung and oesophageal cancer metastatic disease
  • Assessment of response to treatment
    • A decrease in FDG uptake after chemotherapy indicates that the tumor is responding to treatment
  • Routine surveillance following treatment- not commonly preferred.

[[figure-1]]

Not useful in the following situations:

  • High Glycolytic Metabolism tissues: Central nervous system tumors.
  • Inflammation vs. Cancer: Both conditions exhibit increased glucose metabolism.
  • Movement disorders
  • Coronary blood flow

Warburg Effect

  • Cancer cells prefer glycolysis over oxidative phosphorylation, even in the presence of oxygen.
  • This leads to increased glucose uptake and lactate production, common in many cancers.
  • 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG), a glucose analog used in PET imaging, helps study this effect.

Mechanisms of 18F-FDG Accumulation

Mechanism

Description

Aerobic Glycolysis

Cancer cells rely heavily on glycolysis, increasing glucose and 18F-FDG uptake, even with oxygen.

Transport & Trapping

GLUT-1 transporters mediate glucose entry. 18F-FDG is phosphorylated and trapped inside cells.

Tumor Heterogeneity

Differences in tumor subtype, size, and microvasculature affect 18F-FDG uptake.

Clinical Implications of 18F-FDG

Implication

Details

Prognostic Indicator

Higher 18F-FDG uptake correlates with worse prognosis (e.g., shorter DFS in invasive ductal carcinoma).

Reverse Warburg Effect

Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) increase glycolysis in tumor cells via metabolic coupling.

Treatment Monitoring

PET imaging tracks changes in 18F-FDG uptake, reflecting therapy responses targeting glycolysis or mitochondria.

Explanation:

According to the American College of Radiology (ACR) Manual on Contrast Media, Gadolinium-Based Contrast Agents (GBCAs) are classified into three groups based on their risk of causing Nephrogenic Systemic Fibrosis (NSF).

  • Group II agents (such as gadobutrol, gadoterate meglumine, gadoteridol, and gadobenate dimeglumine) are highly stable macrocyclic molecules or stable linear ionic molecules. The risk of NSF with these agents is considered extremely low, even in patients with severe kidney disease.

Because the risk is negligible, the ACR guidelines explicitly state that for Group II agents:

  • No routine renal function screening (eGFR testing) is mandatory.
  • They can be safely administered across all ranges of renal function without specialized precautions.

50-year-old with eGFR <50 mL/min (Condition 1): Safely administered. ACR/NKF consensus guidelines state that Group II agents do not need to be withheld, even if the eGFR drops below 30 mL/min. An eGFR < 50 mL/min is completely safe.

A 30-year-old with no RFT (Renal Function Test) (Condition 2): Safely administered. Since routine laboratory screening is considered optional for Group II agents, a lack of recent RFTs is not a contraindication.

60-year-old with status of renal functions not known (Condition 3): Safely administered. If the patient needs MRI contrast, Group II agents can still be used because they are low NSF risk, and screening is not mandatory in all settings.

Child with normal renal functions (Condition 4): Safely administered. There are no contraindications for pediatric use when renal function is normal.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

X-rays are produced in an X-ray tube when high-speed electrons emitted from the cathode filament strike the tungsten target (anode).

The kinetic energy of these electrons is converted into X-ray photons by two mechanisms:

  • Bremsstrahlung Radiation (Braking Radiation) - Major Mechanism
    • Bremsstrahlung means “braking radiation.”
    • High-speed electrons pass close to the nucleus of tungsten atoms.
    • The attractive force of the nucleus causes deceleration and deflection of electrons.
    • The lost kinetic energy is released as X-ray photons.
    • Produces a continuous spectrum of X-ray energies.
    • Responsible for the majority of diagnostic X-ray production.
  • Characteristic Radiation - Minor Mechanism
    • High-energy electrons strike tungsten atoms and eject inner-shell electrons (usually K-shell).
    • The vacancy is filled by an electron from a higher energy shell.
    • The difference in energy between shells is released as an X-ray photon.
    • Produces X-rays with specific characteristic energies depending on the target material.
    • Contributes less to diagnostic X-ray production.

Photoelectric effect (Option A):

  • X-ray photon is completely absorbed by an inner-shell electron.
  • Causes ejection of a photoelectron.
  • Important in X-ray attenuation and image contrast, not X-ray generation.

Compton effect (Option B):

  • X-ray photon interacts with an outer-shell electron.
  • Causes photon scattering with reduced energy.
  • Responsible for scatter radiation during imaging.

Paired production (Option C):

  • Occurs when high-energy photons (>1.02 MeV) interact with the nucleus.
  • Produces an electron–positron pair.
  • Not involved in diagnostic X-ray production.

  2. https://radiopaedia.org/articles/bremsstrahlung-radiation

The given X-ray finding suggests Scoliosis and Cobb Angle is used to assess the degree of curvature in this condition.

Cobb Angle:

  • It is measured by the intersection of perpendicular lines drawn to the end plates of the most tilted vertebrae in a spinal curve.
  • A Cobb angle greater than 10° in the coronal plane indicates scoliosis.


Codman Angle (Option A) is formed by the intersection of a line along the bone cortex and another line at the point where the periosteum is elevated. This is typically seen in conditions such as Ewing sarcoma and osteosarcoma.

Ferguson Angle (Option C) is the angle formed between the plane of the sacral base (the upper surface of the sacrum) and the horizontal plane, used to assess lumbar lordosis.

Q Angle (Option D) is formed by the intersection of a line drawn from the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) to the centre of the patella and a second line from the centre of the patella to the tibial tuberosity.

The Q-angle assesses knee alignment and is used to evaluate patellofemoral dysfunction and ACL injury risk.

  • The above radiograph shows Terry Thomas sign, i.e increased gap between the scaphoid and lunate bones which is indicative of Scapholunate ligament dissociation.
  • This ligament tear commonly occurs after a fall onto an outstretched hand or may occur secondarily following a radial styloid fracture or a scaphoid fracture.

Category

Scapholunate dislocation

Scaphoid fracture

Definition

This occurs when an injury disrupts the scapholunate ligament, leading to instability between the scaphoid and lunate bones.

It can occur in 3 sites.

• Distal tubercle

• Waist (Common)

• Proximal pole

[[figure-1]]

Mechanism of injury

• Fall on the dorsiﬂexed hand

• Fall on outstretched hand

• Secondary to radial-styloid fracture

Signs & Radiological findings

Terry Thomas sign (increased gap between the scaphoid and lunate bones)

[[figure-2]]

• Tenderness over anatomical snuff box.

• A ‘Humpback sign’ is observed in displaced fractures.

[[figure-3]]

Waistline fracture of scaphoid (Option B)

Treatment

• Early detection: Surgical repair with K-wire fixation is done

• Chronic case (without arthritis): Ligament repair is preferred.

• Chronic case (with arthritis): Proximal row carpectomy, four-corner fusion or radio scapholunate arthrodesis is preferred.

• Immobilization with Scaphoid cast or Bohler-Gauntlet scaphoid cast for undisplaced fractures

• ORIF with Herbert's screw.

Complications

• Carpal instability

• Increased risk of osteoarthritis.

• Avascular necrosis (Option A) is common in proximal pole fractures of the scaphoid due to the radial artery primarily supplying the distal pole.

It may show a ground-glass appearance, increased bone density, and, occasionally, collapse and fragmentation on X-ray.

[[figure-4]]

• Non-union

[[figure-5]]


Radial styloid fracture, also known as a Chauffeur's fracture (Option C), is an intra-articular injury to the distal radius. The force responsible for this fracture may also cause a scaphoid fracture and damage to carpal ligaments, potentially leading to carpal instability.

[[figure-6]]

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The given X-ray depicts an intra-articular fracture of the distal radius, called Barton’s fracture.
  • It is usually accompanied by a dislocation of the radiocarpal joint.

Barton’s fracture

Site

Distal radius

Mechanism of injury

Fall on an outstretched hand

Displacement
  • Volar Barton’s fracture: Anterior displacement of the fracture fragment.
  • Dorsal Barton’s fracture: Posterior displacement of the fracture fragment.

Management
  • Closed reduction
  • Open Reduction and Internal Fixation (ORIF)

X-ray

Hutchinson fracture (Option A), also called Chauffeur's fracture, is an intra-articular fracture of the radial styloid process at the distal radius caused by a fall or by direct impact in a car accident and commonly associated with carpal ligament injury.


Colles fracture (Option B) is an extra-articular distal radius fracture characterised by dorsal angulation and displacement, caused by a fall on an outstretched hand and commonly present with Dinner-fork deformity.

Smith fracture (Option C), also called Reverse-Colles fracture, involves a fracture of the distal radius with ventral displacement of the distal fragment. This fracture commonly occurs from a fall onto a flexed wrist, leading to a garden-spade deformity, along with wrist pain, swelling, and limited range of motion.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The depicted radiograph is a CT scan of the cervical spine showing a Jefferson burst fracture of the C1 vertebra (atlas).
  • This fracture typically results from an axial load, such as a fall onto the head or a direct blow, causing a burst-type injury.
  • Features:
    • Lateral displacement of the lateral masses of C1 relative to C2.
    • Fracture lines in the anterior and posterior arches of C1.
    • Potential instability if there is transverse ligament rupture.
    • Unstable fractures: Posterior fixation with pedicle screw system



Chance fracture (Option A) is a seatbelt injury that results from a flexion-distraction mechanism. It involves disruption of the posterior column structures and is frequently associated with intra-abdominal injuries. Radiographic findings show a horizontal fracture through the posterior elements or disruption of the facet joints and spinous processes.



Hangman's fracture (Option B) refers to a bilateral fracture of the pedicles of the C2 vertebra caused by hyperextension and axial loading of the cervical spine. The lamina, pedicles, and other parts of the posterior axis may also be involved in this type of fracture.

Clay shoveller’s fracture (Option C) is an avulsion fracture of the spinous process in the lower cervical or upper thoracic spine. It typically occurs due to sudden muscle contraction or direct trauma to the upper back.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical presentation and X-ray findings show increased density in the distal fibula due to tumour-induced bone production, along blood vessels creates a radiographic appearance resembling sun rays, which strongly suggests Osteosarcoma.
  • It is the second most common and highly malignant primary bone tumor of mesenchymal cells.
  • It commonly occurs in the metaphysis of the lower end of the femur, the upper end of the tibia, and the upper end of the humerus.
  • Radiological Findings:
    • Irregular destruction in the metaphysis, often with new bone formation.
    • Periosteal reaction: Irregular, intense periosteal reaction distinct from the smooth, layered reaction seen in osteomyelitis.
    • Codman's Triangle: A triangular area of subperiosteal new bone at the tumour-host cortex junction.

      [[figure-1]]

    • Sun-Ray Appearance: New bone formation along blood vessels creates a radiographic appearance resembling sun rays.

[[figure-2]]



Ewing's Sarcoma (Option A) is an aggressive tumor that primarily affects children and presents as a diaphyseal lesion with an "onion peel" appearance on imaging.

[[figure-3]]



Osteoblastoma (Option C) is a benign tumor typically occurring in the jaw and spine, and in long bones, it is found in the diaphysis or metaphysis. Radiologically, it appears as a well-defined, expansile radiolucent bone lesion and won’t show a cortical reaction and aggressive features as in osteosarcoma.

[[figure-4]]

Osteochondroma (Option D) typically manifests as an exophytic growth from the bone surface.

[[figure-5]]



Reference:

J.Maheshwari Essential Orthopaedics, 5th Edition, Page 239, 240
question: A 17-year-old male presents with a 3-month history of persistent pain and swelling above the left ankle, with constant and worsening discomfort, especially during physical activity. On examination, there is tenderness and a palpable mass over the lateral aspect of the distal fibula. An X-ray shows characteristic findings depicted in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The given clinical scenario, along with the X-ray finding showing lobulated lucent cystic lesions with disruption of the anterior cortex in the tibia, points towards Adamantinoma.


Adamantinoma: (Rare, low-grade malignant tumor)

  • It primarily affects the tibial diaphysis in up to 90% of cases.
  • Commonly occurs in individuals aged 20 to 40 years
  • Typically present with pre-tibial pain, swelling, and occasionally fractures.
  • Radiological Features:
    • Expansive, lobulated, lucent cystic lesion with disruption of the anterior cortex.
    • Lytic Lesions: Characterized by multiple well-defined lucencies (Honeycomb-like Appearance).
    • Sclerosis: Interspersed sclerotic areas within the lytic regions.
      • Extra-osseous Extension: 30% of cases


Most Common Sites of Primary Bone Tumor:

Epiphysis

Metaphysis

Diaphysis
  • Chondroblastoma: Most common before puberty.
  • Osteoclastoma/GCT(Giant Cell Tumor): Most common after puberty.
  • Chondrosarcoma
  • Osteochondroma
  • Bone Cyst
  • Enchondroma
  • Osteosarcoma
  • Osteoclastoma
  • Ewing’s Tumor
  • Lymphoma
  • Multiple Myeloma
  • Adamantinoma
  • Osteoid Osteoma


Giant Cell Tumor (Osteoclastoma) (Option B) typically occurs in the epiphyseal region of long bones, especially around the knee, after puberty. It is characterized by a distinct "soap-bubble appearance" on imaging due to multiloculated lytic lesions.


Simple Bone Cyst (Option A) typically appears as a well-defined, unilocular lytic lesion with a thin, sclerotic border in the metaphysis of long bones. It does not disrupt the cortex or cause significant soft tissue mass.


Aneurysmal Bone Cyst (Option C) appears as an expansile, lytic lesion with a "multilocular" appearance. It typically affects the metaphysis and may cause cortical thinning or disruption. MRI often shows a blood-filled cystic structure with fluid levels.



Reference:
  1. Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Page 219

  • The pathognomonic MRI finding of acute osteomyelitis is bone marrow edema, which appears as high signal intensity on T2-weighted images and low signal intensity on T1-weighted images & is one of the earliest radiological signs and appears within 24 hours (Earliest- Bone scintigraphy)
  • The penumbra sign (Option A) (Ring enhancement due to granulation tissue) is pathognomonic for subacute osteomyelitis, especially in cases of Brodie's abscess.
  • Sequestrum (Option C) refers to a piece of dead bone that has separated from healthy bone, commonly seen in chronic osteomyelitis.
  • Involucrum (Option D) is the new bone formation that develops around the sequestrum, indicative of chronic osteomyelitis.



Characteristic Radiological Features of Osteomyelitis:

Imaging Modality

Acute Osteomyelitis

Subacute Osteomyelitis

Chronic Osteomyelitis

Plain Radiograph

(5-7 days to appear)

marrow edema

Bone scintigraphy

Increased uptake

Diabetic Foot Osteomyelitis: T1-weighted images show low signal intensity in the marrow near an ulcer or sinus tract as the main indicator of osteomyelitis.

question: A 10-year-old patient presents with symptoms suggestive of osteomyelitis. An MRI is performed, and the radiologist notes a finding indicative of acute osteomyelitis. Which of the following findings is considered pathognomonic for this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical scenario of left arm pain and swelling, along with an X-ray showing a well-defined, unilocular lytic lesion in the metaphysis of the left humerus, without infection or soft tissue involvement, suggests a diagnosis of a simple bone cyst.

Fallen fragment sign:

Features

Simple Bone Cyst (SBC)

(Option A)

Aneurysmal Bone Cyst (ABC)

(Option B ruled out)

Nature

Solitary, unilocular

Benign, expansile, multi-cystic

Children and teenagers

Brodie Abscess (Option C) involves a chronic bone abscess where the body has contained an infection, resulting in pus or jelly-like granulation tissue, surrounded by a sclerotic zone & has associated features of infection.

Sequestrum (Option D) is a piece of dead bone separated from living bone, often due to infection or chronic inflammation. On X-ray, it appears as a dense, irregularly shaped area within the bone, often surrounded by a zone of lucency. question: A 10-year-old boy presents with mild left arm pain, which has worsened over the past few months, particularly after a recent fall while playing. There are no signs of infection or soft tissue involvement. An X-ray shows the findings depicted in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The deformity described is the shepherd's crook deformity of the femur, characterized by a bowing of the proximal femur.
  • It results in a reduction of the femoral neck angle to nearly 90°, leading to a coxa vara deformity.
  • This is commonly seen in conditions like Paget's disease of bone, osteogenesis imperfecta, and fibrous dysplasia. However, osteopetrosis (Option C), a condition marked by excessive bone density, is not typically associated with this deformity.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]



  • Osteopetrosis is a condition characterized by excessive bone density and is typically associated with Erlenmeyer flask deformity, also known as metaphyseal flaring.

[[figure-3]]

Paget's disease of bone (Option A): This condition involves abnormal bone remodeling that can lead to softened, enlarged bones prone to bowing and the characteristic "shepherd's crook" deformity, especially in the femur.

Osteogenesis imperfecta (Option B): Due to defective collagen, bones are brittle and prone to recurrent fractures and progressive bowing deformities, including the "shepherd's crook" shape, from normal weight-bearing.

Fibrous dysplasia (Option D): Replacement of normal bone with fibrous tissue, particularly in the proximal femur, results in weakened areas that can progressively bow into the distinct "shepherd's crook" deformity under mechanical stress.



Reference:

Grainger and Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 1038,1908

question: A 30-year-old male presents with pain in the thigh and a noticeable deformity, as shown in the image. This deformity can be seen in all the following conditions except?

correctAnswer: D. CT scan of the femur
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical presentation and radiographic findings suggest Osteoid osteoma, characterized by nocturnal pain that is relieved by NSAIDs.
  • This benign bone tumor commonly affects young adults and is often located in the cortex of long bones, particularly the femur and tibia.
  • Characterized by a nidus that secretes prostaglandins, leading to intense nocturnal pain.
  • A CT scan is the investigation of choice (Osteoid osteoma is a cortical tumor. Hence, CT is superior to MRI which evaluates bone marrow & extent of tumors), revealing a central radiolucent nidus accompanied by surrounding sclerosis and a Vascular groove sign (thin channel in the thickened bone around the nidus)
  • It is managed by radiofrequency ablation.

[[figure-1]]


X-ray (Option A) is used to diagnose fractures, joint conditions, tumours, and chest issues, as well as in dental assessments. It also guides treatment. Though an X-ray is the initial test for osteoid osteoma, CT provides better visualisation and confirms the diagnosis.


MRI (Option B) is used to diagnose soft tissue pathologies, bone marrow conditions, and neurological disorders, but it is not preferred for osteoid osteoma as it can obscure the nidus.


DEXA scan (Option C) measures bone mineral density to diagnose osteoporosis and assess fracture risk but is not preferred for osteoid osteoma as it does not provide detailed visualization of the lesion.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • A Dual Energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) scan is primarily used to diagnose osteoporosis, assess fracture risk, and monitor drug therapy.
  • The DXA scanner uses X-rays with two energy peaks, enabling the differential absorption of radiation by bone and soft tissue, which facilitates the calculation of bone mineral density (BMD).
  • Interprets results using T-scores and Z-scores.
  • T-score: It compares a patient's BMD to the average BMD of a healthy young adult of the same sex. It indicates how much the patient's bone density deviates from the optimal peak bone mass.

WHO Criteria for Osteoporosis

T score

Interpretation

>-1.0 (Option A)

Normal BMD (bone mineral density)

-1.0 to -2.5 (Option B)

Osteopenia

<-2.5 (Option C)

Osteoporosis

<-2.5 with fracture (Option D)

Severe osteoporosis

  • Z-score: It compares the patient's BMD to the average BMD of individuals of the same age and sex. It helps assess whether the bone density is within a normal range for that specific demographic group.

Interpretation: A Z-score of -2.0 or lower may suggest significantly lower bone density compared to age-matched peers and may warrant further investigation into secondary causes of bone loss.

Ankylosing spondylitis (Option A) shows sacroiliac joint erosions, bamboo spine and dagger sign.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The scenario describes a case of Scurvy, which is characterised radiologically by the presence of Wimberger’s ring (ring epiphysis).

Scurvy

Rickets

Deficient vitamin

Vitamin C

Vitamin D

Reduced levels of

Collagen

Calcium
Clinical features
  • Increased capillary fragility
  • Appearance of petechiae on the skin
  • Delayed wound healing
  • Bleeding gums
  • Perifollicular hemorrhage
  • Frog-like posture (semiflexion at hips and knees): Due to the inability to move limbs due to pain (pseudoparalysis).
  • Scorbutic rosary (angular swellings at the costochondral junction arising due to subperiosteal bleed)
  • Genu varum (bow-legs) or Genu valgum (knock-knees)
  • Double-malleoli sign: The lateral malleolus of the ankles has two bony prominences instead of one.
  • Waddling gait
  • Frontal bossing
  • Delayed closure of anterior fontanelle
  • Craniotabes (soft skull bones with ping-pong ball consistency)
  • Delayed dentition and enamel hypoplasia.
  • Rachitic rosary (anterior chest wall has a beaded appearance due to swelling of costochondral cartilage junctions)
  • Harrison sulcus: Depression along the lower border of the chest at the site of insertion of the diaphragm.
  • Deformity of the hips: Coxa valga (femoral neck-shaft angle is increased) or coxa vara (femoral neck-shaft angle decreased)

Radiological features

  • Pencil-thin cortex
  • A white line of Frankel is present (dense zone of provisional calcification at the growing metaphysis, giving a white line)
  • Trummerfeld’s zone or Scorbutic zone (black area adjacent to the white line of Frankel, due to lack of mineralisation of osteoid)
  • Wimberger's ring (epiphysis is small with a well-defined sclerotic margin, ring-shaped)
  • Pelkan's spur (extensions at the metaphysis)
  • Widening of the growth plate (Option A).
  • White Line of Frankel: Absent in active rickets (Option D); present in healing rickets after treatment.
  • Splaying (widening) of bones.
  • Cupping (concavity) (Option B) and fraying or (irregular margin) of bone ends.

  • Protrusio acetabuli and triradiate deformity of the pelvis.

Explanation:

  • A fall on an outstretched hand (FOOSH) with pain and tenderness in the anatomical snuff-box, with imaging showing carpal instability, the most likely diagnosis is scapholunate dissociation, caused by rupture of the scapholunate interosseous ligament.
  • Clinical features: pain and swelling with tenderness over the dorsum just distal to Lister’s tubercle.
  • Watson’s test - Pushing backwards on the scaphoid tubercle is very painful and, if performed while moving the wrist radialwards and ulnarwards, it can elicit a clunk.
  • Scapholunate ligament disruption leads to an increased gap between the scaphoid and lunate. If the gap is greater than 3-4 mm, radiographs show the Terry-Thomas sign.
  • The scaphoid may appear foreshortened, with a typical cortical ring sign.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

  • If left untreated, it can progress to chronic wrist pain and degenerative changes (SLAC wrist).

Radiocarpal dislocation (Option A): It is a high-energy wrist injury with displacement of the entire carpus relative to the distal radius.

[[figure-3]]

Midcarpal dislocation (Option C): Midcarpal dislocations disrupt colinearity of radius and lunate with volar tilt and volar subluxation of lunate and dorsal subluxation of capitate and middle finger metacarpal.

[[figure-4]]

Triquetrolunate dislocation (Option D): It is a rare perilunate wrist injury in which the triquetrum is displaced relative to the lunate, usually as part of a perilunate dislocation spectrum, caused by high-energy trauma, most commonly a fall on an outstretched hand, with the wrist typically in hyperextension with ulnar deviation. It represents a progressive ulnar-sided carpal instability.

[[figure-5]]

X-ray anteroposterior view (a) showing lunotriquetral dissociation and lateral view (b) showing classical spilled tea cup sign.

explanationHtml:
• MRI is the imaging modality of choice for early detection of septic arthritis in children, as it can identify joint effusion, synovial inflammation, and adjacent bone marrow changes before they appear on X-ray.

MRI in Pediatric Septic Arthritis

  • Early Detection:
    • MRI can detect joint effusion and synovial thickening within hours of symptom onset.
    • Shows bone marrow oedema indicating early osteomyelitis.
  • High Sensitivity:
    • Superior soft tissue contrast compared to X-ray or CT.
    • Visualises cartilage, ligaments, and surrounding soft tissues.
  • Sequences Used:
    • T2-weighted or STIR sequences highlight fluid and oedema.
    • Post-contrast T1-weighted images show synovial enhancement and abscess formation.

Clinical Importance

  • Rapid diagnosis prevents joint destruction.
  • Guides early surgical or antibiotic management.

Ultrasound-guided aspiration (Option B): Useful for fluid sampling, but cannot visualise bone marrow or early cartilage changes.

X-ray (Option C): Often normal in early infection; shows late changes like joint space narrowing or periosteal reaction.

CT scan (Option D): Less sensitive than MRI for soft tissue and marrow oedema; involves radiation.



Reference:

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 1205.

  • Technetium-99m MDP is the most commonly used radiopharmaceutical for skeletal scintigraphy because it localizes to areas of active bone turnover, enabling sensitive detection of fractures, tumors, and metabolic bone disease.

Mechanism of Uptake

  • Binds to hydroxyapatite crystals in bone
  • Accumulates at sites of increased osteoblastic activity
  • Highlights both focal and diffuse skeletal pathology

Imaging Advantages

  • Emits gamma radiation suitable for scintigraphy
  • Allows whole-body skeletal survey
  • Provides early detection of bone lesions before plain radiographs

Gallium-67 (Option A): Localizes to sites of infection, inflammation, and tumors; not specific for bone pathology.

Technetium-sulphur colloid (Option C): Used for liver, spleen, and bone marrow imaging; unsuitable for skeletal scans.

Technetium-99m (Option D): Accumulates in thyroid, salivary glands, and stomach; does not target bone.



Reference:

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 854.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Cervical rib is identified by the presence of an accessory rib arising from the cervical spine, most commonly from the C7 vertebra, seen on chest or neck radiographs.

Radiological Features

  • Appears as an extra bony projection above the normal first rib
  • Originates from the seventh cervical vertebra (C7)
  • May be complete or incomplete, unilateral or bilateral
  • Best visualised on:
    • Chest X-ray
    • Cervical spine radiograph

Clinical Significance

  • Often asymptomatic and incidentally detected
  • Can cause thoracic outlet syndrome due to compression of:
    • Subclavian vessels
    • Brachial plexus
  • Symptoms may include pain, numbness, or vascular insufficiency in the upper limb.

Costochondritis (Option A): An inflammatory condition affecting costochondral junctions; radiographs are usually normal and do not show extra bony structures.

Spondylolisthesis (Option B): Involves anterior or posterior displacement of a vertebra, typically seen in the lumbar spine, not as an accessory rib.

Rib fracture (Option C): Shows cortical discontinuity or callus formation following trauma, not a well-formed additional rib.



Reference:

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 39.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The empty thecal sac sign on MRI is a characteristic feature of arachnoiditis caused by chronic inflammation leading to adhesion and clumping of spinal nerve roots.

Empty Thecal Sac Sign

  • Seen on MRI spine, especially T2-weighted images
  • Normal nerve roots should be freely floating in CSF
  • In this sign:
    • Nerve roots are clumped and adherent to the dural margins
    • Central CSF space appears empty

[[figure-1]]

Pathophysiology of Arachnoiditis

  • Inflammation of the arachnoid mater
  • Leads to:
    • Fibrosis
    • Adhesions
    • Nerve root entrapment
  • Common causes:
    • Prior spinal surgery
    • Intrathecal contrast
    • Chronic infection
    • Trauma

MRI Patterns of Arachnoiditis

  • Type I: Clumped nerve roots
  • Type II: Empty thecal sac sign (most tested)
  • Type III: Soft tissue mass replacing CSF

Discitis (Option A): Shows disc space narrowing, endplate erosion, and paraspinal soft tissue changes, not nerve root clumping.

Vertebral osteomyelitis (Option B): MRI shows vertebral marrow oedema and destruction with possible abscess formation.

Tethered cord syndrome (Option C): Characterised by a low-lying conus medullaris and thickened filum terminale, not an empty thecal sac.



Reference:

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 1330.
question: A patient with chronic low back pain undergoes an MRI of the lumbar spine. The scan shows peripheral clumping of nerve roots with a centrally empty thecal sac. This MRI finding is most commonly seen in which condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Myelography is a contrast study used to visualise the spinal canal, nerve roots, and thecal sac by intrathecal injection of contrast material.

Principle of Myelography

  • Involves intrathecal injection of iodinated contrast into the subarachnoid space.
  • Contrast outlines:
    • Thecal sac
    • Spinal cord
    • Nerve roots

[[figure-1]]

Imaging Appearance

  • Contrast column seen within the spinal canal.
  • Indentations or blockages suggest:
    • Disc herniation
    • Spinal stenosis
    • Tumors
    • Arachnoiditis

Clinical Utility

  • Used when MRI is contraindicated or inconclusive.
  • Often combined with CT myelography for detailed evaluation.

Angiography(Option A): Visualises blood vessels using intravascular contrast, not the spinal canal.

Projectional radiography (Option B): Plain X-ray technique without contrast injection.

DEXA(Option D): Used to measure bone mineral density, not spinal canal anatomy.



Reference:

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 1231.
question: Which radiological procedure is being performed as shown in the image below?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • MRI is the investigation of choice for detecting early avascular necrosis of the femoral head when plain radiographs are normal, particularly in patients on long-term steroid therapy.

Avascular Necrosis - Pathophysiology

  • Chronic steroid use causes fat embolism, marrow ischemia, and osteocyte death.
  • Early disease involves bone marrow changes without cortical collapse.

Imaging:

  • Plain X-ray remains normal in early AVN.
  • Diagnosis requires an imaging modality sensitive to marrow pathology.

[[figure-1]]

Role of MRI:

  • MRI detects ischemic marrow changes before structural deformity.
  • Characteristic findings include:
    • T1: Low-signal intensity serpiginous line
    • T2: Double-line sign (inner bright, outer dark rim)
  • Highest sensitivity and specificity among all modalities for early AVN.

Bone scintigraphy(Option A): Shows increased uptake but lacks specificity and detailed anatomical localisation.

CT scan(Option B): Useful for detecting subchondral fractures and collapse, but insensitive in early marrow-stage disease.

PET scan(Option C): No established role in routine diagnosis of avascular necrosis.



Reference:

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Musculoskeletal Imaging, Page 996.
question: A middle-aged man with a history of prolonged corticosteroid therapy complains of an insidious onset of hip pain. The initial pelvic radiograph does not reveal any abnormality. Which investigation is most appropriate to confirm the suspected diagnosis at this stage?

correctAnswer: A. Bipolar prosthesis with displacement of the inner head
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Bipolar prosthesis with displacement of the inner head is diagnosed when the inner femoral head is eccentrically displaced within the outer metallic shell while the outer head remains seated in the acetabulum.

Bipolar Hemiarthroplasty - Radiographic Concept

  • A bipolar prosthesis has two articulations:
    • Inner articulation: femoral head with polyethylene liner
    • Outer articulation: metallic shell with native acetabulum
  • Normal alignment shows concentric positioning of inner and outer heads.

Radiological Features of Bipolar Head Dislocation

  • The outer metallic head remains within the acetabulum
  • The inner femoral head is eccentrically displaced
  • Loss of concentric relationship between the two heads
  • No acetabular cup is present (unlike total hip replacement)

Mechanism

  • Occurs due to:
    • Polyethylene liner failure
    • Trauma or excessive motion
    • Chronic mechanical wear

Normal total hip replacement in situ(Option B): Shows a single femoral head articulating with an acetabular cup; dual articulation is absent.

Dislocated total hip replacement (Option C): Both the femoral head and prosthetic head are displaced out of the acetabular cup.

Normal bipolar hemiarthroplasty in situ(Option D): Inner and outer heads are concentrically aligned with no eccentric displacement.



Reference:

Spontaneous dissociation of bipolar hip hemiarthroplasty in a patient with nerve palsy: A case report and review of the literature - ScienceDirect

question: A patient who underwent hip surgery in the past presents for routine follow-up. A pelvic radiograph is provided. Based on the radiographic appearance, what is the most appropriate description of the prosthesis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Medial meniscal tears are common in athletes with twisting knee injuries, and MRI is the imaging modality of choice to identify these tears, including characteristic signs like the double PCL sign.

Anatomy & Function of Meniscus

  • Medial meniscus: C-shaped fibrocartilaginous structure on the medial tibial plateau
    • Absorbs shock
    • Distributes load across the knee joint
    • Stabilises the knee, especially against rotational forces

Mechanism of Injury in Athletes

  • Twisting or pivoting movements on a flexed knee
  • Direct trauma during tackles or sudden changes in direction
  • Often associated with ACL injuries, but can occur in isolation

Radiological Findings on MRI

  • Sagittal and coronal T2-weighted images are most informative
  • Double PCL sign:
    • Linear low-signal band running parallel and anterior to the posterior cruciate ligament
    • Indicates a displaced bucket-handle tear of the medial meniscus
  • Other supportive findings:
    • High signal intensity within the meniscus extending to the articular surface
    • Joint effusion may be present

[[figure-1]]

Clinical Relevance

  • Bucket-handle tears may cause locking and a restricted range of motion
  • Early MRI diagnosis guides arthroscopic repair vs partial meniscectomy

Posterior cruciate ligament tear (Option A): Usually caused by hyperflexion or dashboard injuries; MRI shows discontinuity or increased signal in the PCL itself.

Tear of the lateral collateral ligament (Option B): Rare; MRI shows high signal at the lateral ligament with lateral joint line tenderness.

Tear of the medial collateral ligament (Option C): Typically due to valgus stress; MRI shows ligament fibre disruption and medial joint line oedema.



Reference:

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 998.

options.text: Tear of the lateral collateral ligament
Tear of the medial collateral ligament
