Sagittal MRI demonstrates a linear low-signal band running parallel to the posterior cruciate ligament in the intercondylar notch. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Ewing’s sarcoma is a diaphyseal bone tumour in children with a permeative lytic lesion, lamellated (onion-skin) periosteal reaction, and possible soft tissue mass, best evaluated by X-ray and MRI for extent.

Radiological Features:

  • Location:
    • Diaphysis of long bones (femur, tibia, humerus)
    • Rarely involves the metaphysis or epiphysis
  • Lesion Appearance:
    • Permeative lytic lesion with poorly defined margins
    • Aggressive cortical destruction
    • Sometimes associated with a soft tissue mass
  • Periosteal Reaction:
    • Onion-skin (lamellated) appearance due to repeated periosteal elevation
    • Less commonly Codman triangle may be seen

[[figure-1]]

  • Soft Tissue Involvement:
    • An extraosseous mass is frequently present without calcification
  • Additional Imaging:
    • MRI: Defines marrow and soft tissue extension, helps in pre-surgical planning
    • CT: Useful for cortical breach assessment
    • Bone Scan: Shows increased uptake in affected bone and detects skip lesions

Osteosarcoma (Option A): Metaphyseal location, mixed lytic-sclerotic lesion, sunburst appearance, Codman triangle; differs from diaphyseal Ewing’s sarcoma.

Giant cell tumour (Option B): Epiphyseal, expansile, well-defined, usually in skeletally mature patients; lacks periosteal reaction.

Unicameral bone cyst (Option C): Centrally located metaphyseal lesion, well-marginated, often discovered after fracture; no aggressive periosteal reaction.



Reference:

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 1012.
question: A 10-year-old child presents with localised pain and swelling in the midshaft of the femur. Radiographs reveal a permeative lytic lesion with onion-skin periosteal reaction. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Hurler syndrome is a mucopolysaccharidosis type I disorder caused by alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency, leading to the accumulation of dermatan and heparan sulfate in multiple tissues. The skeletal manifestations (dysostosis multiplex) are key radiologic features.

Skeletal Manifestations in Hurler Syndrome

  • Cranial changes
    • Thickened calvaria due to abnormal bone deposition
    • J-shaped sella turcica (flattened anterior wall, rounded posterior wall)
    • Enlarged fontanelles in infants
  • Facial and skull features
    • Coarse facial features (frontal bossing, depressed nasal bridge)
    • Macrocephaly
    • Prognathism
  • Other skeletal deformities
    • Erlenmeyer flask deformity: flaring of the distal femur and tibia metaphyses
    • Short stature and broad ribs
    • Vertebral anomalies (platyspondyly)
  • Pathophysiology
    • Accumulated glycosaminoglycans disrupt normal bone modelling
    • Leads to thickened skull, dysostosis multiplex, and joint stiffness

Sanfilippo syndrome (Option B): Primarily causes severe neurocognitive decline; skeletal changes are mild, and corneal clouding is rare.

Gaucher’s disease (Option C): Manifests with hepatosplenomegaly, anaemia, and Erlenmeyer flask deformities, but skull changes like J-shaped sella are absent.

Morquio syndrome (Option D): Normal intelligence, skeletal dysplasia primarily affects the spine, hips, and chest; corneal clouding may occur, but the cranial vault is usually normal.



Reference:

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 1624.
question: A 1.5-year-old child presents with developmental delay, coarse facial features, and a distended abdomen. Ophthalmologic exam shows corneal clouding. Skull radiographs reveal thickened calvaria and a J-shaped sella turcica. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
• The X-ray is suggestive of Erlenmeyer flask deformity, which is least likely to be associated with Hunter’s disease.
  • The Erlenmeyer flask deformity refers to flaring of the metaphysis with loss of normal diaphyseal constriction, producing a flask-shaped appearance on long-bone radiographs. It results from defective metaphyseal remodelling, commonly due to marrow expansion or infiltrative disorders.

Erlenmeyer flask deformity is seen in the following conditions:

  • Marrow infiltration/expansion:
    • Lysosomal storage disease
      • Gaucher disease: osteopenia with Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease or Hass disease
      • Niemann-Pick disease (type B)
    • Hemoglobinopathies
      • Thalassemia: coarsened trabeculation, cobweb appearance, especially if treated with deferoxamine
      • Sickle cell disease
    • Membranous lipodystrophy
    • Fetal magnesium toxicity
    • Chronic lead toxicity
  • Bone dysplasias
    • Fibrous dysplasia
    • Achondroplasia
    • Ollier’s disease
    • Multiple hereditary exostoses

Hunter’s Disease (Mucopolysaccharidosis Type II)

  • Genetic Basis: X-linked lysosomal storage disorder due to iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency.
  • Skeletal Manifestations:
    • Mild or absent marrow changes
    • Dysostosis multiplex may be present (e.g., thickened ribs, vertebral anomalies)
    • Long bone deformities, like an Erlenmeyer flask, are uncommon
    • Rarely shows cortical thinning or metaphyseal flaring
  • Clinical Relevance: Radiographs are often less striking compared to hematologic disorders like Gaucher’s disease, Thalassemia, or Leukaemia.


Reference:

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Pages 1727 &1931.
question: A patient’s long bone radiograph shows characteristic marrow and cortical changes. Which of the following conditions is least likely to produce such findings?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Radiographs of the child show short, thick long bones with metaphyseal flaring.

  • Achondroplasia is the most common skeletal dysplasia, causing disproportionate dwarfism.
  • It is characterised by rhizomelic shortening (proximal limb shortening)
  • Frontal bossing and midface hypoplasia are classic clinical features
  • Radiographs show short, thick long bones with metaphyseal flaring
  • Caused by an activating mutation of the FGFR3 gene, which inhibits endochondral ossification

[[figure-1]]

In the image:

(A) Generalised platyspondyly leading to an increased height of the intervertebral spaces. The pelvis shows a squared configuration with a horizontalized acetabular roof and a narrow sciatic notch. Pubis and mainly the ischia are broad. The long tubular bones are shorter with metaphyseal irregularity, and the fibulae are longer than the tibia. Note the oval-shaped lucent appearance of the proximal femora.

(B) Lateral view showing an increased lumbar lordosis.

(C) The cranium is large, and both frontal and occipital regions are prominent.

(D) The hand shows shortening of all tubular bones - metacarpal and phalanges

Osteogenesis imperfecta (Option A): Presents with bone fragility, multiple fractures, and blue sclera rather than limb shortening.

Hypothyroidism (Option C): Causes proportionate dwarfism with delayed bone age, not rhizomelic shortening.

Rickets (Option D): Shows widened growth plates, cupping, and fraying due to vitamin D deficiency.



Reference:

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 1887,1893.
question: A child presents with disproportionate short stature, rhizomelic shortening of limbs, frontal bossing, and lumbar lordosis. Radiographs of the child are given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The above clinical scenario with radiological investigation points towards a Colles’ fracture, as evidenced by dorsal displacement of the distal radius (“dinner-fork deformity”) after a fall on an outstretched hand (FOOSH).

Etiology:

  • Most common distal radius fracture in elderly, especially postmenopausal women.
  • Mechanism: Fall on an extended wrist.
  • Typically extra-articular.

Radiological Features:

  • Dorsal displacement and angulation of the distal fragment.
  • Radial shortening may be present.
  • No articular involvement (extra-articular).

[[figure-1]]

Clinical Features:

  • Dinner-fork deformity visible on inspection.
  • Pain, swelling, and tenderness over distal radius.
  • Restricted wrist movements.
  • Complications may include median nerve compression, malunion, and post-traumatic arthritis.

Reverse Barton’s fracture (Option A):

  • Intra-articular fracture with volar displacement of distal fragment.
  • Often unstable, requiring surgical fixation.
  • Mechanism: direct trauma or fall on dorsiflexed wrist with axial load.

[[figure-2]]

Smith’s fracture (Option B):

  • Volar displacement of distal fragment, opposite of Colles’.
  • Mechanism: fall on flexed wrist.
  • May result in pronator quadratus injury and median nerve compression.
  • Extra-articular or intra-articular depending on fracture line.

[[figure-3]]

Rolando’s fracture (Option D):

  • Comminuted intra-articular fracture of the base of first metacarpal.
  • Often unstable, frequently requiring surgical intervention.
  • Can result in thumb function impairment if not reduced accurately.
  • Mechanism: axial load on partially flexed thumb.

[[figure-4]]



Reference:

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 1154.
question: A 65-year-old falls on her outstretched hand and presents with pain, swelling, and visible deformity of the wrist. On examination, the wrist shows dorsal prominence of the distal radius. Which of the following is the most likely type of fracture?

correctAnswer: B. Median nerve injury causes pointing index
explanationHtml:
The above clinical scenario with radiological investigation points towards a supracondylar fracture of the humerus with acute median nerve involvement, as evidenced by weakness of wrist and finger flexion (“pointing index” sign).

Etiology:

  • Most common elbow fracture in children, usually aged 5-8 years.
  • Mechanism: Fall on outstretched hand (FOOSH) with elbow in extension.
  • Classified as extension-type (most common) or flexion-type based on displacement.

Acute Complications:

  • Median nerve injury: Causes “pointing index” sign, inability to flex the index finger or thumb.
  • Vascular compromise: Brachial artery injury may lead to Volkmann ischemic contracture if untreated.
  • Acute compartment syndrome: Rare but limb-threatening; requires urgent attention.

Late Complications:

  • Cubitus varus (“gunstock deformity”): Most common late deformity due to malunion.
  • Myositis ossificans: Heterotopic ossification developing weeks after trauma.
  • Non-union: Extremely rare in supracondylar fractures.

Non-union is common (Option A): Rare; pediatric supracondylar fractures heal reliably with proper alignment and immobilization.

Cubitus valgus is common (Option C): Typically occurs after lateral condyle fractures, not classic supracondylar fractures.

Myositis ossificans is one of the acute complications (Option D): Occurs weeks later, considered a late complication rather than acute.



Reference:

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 1150.

options.text: Median nerve injury causes pointing index
Myositis ossificans is one of the acute complications

question: A 7-year-old child falls on an outstretched hand while playing. On examination, there is pain, swelling around the elbow, and limited movement. Neurological assessment reveals weakness of wrist and finger flexion. An X-ray of the child is given below. Which of the following is the most likely complication?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Luxatio erecta is a rare inferior shoulder dislocation.
  • Typically occurs after forceful hyperabduction of the arm.
  • The arm is fixed in extreme abduction, often above the head.
  • Radiograph shows the humeral head lying inferior to the glenoid.
  • High risk of neurovascular injury, particularly the axillary nerve and artery.
  • Prompt recognition and reduction are essential.

Bankart lesion (Option A)

  • Labral tear of the anterior-inferior glenoid.
  • Typically associated with recurrent anterior dislocations.
  • Does not represent a dislocation itself.

[[figure-1]]

Posterior dislocation (Option C)

  • Usually occurs after seizures, electric shock, or trauma.
  • Humeral head displaced posteriorly.
  • Radiographic signs: light-bulb sign, trough line sign, loss of half-moon overlap.

[[figure-2]]

Anterior dislocation (Option D)

  • Most common shoulder dislocation.
  • Humeral head displaced anteriorly and inferiorly.
  • Arm usually in slight abduction and external rotation.
  • Can be associated with Hill-Sachs lesion and Bankart lesion.

[[figure-3]]



Reference:

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 1149.
question: A 30-year-old man presents to the emergency department after a fall during a gymnastics routine, where his arm was forcefully abducted overhead. He is unable to lower his arm, which is fixed in full abduction. The shoulder X-ray shows the humeral head displaced inferior to the glenoid. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Posterior dislocation is commonly caused by seizures, electric shock, or fall on a flexed, adducted arm after direct trauma to the front of the shoulder or due to fall on the outstretched hand.
  • Often missed on AP view, requiring axillary or scapular Y view for confirmation.
  • Light-bulb sign: Fixed internal rotation of the humeral head giving a rounded appearance.
  • Trough line sign: Dense vertical line in the medial humeral head due to impaction.
  • Loss of normal half-moon overlap sign: Glenoid appears vacant because of the lateral displacement of the humeral head.
  • Rim sign: Widened glenohumeral joint >6 mm.
  • Acute angle of the scapulohumeral (Moloney) arch: Helps distinguish from anterior dislocation

Inferior dislocation (Option A)

  • Arm is fixed overhead in abduction.
  • Rare, usually traumatic.
  • Humeral head displaced inferiorly.

Anterior dislocation (Option C)

  • Most common type of shoulder dislocation.
  • Humeral head displaced anteriorly and inferiorly.
  • Arm usually in slight abduction and external rotation.

Fracture neck of humerus (Option D)

  • Shows a visible fracture line in the humeral neck.
  • No classic internal rotation deformity or light-bulb sign.
  • May accompany dislocation but is a separate entity.


Reference:

Apley’s System of Orthopaedics and Fractures, 10th Edition, Page 764.
question: A 25-year-old man presenting to the emergency department after a generalised tonic-clonic seizure. He complains of pain and restriction of movement in the right shoulder. The radiograph of his shoulder is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The above question refers to a greenstick fracture, which is a type of incomplete fracture seen predominantly in children due to the elastic nature of immature bones.

In a greenstick fracture, a bending force is applied to the bone. As a result:

  • The convex (outer) cortex fails and breaks
  • The concave (inner) cortex does not break but bends

[[figure-1]]

Hence, the statement that best describes a greenstick fracture is that the inner cortex bends, making Option A correct.

Buckling with intact cortices (Option B):This describes a torus (buckle) fracture, commonly seen at the metaphysis in children.

Outer cortex bends (Option C):Incorrect because the outer cortex is the one that breaks, not bends.

Inner cortex breaks (Option D):Incorrect as the inner cortex remains intact and only bends in greenstick fractures.



Reference:

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 1147.

Explanation:

  • The next best step to evaluate this child is with an MRI, since there is weakness in the bilateral upper and lower extremities, but without radiological evidence, suggestive of SCIWORA (Spinal Cord Injury Without Radiographic Abnormality).
  • MRI evaluates the spinal cord, ligaments, and soft tissue lesions.

CT scan (Option A): Useful for fractures but poor for cord and ligament evaluation

Physiotherapy (Option C): Contraindicated before ruling out spinal cord injury

Reassurance (Option D): Unsafe without definitive imaging



Reference:

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 1948.
question: A 11-year-old child presents after a minor fall with weakness in both upper and lower limbs. Cervical spine X-ray shows normal alignment with no fracture. Which is the next best investigation to evaluate this child?

explanationHtml:
The bone-within-bone appearance on radiographs is least likely to be seen in hyperparathyroidism because this condition is predominantly osteolytic rather than sclerotic.

Bone-within-Bone Appearance

  • Appears as concentric layering of dense bone within the medullary cavity
  • Represents growth arrest lines or repeated episodes of abnormal bone remodeling
  • Seen in conditions with:
    • Cyclical sclerosis
    • Impaired bone turnover
    • Marrow expansion with reparative bone formation

Hyperparathyroidism

  • Primary pathology is increased osteoclastic bone resorption
  • Leads to:
    • Subperiosteal bone resorption
    • Cortical thinning
    • Brown tumors
  • Sclerosis is not a feature, hence bone-within-bone pattern is not produced

Sickle cell disease (Option B):
Repeated marrow infarctions cause growth arrest lines, producing a classic bone-within-bone appearance, especially in long bones.

Paget’s disease (Option C):
Characterized by repeated cycles of bone resorption and excessive sclerosis, which can give rise to layered bone appearance.

Caffey disease (Option D):
Infantile cortical hyperostosis shows periosteal new bone formation and cortical thickening, which can simulate layered bone patterns in infants.



Reference:

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition,page no.1153.
question: A radiograph of a long bone (image shown) demonstrates a bone-within-bone appearance. Which of the following conditions is least likely to produce this radiographic appearance?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The doughnut sign on bone scintigraphy refers to increased peripheral radiotracer uptake with central photopenia, producing a ring-like appearance. This pattern reflects a reactive, metabolically active peripheral zone surrounding a central non-osteoblastic or necrotic area.

[[figure-1]]

Bone scan demonstrates the "doughnut sign" of aneurysmal bone cyst: peripheral uptake with a photopenic center.

  • Multiple myeloma produces purely lytic lesions due to osteoclastic activation without osteoblastic response. As a result, bone scintigraphy often shows photopenic (“cold”) lesions rather than peripheral tracer uptake. Hence, the classic doughnut (ring) sign is not seen in multiple myeloma.
  • Conditions in which the doughnut sign on bone scan is seen:
    • Giant cell tumour
    • Aneurysmal bone cyst
    • Telangiectatic osteosarcoma
    • Chondrosarcoma


Reference:

https://radiopaedia.org/articles/doughnut-sign-disambiguation
question: The doughnut sign on bone scintigraphy shows peripheral tracer uptake with central photopenia. Which condition is NOT associated with this sign?

correctAnswer: C. Type I is the most lethal form
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Osteogenesis imperfecta (also known as brittle bone disease) is caused by defective type I collagen synthesis.
  • The genes involved: COL1A1, COL1A2; Autosomal dominant inheritance is the most common (Option A).
  • Radiological features include multiple wormian bones in the skull (Option B), osteopenia, bow-shaped long bones, thin cortices and multiple diaphyseal fractures at different stages of healing.
  • Common differentials include:
    • Battered baby syndrome (child abuse) (Option D) - Metaphyseal fractures are seen.
    • Rickets
    • Hypophosphatasia

Type

Severity

Clinical Features

Prognosis

Type I

Mild

Blue eyes, recurrent fractures, hearing loss, dentinogenesis imperfecta, hyperextensible joints, easy

bruising, thin skin, joint laxity, scoliosis, wormian bones, hernia, and

mild short stature

Best prognosis

Type II

Severe

Intrauterine fractures of long bones, beaded ribs, micromelia and bowing of extremities

Most lethal in the perinatal period (Option C)

Type III

Severe, progressive

Short stature, bone deformities

Most severe non-lethal form of OI

Type IV

Moderate

Normal sclera, fractures

Variable

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 1097.

question: A child with recurrent fractures following trivial trauma and blue sclera is diagnosed with osteogenesis imperfecta. The skull radiograph shows multiple wormian bones. Which of the following statements regarding this condition is NOT true?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Dense metaphyseal bands are not seen in primary hyperparathyroidism since increased bone resorption occurs in this condition.
  • Dense metaphyseal bands, also known as dense metaphyseal lines, transverse bands or “lead lines” indicate increased mineralisation or healing response, seen as radioopaque bones (thicker than diaphyseal cortex) at the metaphysis of growing, particularly at the wrists and knees.

[[figure-1]]

Dense metaphyseal bands are seen in:

  • Lead poisoning
  • Healing rickets
  • Scurvy (after treatment) (Option B)
  • Chronic renal failure / Renal osteodystrophy
  • Bisphosphonate therapy (e.g., pamidronate)
  • Congenital syphilis and TORCH infections (Option A)
  • Vitamin D intoxication (Option D)
  • Hypoparathyroidism
  • Hypothyroidism


Reference:
  1. Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 1913, 1929.
  2. https://pubs.rsna.org/doi/abs/10.1148/radiology.211.3.r99jn13773?journalCode=radiology
question: Dense metaphyseal bands are seen in several metabolic and infectious disorders. Which of the following conditions does NOT cause dense metaphyseal bands?

  • It articulates proximally with the talus, distally with the three cuneiform bones, and laterally with the cuboid.
  • On a dorsoplantar (DP) or oblique foot X-ray, it is seen on the medial side between the talus and cuneiforms.

[[figure-1]]

Cuboid (Option B): Found on the lateral aspect of the foot between the calcaneus and 4th–5th metatarsals.


Intermediate cuneiform (Option C): Located between medial and lateral cuneiforms, distal to the navicular.


Lateral cuneiform (Option D): Positioned between the intermediate cuneiform and cuboid, articulating with the 3rd metatarsal.

explanationHtml:
1. Plain Radiographs (X-rays):

  • Often Normal: Plain X-rays are notoriously insensitive for detecting acute sacral insufficiency fractures, especially in the early stages. The subtle nature of the fracture and overlying bowel gas can obscure them.
  • Subtle Sclerosis: In later stages or chronic cases, a vague vertical band of increased bone density (sclerosis) may be noted in the sacral ala (wing) parallel to the sacroiliac joint. This represents healing bone or callus formation.

2. Bone Scintigraphy (Nuclear Medicine Bone Scan):

  • Highly Sensitive: Bone scans (using technetium-99m methylene diphosphonate, 99mTc-MDP) are very sensitive for detecting SIFs, often showing uptake earlier than other modalities.
  • "H-Sign" or "Honda Sign": This is a classic and highly characteristic finding, though not present in all cases (occurs in 20-78% of cases). It refers to a pattern of increased radionuclide uptake resembling the letter "H".

3. Computed Tomography (CT Scan):

  • Better for Bony Detail: CT is superior to plain X-rays for visualizing subtle cortical breaks and fracture lines.
  • Fracture Line: A low-attenuation (dark) fracture line may be seen, often with surrounding ill-defined sclerosis representing callus formation.
  • Sclerosis: Broad regions of sclerosis adjacent to the fracture line can be present.


Reference:

Sacral insufficiency fracture

question: Identify the condition associated with the image shown below:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Metastatic bone disease is the most common cause of lytic bone lesions in elderly patients with a history of weight loss.
  • The femur and pelvis are common sites for metastatic deposits, especially from primary malignancies like breast, lung, prostate, and renal cell carcinoma.
  • Pathological fractures following trivial trauma are characteristic.
  • The X-ray shows focal bony destruction of the acetabulum, causing abnormal joint orientation, but the femoral articular surface remains normal, suggesting a bone lesion rather than joint pathology.

Metastatic Tumors to Bone

Common Metastatic Tumors
  • Lung carcinoma (male)
  • Breast carcinoma (female)
  • Prostate carcinoma (Osteoblastic)
  • Thyroid carcinoma

Clinical Features
  • Known Primary Malignancy:
    • Bone pain (common in spine, ribs, extremities)
    • Pathological fracture (common in spine)
  • Unknown Primary Malignancy:
    • Bone pain leading to destructive lesion diagnosis
    • Pathological fracture due to weakened bone

Malignancies Presenting with Silent Primary
  • Thyroid carcinoma
  • Renal cell carcinoma
  • Bladder carcinoma

Common Sites of Metastasis
  • Vertebral bodies
  • Ribs
  • Pelvis
  • Humerus
  • Femur
  • Uncommon distal to elbow and knee

Eosinophilic Granuloma (Option A): Primarily affects children, commonly involving the skull and vertebral bodies, not typical in elderly patients.

Disseminated TB (Option B): Typically involves the hip joint (Tuberculous arthritis), leading to joint space narrowing and articular surface destruction, which is not seen here.

Brown Tumor (Option C): Seen in hyperparathyroidism, with multiple lytic lesions and associated systemic features, which are not mentioned in the case.



Reference:

Apley and Solomon’s System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th Edition, Pages 220-227
question: A 60-year-old patient presents with an inability to bear weight following a trivial trauma. X-rays of the pelvis and thigh reveal lytic lesions with cortical destruction. She has a history of weight loss. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option C – Chance fracture:

  • The given radiograph shows a chance fracture. Chance fracture usually occurs at the thoracolumbar junction (T10-L2). It is a horizontal fracture that extends through the spinous process, pedicles, and vertebral body, affecting the posterior and middle columns of the spine. It characteristically shows anterior compression of vertebral body, posterior distraction (splitting posterior elements horizontally)

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Burst Fracture:

  • The vertebral body is shattered, with fragments extending into the spinal canal, potentially causing spinal cord compression.
  • Axial loading fracture where vertebral body shatters and retropulses fragments into the canal
  • Fracture lines are vertical, not horizontal
  • Posterior elements are usually not distracted.

Option B - Compression Fracture: The vertebral body becomes wedge-shaped due to the collapse of the anterior portion, with the posterior height usually preserved.

Option D - Impacted fracture: Impacted Fracture shows overlapping bone fragments leading to increased density at the site of injury.



Reference:

.
question: Identify the given fracture:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) is a key ligament in the knee joint, located at the back of the knee. It prevents the tibia from sliding backward relative to the femur and provides stability, especially during activities like walking, running, and jumping.

Knee Ligaments

  • The knee joint is stabilized by several ligaments, including the PCL, ACL, and other supportive ligaments like the patellar tendon. Each of these ligaments plays an important role in maintaining the structural integrity of the knee, facilitating movement, and preventing injury.

Comparison of Knee Ligaments and Tendons

Structure

Location

Function

Injury Characteristics

PCL (Posterior Cruciate Ligament)

Back of the knee joint

Prevents tibia from sliding backward, stabilizes knee

Less common than ACL injury; caused by high-impact trauma (e.g., car accidents, contact sports); symptoms include instability, pain, and swelling

ACL (Anterior Cruciate Ligament)

Front of the knee joint

Prevents tibia from sliding forward, controls rotational movement

Common in sports with sudden stops, direction changes, or jumps (e.g., football, basketball, skiing); symptoms include pain, swelling, and functional loss

Patellar Tendon

Connects patella (kneecap) to tibia

Enables knee extension during walking and running

Injured due to trauma or overuse; symptoms include pain, swelling, and difficulty straightening the knee

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

ACL (Option B): The anterior cruciate ligament is located in the front of the knee, preventing excessive forward movement of the tibia. This is not the ligament in question here.

Patellar Tendon (Option C): The patellar tendon connects the patella to the tibia and does not function in the same way as the cruciate ligaments, which control the motion of the tibia in relation to the femur.

None of the Above (Option D): This option is incorrect because the marked ligament is clearly identified as the PCL.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Bone marrow is the most radiosensitive tissue in the human body because it contains rapidly dividing hematopoietic stem cells, which are highly vulnerable to ionizing radiation. Radiation exposure can lead to pancytopenia, increasing the risk of infections, anemia, and bleeding.

Radiosensitivity of Different Tissues

Tissue

Radiosensitivity

Reason

Bone marrow

Highly radiosensitive

Contains rapidly dividing stem cells for blood cell production

Lymphoid tissue

Highly radiosensitive

Rapid cell turnover, easily damaged by radiation

Gastrointestinal mucosa

Moderately radiosensitive

Epithelial cells divide rapidly

Skin

Moderate

Basal layer is sensitive, but outer layers provide some protection

Muscle

Radioresistant

Cells do not divide frequently

Nervous tissue

Highly radioresistant

Neurons are non-dividing cells and less affected by radiation

Skin (Option A): Moderately radiosensitive due to the presence of basal cell layers, but not as sensitive as bone marrow.

Muscles (Option B): Incorrect because muscle cells are highly radioresistant as they do not actively divide.

Nervous tissue (Option D): Incorrect because neurons are non-dividing and among the most radioresistant cells in the body.

question: What is the most radiosensitive tissue in our body?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The arrow marking as 2 is psoas muscles and in the context of a 15-year-old patient with a history of spinal tuberculosis and presenting with low-grade fever, dull backache, and persistent flexion of the hip joint, the involvement of the psoas muscle is highly suggestive of a psoas abscess.
    • Muscle from anterior aspect crossing hip joint anteriorly - Iliopsoas muscle.
    • Pulling the femur anteriorly causing the hip flexion- Iliopsoas muscle (Proximal muscle) - Chief muscle for hip flexion.
  • The psoas muscle is a large muscle located in the lower back that plays a key role in hip flexion and stabilization of the spine.
  • Psoas abscesses can occur as a complication of spinal tuberculosis, with the infection spreading from the vertebral column to the adjacent psoas muscle.

[[figure-1]]

Spinal TB (Pott’s Disease)

Involves lower thoracic and upper lumbar vertebrae in adults; and upper thoracic spine in children.

Lesions spread to adjacent vertebrae and intervertebral disks.

Advanced Disease
  • Collapse of vertebrae leads to kyphosis (gibbus deformity).
  • Paravertebral cold abscesses:
    • Upper spine: Abscess may penetrate the chest wall as a soft tissue mass.
    • Lower spine: May track to the inguinal region or form a psoas abscess.

Diagnosis of Spinal TB
  • Imaging (CT/MRI): Shows characteristic lesions, suggesting TB aetiology.
  • Differential Diagnosis: Includes tumours and infections like pyogenic bacterial osteomyelitis.
  • Confirmation: Aspiration or biopsy confirms TB via positive cultures and typical histology.

Complications
  • Paraplegia: Due to abscess or spinal cord compression; requires emergency drainage if caused by a large abscess.

1 (Option A): Abdominal wall muscles, including the rectus abdominis, external oblique, internal oblique, and transversus abdominis, are responsible for core stability and movement of the trunk. In the given scenario, the symptoms and CT image findings are not indicative of abdominal wall muscle involvement.

3 (Option C): The adductor muscles, including the adductor longus, adductor brevis, and adductor magnus, are located in the inner thigh and are responsible for hip adduction. They are not directly related to the symptoms and CT findings described in the scenario.

question: A 15-year-old patient with a history of spinal tuberculosis was brought to the hospital with low-grade fever, dull backache, and persistent flexion of the hip joint. Hip joint motion was limited and painful. Identify the muscle affected in the CT image.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE) is a disorder of adolescents in which the growth plate is damaged and the femoral head moves (“slips”) with respect to the rest of the femur.
  • It results in a non-traumatic painful hip of adolescence. Usually, an anteroposterior view of the pelvis and frog lateral views of both hips helps in the diagnosis of SCFE.

Frog Leg Lateral View:

Indication: Used in the assessment of:

  • Slipped capital femoral epiphysis
  • Perthes disease
  • Procedure:
    • The patient is supine with the affected limb flexed at the knee approximately 30° to 40°, and the hip is abducted 45°. The beam is focused midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis.
    • If it is a bilateral examination, both knees are to rest on sponges, giving the appearance of "frog legs."

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Perthes disease (Option B) is a childhood disease that occurs when the blood supply to the femoral head of the hip joint is temporarily interrupted and the bone begins to die. This can cause pain, limping, and limited movement of the hip joint. The early signs of Perthes disease may be joint effusion and widening of medial joint space. In the advanced burnt-out stage femoral head and neck deformity occur.

Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) (Option C) is a disorder that is due to abnormal development of the acetabulum with or without hip dislocation. This condition may occur at any time, from conception to skeletal maturity and the child may be born with dislocation or instability of the hip joint which then may result in hip dysplasia.

Ankylosing spondylitis (Option D) is a chronic, inflammatory disease of the axial spine. There is a fusion of both SI joints and thin, symmetrical syndesmophytes bridging the Intervertebral disc spaces are seen as depicted in the x-ray of sacroiliac joints.



Reference:

Grainger and Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page no: 230

question: A 13-year-old boy presents to you with a limitation of abduction and internal rotation of the left hip. The x-ray appearance of his left hip joint is shown in the below image. What is the diagnosis of this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Idiopathic scoliosis is the most common type of scoliosis, accounting for the majority of cases.
  • It refers to scoliosis of unknown cause and typically develops during adolescence.
  • The age of the patient in this scenario aligns with the typical onset of idiopathic scoliosis, making it the most likely cause.

Scoliosis:

Scoliosis is defined as a lateral curvature of the spine with a Cobb angle of >10°, as measured on a standing radiograph. It commonly develops during adolescence.

Causes:

  1. Idiopathic Scoliosis: Most common, with no known cause. Typically develops in adolescence.
  2. Congenital Scoliosis: Results from abnormal fetal spinal development.
  3. Neuromuscular Scoliosis: Associated with neurological or muscular disorders like cerebral palsy or muscular dystrophy.
  4. Degenerative Scoliosis: Caused by age-related degeneration, often seen in older adults.

Types:

  1. Structural Scoliosis: Permanent curvature of the spine.
  2. Nonstructural Scoliosis: Functional or temporary, often corrects when lying down.

Clinical Features:

  1. Uneven shoulders or hips.
  2. Leaning to one side due to spinal curvature.
  3. Prominent ribs or shoulder blade on one side.
  4. Asymmetrical back appearance, especially when bending forward.
  5. Muscle imbalances causing fatigue and discomfort.
  6. Back pain, especially during prolonged sitting or standing.

Incorrect Options:

Congenital (Option A): Congenital scoliosis occurs due to malformation of the vertebrae during fetal development and is usually detected much earlier (infancy or early childhood).

NF1 (Option B): Neurofibromatosis type 1 can cause scoliosis, but it’s associated with other features like café-au-lait spots, neurofibromas, or a family history.

Neuromuscular (Option D): Neuromuscular scoliosis is seen in children with neurological or muscular disorders like cerebral palsy or muscular dystrophy, which would have associated clinical findings.

  • Grainger and Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 1265,1266

question: A 14-year-old boy presents with pain and swelling over the right humerus for 2 months. He also has a fever and raised ESR. Blood tests show leucocytosis with neutrophilia. An X-ray of the humerus is shown below. Which of the following is the next step for this patient?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option D- Pott’s spine:

  • Pott’s spine is an extrapulmonary manifestation of TB. Disc Space Narrowing, paravertebral abscess, and vertebral lysis are common features observed in the case of Pott’s spine x-ray.

The sagittal T1 image of the lumbar spine should show a salt-and-pepper appearance of the vertebral marrow in the patient. Since none of them are observed, it is an incorrect choice.

Option B - Ankylosis Spondylitis: It shows features of Sacroiliitis, i.e., inflammation of the sacroiliac joint on Radiology, which isn’t observed in the given MRI image. Thus, it is an incorrect choice.

Option C - Pyogenic Spondylitis: It presents with an abscess in proximity to the spine. Regional osteopenia, new bone apposition, and peripheral sclerosis are some of the radiographic features. Since the given MRI doesn’t show any abscess, it is concluded that option c is an incorrect choice.

It is a glucose analog that is taken up by high-metabolism tissues (like tumors, which exhibit the Warburg effect) but cannot be fully metabolized, thus trapping the tracer and allowing imaging of metabolically active sites.

In a young patient with marfanoid habitus, sudden acute dyspnoea is classically due to primary spontaneous pneumothorax caused by rupture of apical blebs.

  • Marfan syndrome predisposes to:
    • Apical subpleural blebs
    • Spontaneous rupture leading to pneumothorax
  • Presents with sudden breathlessness ± pleuritic chest pain

Chest X-ray Features of Pneumothorax

  • Thin visceral pleural line visible
  • Absence of lung markings beyond this line
  • Increased radiolucency of the affected hemithorax

The most common HRCT finding in COVID-19 is ground-glass opacities.


CT Findings of COVID-19:

question: The most common HRCT finding in a patient with COVID-19 is:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation includes progressive dyspnea, a dry cough, and clubbing, which are common in interstitial lung diseases, and the Predominantly subpleural reticular pattern with honeycombing, especially in the lower lobes confirm UIP.

Usual Interstitial Pneumonia (UIP)

Non-Specific Interstitial Pneumonia (NSIP) (Option A)

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]
  • It presents as a mainly subpleural bibasal reticular pattern with areas of honeycomb (subpleural cystic airspaces with discrete, thickened walls that are stacked or lined up in a row) destruction.
  • As the disease advances, it tends to spread along the lung periphery, affecting the anterior parts of the upper lobes, referred to as the 'propeller blade distribution.'
  • There are signs of traction bronchiectasis and bronchiolectasis.
  • Ground-glass opacities are not predominant.
  • Bilateral ground-glass opacities accompanied by fine reticular patterns.
  • Primarily peripheral in distribution, but may also appear patchy or band-like.
  • Minimal or absent honeycomb pattern.
  • Presence of traction bronchiectasis and bronchiolectasis.
  • Subpleural sparing is seen.

Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (Option C)

[[figure-3]]

  • Opacities may appear consolidative, ground-glass, nodular, or mass-like.
  • Typical distribution is subpleural or peribronchovascular.
  • A common appearance is the perilobular pattern, which features linear or band-like opacities arranged in an arcade or polygonal shape.
  • The “atoll” or “reversed halo sign” is characterized by central ground-glass opacity with a surrounding consolidative edge.

Sarcoidosis generally features bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with egg shell calcification of hilar lymph nodes and ground-glass opacities. (Option D)

question: A 60-year-old man with a history of working as a shipyard worker presents with progressive dyspnea, a persistent dry cough, and chest tightness. He also reports recent weight loss and has experienced crackles upon auscultation. A CT scan of the chest reveals a distinct structure. What could be the underlying mechanism responsible for the observed sign on the CT image?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical features of Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) combined with brachial plexopathy (arm weakness, pain, and numbness) strongly suggest a Pancoast tumor, which is a lung apex tumor often affecting the sympathetic chain and brachial plexus. MRI is the preferred imaging modality as it provides detailed visualization of soft tissues, including the tumor’s invasion into surrounding structures like the brachial plexus.

CT Scan (Computed Tomography):

  • Modality of choice for the detailed evaluation of lung tumors.

[[figure-1]]

PET-CT (Positron Emission Tomography-CT):

  • Modality of choice for staging and assessing metastatic spread, as malignant cells show increased glucose metabolism.
  • Combines metabolic imaging (via PET) with anatomic detail (via CT).

MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging):

  • Not routinely used for lung tumors, but valuable in specific cases.
  • Superior sulcus tumors (Pancoast tumors): Investigation of choice in pancoast tumors to assess brachial plexus involvement or spinal cord invasion.

Chest X-ray (Option A):
Incorrect — suggests the presence of mass but does not define nerve or soft tissue invasion.

CT Scan (Option C):
Incorrect — good for bony detail but not optimal for brachial plexus or sympathetic chain evaluation.

PET Scan (Option D):
Incorrect — useful for staging, not for assessing local neurological invasion.



Reference:
  1. Grainger & Allison's Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 40-43.
  2. Fred A. Mettler Essentials of Radiology, 4th Edition, Page 72-75.

question: A 55-year-old male presents with drooping of the right eyelid, a constricted right pupil, and lack of sweating on the right side of his face. He also reports weakness, pain, and numbness in his right arm. Chest x-ray reports an apical lung mass on the right side. What is the imaging modality of choice to identify the underlying cause of his symptoms?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

MRI is the preferred imaging modality for posterior mediastinal masses, particularly those suspected to arise from neural structures. It provides excellent soft tissue contrast and allows detailed visualization of the mass and its relationship with surrounding tissues, making it ideal for evaluating neurogenic tumors.

Felson classification of the mediastinum:

Felson classification divides the mediastinum into three anatomical compartments to assist in the localization and diagnosis of mediastinal masses. These compartments are based on lateral chest radiographs.

[[figure-1]]

Compartment

Boundaries

Common Masses/Abnormalities

Anterior (Prevascular)

Posterior sternum to anterior heart and great vessels
  • Thymic masses: Thymoma, thymic hyperplasia, thymic carcinoma
  • Germ cell tumors: Teratoma
  • Thyroid masses: Ectopic thyroid, substernal goiter
  • Lymphoma: Hodgkin's, non-Hodgkin's

Middle (Visceral)

Between anterior and posterior compartments

Contains heart, great vessels, trachea, esophagus, lymph nodes
  • Bronchogenic cysts
  • Pericardial cysts
  • Lymphadenopathy (metastasis, lymphoma, sarcoidosis)
  • Aortic aneurysms, vascular abnormalities

Posterior (Paravertebral)

Posterior heart and great vessels to anterior vertebrae
  • Neurogenic tumors: Schwannomas, neurofibromas, ganglioneuromas
  • Esophageal lesions: Tumors, diverticula
  • Spinal abnormalities: Vertebral infections, hernias, masses


Reference:
  1. Grainger & Allison's Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 69
  2. Fred A. Mettler Essentials of Radiology, 4th Edition, Page 86-92.

To confirm the diagnosis and further evaluate the mass, the physician orders additional imaging. What is the most appropriate imaging modality to confirm the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The acromion process of the scapula develops from multiple secondary ossification centers, which typically appear around 14–16 years and fuse between 18–25 years.

The presence of a visible, unfused acromial epiphysis on radiography indicates that skeletal maturity has not yet been achieved, but the individual is older than mid-adolescence, placing the age most consistently in the 16–18 year range.

12–14 years (Option A): At this age, acromial ossification centers are usually not yet well formed.

14–16 years (Option B): Ossification begins in this period, but the degree of development seen here suggests a later adolescent stage.

18+ years (Option D): After 18 years, fusion of the acromial epiphysis begins, and a clearly separate ossification center would be less likely.

explanationHtml:
• The posteroanterior (PA) view is the standard projection for routine chest X-rays because it provides optimal visualisation of the heart, lungs, and mediastinum with minimal magnification of cardiac structures.

Principles of PA Chest X-ray

  • The patient stands facing the detector with the chest against it
  • The X-ray beam passes from posterior to anterior
  • Scapulae are rotated out of the lung fields
  • Provides a more accurate representation of heart size compared to AP

[[figure-1]]

Advantages

  • Minimal magnification of the heart
  • Clear lung fields for detecting infiltrates, masses, or pneumothorax
  • Standard baseline for follow-up imaging

Technique Notes

  • Full inspiration is requested for maximum lung expansion
  • Patient upright for better air-fluid level detection

Incorrect Options:

AP view (Option B): Used when patients cannot stand; the heart appears artificially enlarged.

Lateral view (Option C): Provides additional information about retrosternal and retrocardiac areas, but not for routine baseline imaging.

Oblique view (Option D): Rarely used; mainly for specific mediastinal or lung lesion localisation.



Reference:

David Sutton’s Textbook of Radiology and Imaging, Part 1, 7th Edition, Page 1.
question: A patient comes for a routine chest examination. Which X-ray projection is typically preferred for standard imaging?

explanationHtml:
• The left anterior oblique (LAO) view is the preferred chest X-ray projection for optimal visualisation of the right lung, as it exposes the maximum area of the right lung field by rotating it away from the mediastinum. Conversely, the right anterior oblique (RAO) view best demonstrates the left lung.
  • In addition to lung assessment, the LAO view is useful for evaluating cardiac and mediastinal structures such as both ventricles, left atrium, aortic window, and the aorta, while the RAO view highlights the pulmonary artery, right atrium, and right ventricle. Both oblique projections are also routinely utilised during coronary angiographic evaluation for better anatomical delineation.

[[figure-1]]

Incorrect Options:

Right anterior oblique (Option A) :This view demonstrates the maximum area of the left lung, not the right lung. It is mainly used to assess the right atrium, right ventricle, and pulmonary artery, making it unsuitable for optimal right lung visualisation.

Right posterior oblique (Option C) :Posterior oblique views are not routinely used for targeted lung field assessment. They do not provide maximal exposure of the right lung compared to anterior oblique projections.

Left posterior oblique(Option D) :Similar to other posterior oblique views, this projection does not adequately separate the right lung from mediastinal structures, resulting in suboptimal visualisation of the right lung field.



Reference:

https://www.hmpgloballearningnetwork.com/site/cathlab/clinical-editors-corner/chest-x-ray-interpretation-made-easy-understanding-cardiac
question: Which oblique chest X-ray projection provides optimal visualisation of the right lung field?

explanationHtml:
• The oblique chest view is the most useful projection for evaluating right middle lobe pathology, as it helps separate the middle lobe from overlapping lung segments.

Radiographic Principle

  • The right middle lobe is located anteriorly and medially, between the right upper and lower lobes.
  • On a standard PA view, this lobe is frequently obscured by the heart and mediastinum.

Role of the Oblique View

  • Oblique positioning rotates the thorax, reducing overlap of lung fields.
  • Enhances visualization of:
    • Right middle lobe consolidation
    • Collapse (middle lobe syndrome)
    • Localized masses or infections
  • Especially helpful when PAs' view findings are inconclusive.

Incorrect Options:

Lordotic view (Option A): Best for lung apices and clavicle-related pathology.

PA view (Option B): Routine screening view, but limited for isolated middle lobe lesions.

Left anterior oblique view (Option D): Primarily useful for left lung and cardiac border assessment.



Reference:

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 171.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Pulmonary hamartoma is the most common benign tumor of the lung.

  • A characteristic imaging feature is coarse "popcorn" calcification, and CT often demonstrates intralesional fat, a highly specific finding that strongly supports the diagnosis.

[[figure-1]]

  • Hamartomas are the most common benign lung tumors,
  • Generally asymptomatic and often discovered incidentally
  • Radiographic Features:
    • Typically present as a solitary peripheral pulmonary nodule or mass.
    • Size usually ranges from 1 to 4 cm.
    • Well-circumscribed, round or oval shape with smooth or lobulated margins.
    • Internal calcifications, often with a "popcorn" appearance
    • CT scans effectively reveal internal fat, which is pathognomonic for hamartomas.
  • Hamartomas may be multiple, grow slowly, and do not cavitate or invade adjacent structures.

Angioinvasive aspergillosis (Option A): Typically shows multiple pulmonary nodules with a halo sign in the early stage and an air crescent sign during recovery, not popcorn calcification.

Aspergillus mycetoma (Option B): Appears as a fungal ball within a pre-existing lung cavity, producing the air crescent (Monod) sign, rather than popcorn calcification.

Bacterial pneumonia (Option C): Usually presents with air-space consolidation or bronchopneumonic infiltrates. Popcorn calcification is not a feature.

• Pneumomediastinum is the most likely diagnosis in a term neonate with mild respiratory distress and preserved oxygen saturation following assisted delivery.

Pathophysiology and Mechanism

  • Caused by alveolar rupture due to increased intrathoracic pressure during birth or initial breaths
  • Escaped air tracks along bronchovascular sheaths into the mediastinum (Macklin effect)
  • Commonly associated with vacuum or forceps-assisted deliveries

Radiographic Features

  • Air outlining mediastinal structures on chest X-ray
  • Elevation and outlining of the thymus produces the classic “spinnaker sail sign.”
  • Lungs remain expanded with no significant collapse
  • Usually no significant cardiopulmonary compromise

[[figure-1]]

Clinical Course

  • Typically benign and self-limiting
  • Most neonates remain hemodynamically stable
  • Managed conservatively with observation

Incorrect Options:

Pneumothorax (Option A): Shows peripheral hyperlucency with absent lung markings and lung collapse; often causes desaturation.

[[figure-2]]

Consolidation (Option B): Appears as alveolar opacities with air bronchograms; associated with infection and worsening respiratory distress.

[[figure-3]]

Pneumoperitoneum (Option D): Demonstrates free air under the diaphragm on erect films; related to gastrointestinal perforation, not primary respiratory symptoms.

[[figure-4]]



Reference:

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 92.
question: A term neonate born by vacuum-assisted delivery developed mild respiratory distress 1 hour after birth. Arterial oxygen saturation remained >95% without supplemental oxygen. Chest radiography performed 6 hours after birth is given below. What is the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Pleural effusion is best demonstrated on a lateral decubitus chest radiograph because free pleural fluid layers dependently and become clearly visible even in small volumes.

Radiographic Evaluation of Pleural Effusion

  • Pleural effusion represents the accumulation of fluid in the pleural space.
  • Small effusions may not be visible on a routine erect PA chest X-ray.
  • Detecting fluid mobility helps differentiate free fluid from pleural thickening or consolidation.

Lateral Decubitus View

  • The patient lies on the suspected side with the X-ray beam horizontal.
  • Free pleural fluid layers along the dependent chest wall.
  • It can detect as little as 5-10 mL of pleural fluid.
  • Also helps assess whether the effusion is free-flowing or loculated.

[[figure-1]]

Incorrect Options:

PA view (Option B)

  • Requires at least 200-300 mL of fluid to show costophrenic angle blunting.
  • Less sensitive to small effusions.

Left anterior oblique view (Option C)

  • Primarily used to evaluate mediastinal structures and lung overlap.
  • Not useful for detecting pleural fluid.

Right anterior oblique view (Option D)

  • Helps in assessing hilar or parenchymal lesions.
  • Does not improve the detection of pleural effusion.


Reference:

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 43.
question: A 45-year-old man presents to the emergency department with acute pleuritic chest pain and reduced air entry over the right hemithorax on examination. A small pleural effusion is suspected clinically. Which chest X-ray vie

explanationHtml:
• Pleural calcification occurs as a result of prior pleural injury, inflammation, or exposure. Sarcoidosis predominantly affects the lung parenchyma and mediastinal lymph nodes, and pleural involvement is rare and therefore, it is the least likely condition to present with pleural calcification.

[[figure-1]]

Radiographic Features
On chest X-ray:

  • Linear, focal, or diffuse pleural densities.
  • Commonly along the lower lobes or parietal pleura.
  • May be unilateral or bilateral.
  • A CT scan is more sensitive, showing the extent of plaques and subtle calcifications.

Clinical Relevance

  • Suggests prior pleural insult such as infection, trauma, or occupational exposure.
  • Usually asymptomatic, but recognising it is important for history-taking and differential diagnosis.
  • Helps differentiate from other pleural or parenchymal diseases for proper management.

Incorrect Options:

Asbestosis (Option A): Classic cause of pleural calcification; pleural plaques are characteristic.

Hemothorax (Option B): Calcification may occur as the pleura heals after blood accumulation.

Healed empyema (Option C): Chronic infection or inflammation of the pleura leads to fibrosis and calcification.



Reference:

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 82.
question: A 55-year-old patient undergoes a chest X-ray for evaluation of chronic respiratory symptoms. Multiple pleural calcifications are noted. Which of the following conditions is least likely to present with pleural calcification?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • On a standard posteroanterior (PA) chest radiograph, the hilar shadows are formed mainly by the pulmonary arteries, with contribution from the upper lobe pulmonary veins. The lower lobe pulmonary veins do not normally contribute to the hilar shadow because they course inferiorly and medially toward the left atrium rather than forming part of the central hilar contour.

Incorrect Options:

Bronchus(Option A):Although bronchi are air-filled and usually not visible, they are anatomically located at the hilum and are considered part of the hilar structures rather than excluded from the concept.

Pulmonary artery(Option B):This is the primary and dominant contributor to the hilar shadow on both sides.

Upper lobe veins(Option C):These veins run horizontally and contribute to the upper portion of the hilar vascular shadow, especially on the right side.



Reference:

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 25,26,27.
question: On a standard posteroanterior chest radiograph, which of the following structures does NOT normally contribute to the hilar shadow?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

A loculated pleural effusion is a collection of fluid trapped within pleural adhesions, commonly following infection or inflammation.

Pathophysiology:

  • Pleural inflammation (commonly from pneumonia or empyema) causes fibrin deposition.
  • Fibrin forms septations within the pleural space, leading to loculated fluid collections.
  • Loculated effusions do not freely move with the patient's position.

Radiographic Features:

  • On chest X-ray:
    • Lenticular or biconvex opacity along the lateral chest wall.
    • Margins are obtuse with the chest wall.
    • May not change with decubitus positioning.
  • The adjacent lung may be compressed, but no complete lung collapse.
  • Lateral or oblique views can help localize effusion and confirm lack of mobility.

Clinical Relevance:

  • Often associated with pleuritic chest pain, fever, and restricted chest wall movement.
  • Important to differentiate from pneumothorax or consolidation for management decisions.

Incorrect Options:

Pneumothorax (Option B): Shows a radiolucent area without lung markings; a sharply demarcated pleural line; fluid opacity is absent.

[[figure-1]]

Consolidation (Option C): Airspace opacity with air bronchograms; usually uniform in lung parenchyma; not lenticular or localized along pleural margins.

[[figure-2]]

Fibrosis (Option D): Chronic process with volume loss, reticular pattern, and possibly traction bronchiectasis; no acute fluid collection.

[[figure-3]]



Reference:

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 1790.
question: A 32-year-old male presents with persistent fever and sharp, pleuritic chest pain for one week. He has restricted chest movements on the affected side. Chest radiograph shows a non-dependent, lenticular opacity along the lateral chest wall with obtuse margins. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Westermark sign is a focal oligemia (reduced blood flow) seen distal to a pulmonary embolism on chest X-ray. It is a classic radiologic sign of acute pulmonary embolism (PE), which often presents with sudden pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea, especially in patients with recent immobilisation, long-haul travel, or hypercoagulable states.

Radiographic Features

On chest X-ray:

  • Focal area of decreased pulmonary vascular markings distal to the embolus.
  • It may be subtle and often difficult to detect.
  • Sometimes accompanied by Hampton hump (wedge-shaped infarct opacity).
  • Usually unilateral, corresponding to the affected pulmonary artery.

[[figure-1]]

Clinical Relevance

  • Seen in patients with acute PE, which is a life-threatening condition.
  • Helps raise suspicion, but CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) is the gold standard for diagnosis.
  • Important for prompt anticoagulation or thrombolytic therapy to prevent morbidity and mortality.

Incorrect Options:

Palla's sign (Option A): Enlarged right descending pulmonary artery seen in pulmonary embolism; supportive but less specific.

[[figure-2]]

Sausage sign (Option B): Dilated pulmonary artery with thrombus; seen on imaging like CT.

McConnell's sign (Option C): Regional right ventricular dysfunction seen on echocardiography.

[[figure-3]]



Reference:

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 412.
question: A 50-year-old woman develops sudden pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath two days after a long-haul flight. A chest X-ray is performed. Which of the following radiologic signs is most suggestive of her condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Hypertranslucent lungs on chest X-ray are seen when there is increased air content or decreased pulmonary vasculature. Pulmonary fibrosis involves interstitial scarring and decreased lung compliance, which usually leads to reticular opacities and volume loss, not hyperlucency.

Radiographic Features

  • Hypertranslucent lungs: Increased lucency, decreased vascular markings, may see lung overinflation or bullae.
  • Pulmonary fibrosis: Reticular or reticulonodular opacities, honeycombing, reduced lung volumes, and traction bronchiectasis.

Clinical Relevance

  • Recognizing hypertranslucent lungs helps identify conditions with air-trapping, emphysema, or congenital overinflation.
  • Differentiates from fibrotic or restrictive lung diseases, which present with opaque, scarred lung fields.
  • Important for guiding treatment and prognosis, e.g., bronchodilators for emphysema vs antifibrotic therapy for fibrosis.

Incorrect Options:

Asthma with air-trapping (Option A): Hyperlucency can occur in areas of air-trapping during an acute exacerbation.

Congenital lobar emphysema (Option B): Overinflated lobe appears hyperlucent; vessels may be displaced.

Bullous emphysema (Option D): Large bullae appear as focal hyperlucent areas with thin walls.



Reference:

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 208.
question: A 28-year-old man is evaluated with a chest X-ray for abnormal lung findings. In which of the following conditions is a hypertranslucent lung least likely to be observed?

correctAnswer: B. Lines radiating from the hilum toward the periphery of the lung
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Kerley A lines are long, thin lines extending from the hilum toward the lung periphery, representing interstitial lymphatic engorgement, commonly seen in pulmonary oedema.

Radiographic Features

  • Oblique lines radiating from the hilum toward the periphery (2-6 cm).
  • Do not reach the pleura.
  • Best seen on a frontal chest X-ray.

[[figure-1]]

Clinical Relevance

  • Indicative of interstitial pulmonary oedema and pulmonary venous hypertension.
  • Helps differentiate cardiogenic pulmonary oedema from other lung pathologies.

Incorrect Options:

Short peripheral lines not reaching the pleura (Option A): These describe Kerley B lines, which are short (1-2 cm), horizontal lines seen at the lung bases, running perpendicular to the pleura and extending up to it. They represent interlobular septal thickening and are more commonly seen than Kerley A lines.

Lines running perpendicular to the pleura(Option C): This again corresponds to Kerley B lines, a classic sign of interstitial pulmonary oedema, particularly in left-sided heart failure.

Fine interlacing “spider-web” appearance(Option D): This describes Kerley C lines, which are caused by diffuse interstitial oedema and represent a network of superimposed Kerley A and B lines, producing a reticular or spider-web pattern.



Reference:

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 254.

question: Which of the following correctly describes Kerley A lines on chest X-ray?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Pulmonary oedema produces bilateral, symmetrical perihilar alveolar opacities with relative peripheral sparing, creating the classic bat-wing appearance on chest X-ray.
  • This pattern is due to alveolar flooding from raised pulmonary venous pressure, most commonly secondary to left ventricular failure.

Key Radiological Features of Pulmonary Oedema:

  • Central perihilar fluffy air-space opacities
  • Symmetrical distribution
  • Relative sparing of lung periphery
  • Associated findings (cardiogenic):
    • Cardiomegaly
    • Kerley B lines (interstitial oedema)
    • Pleural effusions

[[figure-1]]

Incorrect Options:

Sarcoidosis (Option B):

  • Classically shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (1-2-3 sign)
  • Upper lobe-predominant interstitial nodules
  • Alveolar bat-wing pattern is not a feature

Pulmonary embolism (Option C):

  • Chest X-ray often normal
  • Specific signs:
    • Hampton hump - peripheral wedge-shaped opacity

[[figure-2]]

[[figure-3]]

  • Westermark sign - focal oligemia

[[figure-4]]

  • Diagnosis confirmed on CT pulmonary angiography

Pneumoconiosis (Option D):

  • Chronic occupational lung disease
  • Radiographic patterns:
    • Small rounded nodules (silicosis, coal workers)
    • Upper lobe fibrosis ± eggshell calcification
  • Does not produce acute alveolar perihilar opacities


Reference:

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 251
question: A patient presents with acute breathlessness and orthopnoea. Chest X-ray shows bilateral central alveolar opacities predominantly around the hila with relative peripheral sparing, producing a bat-wing distribution. This radiographic pattern is most suggestive of:

correctAnswer: C. Posterobasal segment of left lower lobe
explanationHtml:
• Pulmonary sequestration most commonly affects the posterobasal segment of the left lower lobe, due to its embryological origin from an accessory lung bud receiving systemic arterial supply.

Pulmonary Sequestration

  • A congenital lung anomaly characterized by non-functioning lung tissue
  • Lacks normal tracheobronchial connection
  • Receives systemic arterial supply, usually from the thoracic or abdominal aorta

Most Common Site

  • Posterobasal segment of the left lower lobe
    • Seen in both intralobar (more common) and extralobar sequestration
    • Left-sided predominance due to embryologic vascular development

[[figure-1]]

Radiological Importance

  • Appears as a persistent basal opacity on chest X-ray
  • CT angiography demonstrates:
    • Aberrant systemic arterial supply
    • Venous drainage into pulmonary veins (intralobar type)

Incorrect Options:

Posterobasal segment of right lower lobe (Option A): Can be involved but is significantly less common than the left side.

Apical segment of left upper lobe (Option B): Upper lobe involvement is rare and not typical for sequestration.

Apical segment of right upper lobe (Option D): Pulmonary sequestration almost never occurs in the upper lobes.



Reference:

https://radiopaedia.org/articles/pulmonary-sequestration

question: Pulmonary sequestration most frequently involves which of the following lung segments?

Explanation:

Chest X ray reveals signs of pneumomediastinum with the presence of air adjacent to the bronchus highlighting the bronchial wall (double bronchial wall sign). Barcode or stratosphere sign is typically found in patients with pneumothorax, not pneumomediastinum.

Pneumomediastinum:

  • Presence of free air around mediastinal structures.
  • Common Causes:
    • Blunt or penetrating trauma.
    • Esophageal perforation.

[[figure-1]]

  • Hamman's crunch sign: Unusual, adventitious sound heard on auscultation of the chest.
  • Radiographic Signs:
    • Ring around the artery sign: Air around the pulmonary artery (usually the right) outlining the artery.

[[figure-2]]

  • Sail sign: Elevation of the thymus caused by air.

[[figure-3]]

  • Continuous diaphragm sign: Air trapped posterior to the pericardium, appearing as a continuous air collection on an AP projection.(Option C)

[[figure-4]]

  • Tubular artery sign: Air outlines the medial side of major aortic branches, with aerated lung outlining the lateral side. (Option A)

[[figure-5]]

  • Double bronchial wall sign: Air adjacent to the bronchus highlights the bronchial wall. (Option D)

[[figure-6]]

  • Naclerio V-sign: V-shaped air lucency in the left lower mediastinal area.

[[figure-7]]

  • Ginkgo leaf sign: Subcutaneous emphysema over anterior chest wall.

[[figure-8]]

question: A 30-year-old female presents with sudden-onset chest pain and difficulty breathing after a recent blunt trauma to the chest. Chest Xray is taken and is shown below. Which of the following radiological findings is not typically seen in this case?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In expiration, the lung becomes white due to air exhaled out while pneumothorax remains black. So, white lung gives a good contrast to black pneumothorax in expiration.

Chest X-ray in Inspiration: Chest X-rays are typically performed during the inspiration phase, which maximizes lung volume and provides a clearer view of the lung fields. During this phase, the lungs fill with air, and the air appears black on the X-ray due to its low density compared to surrounding tissues.

[[figure-1]]

Chest X-ray in Expiration: Expiratory chest X-rays are utilized for assessing small pneumothoraces and suspected inhaled foreign bodies, while inspiratory chest X-rays are performed in all other cases.

[[figure-2]]

Appearance During Expiration: When a foreign body obstructs the airway, air may become trapped in the lungs, preventing full exhalation. Consequently, during an expiratory X-ray, the obstructed lung appears black (due to retained air), indicating an obstruction on that particular side. A persistent black appearance in the affected lung can confirm an obstruction.

Parameter

Normal Lung

Pneumothorax

Inspiration

Black

Black

Expiration

White

Black

Inspiration Chest X-ray (Option A): Commonly used for general chest imaging but can miss small pneumothoraces since the lungs are fully expanded, hiding air in the pleural space.

Lateral Decubitus Chest X-ray (Option C): Most sensitive chest x-ray view for pleural effusion.

Oblique Chest X-ray (Option D): This view can be helpful for evaluating certain thoracic structures but is not typically used to assess pneumothorax.

question: In a lateral chest X-ray, which area should you focus on to identify pathology in the hilar region?

explanationHtml:
Significant facial swelling, prominent neck veins, and difficulty breathing are characteristic of superior vena cava (SVC) syndrome. This condition arises due to obstruction of the SVC, impairing venous return from the head, neck, and upper limbs.

The SVC is a major vein that collects blood from the upper body and returns it to the heart. When obstructed, venous pressure increases in the areas it drains, leading to facial and neck swelling (often with distended neck veins), dyspnea, and sometimes cyanosis.

In the provided CT scan, structure B represents the SVC. Its obstruction results in the clinical manifestations of SVC syndrome.

[[figure-1]]

Grainger & Allison's Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 27-29.

These findings suggest an obstruction in the venous return from the head, neck, and upper limbs. A CT scan is conducted to assess the cause of these symptoms. he clinical scenario here points to the diagnosis of Poland syndrome, in which the chest radiograph shows a hyperlucent or blackout hemithorax of the affected side (left here), and this black-out lung finding is also found in other conditions like bullous emphysema.

question:
A patient presents to the clinic with the following anomalies of chest and hands.

He has a history of having these anomalies since childhood but has no other symptoms. His chest X-ray shows a left hyperlucent lobe. Which other condition can show a similar chest X-ray picture?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

he above clinical symptoms and the chest X-ray lead to the diagnosis of a right pneumothorax, which causes the lung to collapse and squished towards the hilum, ipsilateral depression of the hemidiaphragm, and contralateral deviation of the mediastinum.

Pathophysiology:

  • The pressure gradient in the thorax changes with pneumothorax. Normally, the pleural space is negative compared to atmospheric pressure.
  • If air enters the pleural space through communication with the alveoli, it alters the pressure gradient, leading to lung collapse.

Radiographic appearance of pneumothorax:

  • Pneumothorax appears as a radiolucent area (black).
  • Pneumothorax pushes the adjacent lung towards the hilum.
  • A sharp radiopaque line separates the pneumothorax from the lung parenchyma.
  • A closed pneumothorax is easily detectable in an expiratory X-ray, as there is a decrease in lung volume. However, the volume of the pneumothorax is not affected by respiration.

Tension Pneumothorax

  • Significant contralateral deviation of the mediastinum (vs Option A)
  • Collapsed lung
  • Depression of ipsilateral hemidiaphragm (vs Option B)

[[figure-1]]

White-out lung (Option D) refers to when there is complete opacification of an entire hemithorax. This is seen in conditions like pneumonia of the entire lung, a large mass in the lung or chest wall, large pleural effusion, etc., which increase the opacity of the lung.



Reference:
  1. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK441885/
  2. David Sutton Textbook of Radiology and Imaging, Volume 1, 8th Edition, Page 928-932.
  3. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7390330/
question:
A patient is brought to the emergency after a fall from a tree. He developed shortness of breath and chest pain, is tachypneic, and has distended neck veins on examination. His chest X-ray:

Which of the following is the correct finding here?

explanationHtml:
A-lines are horizontal reverberation artifacts seen in the presence of pneumothorax; all the other signs are absent in this case of pneumothorax.

Ultrasound findings in pneumothorax

Pleural stripe (Option C)

The echogenic line known as the 'pleural stripe' reflects most of the acoustic energy at the air-pleural interface and is the normal pleura.

Artefacts

  • Vertical echogenic bands called 'comet tails' are absent in pneumothorax.
  • 'A lines' are horizontal reverberation artefacts caused by reflection from the pleura in the presence of pneumothorax.

Lung sliding (Option A)
  • It is a normal finding seen due to the shimmering of the pleural stripe at the pleural surface.
  • This sign disappears in pneumothorax.

Lung point sign

  • Indicates the border between sliding lung and pneumothorax which helps assess size.

Barcode/ stratosphere sign
  • In cases where lung sliding is absent, M-mode images show uniform horizontal straight lines known as the stratosphere sign or barcode sign.
  • This is seen in pneumothorax.
  • Normal lung shows Sea-shore sign (Option B).

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]


Reference:

Grainger and Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology a Textbook of Medical Imaging, 7th Edition, Page 51.
question: A patient with a large tension pneumothorax after experiencing a fall is being examined with ultrasound. Which of the following findings will be present in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Clinical features like breathlessness, cough, and decreased breath sound, along with X-ray findings of large pleural opacity and blunted costophrenic angle, indicate a diagnosis of Pleural effusion.


Pleural Effusion:

  • Pleural effusion is the accumulation of fluid in the pleural space.
  • Effusion Progression: Blunting of costophrenic angles starts at 200-500 mL. Classic signs include opacification of the lower chest with a concave superior margin.

[[figure-1]]

  • Massive Effusions: 1000 mL reaches the fourth anterior rib; cause dense opacification of the hemithorax with contralateral mediastinal shift. Diaphragmatic inversion may occur.
  • Lateral decubitus X-rays: Increase sensitivity for small effusions as the pleural fluid moves with gravity and the lung effectively floats on the effusion.

[[figure-2]]

  • Subpulmonary Effusions: Appear as a "high hemidiaphragm" on x-rays, with an unusual contour that peaks laterally than usual. Ultrasound or CT confirms the diagnosis.
  • In an upright PA view, the meniscus sign indicates the presence of a significant amount of pleural fluid, typically exceeding 200 mL and blunting the costophrenic angle.

[[figure-3]]


Lung abscess (Option A) typically presents with a cavitary lesion on imaging, often accompanied by a gas-fluid level, rather than a pleural opacity with a blunted costophrenic angle indicative of fluid accumulation seen in pleural effusion.

[[figure-4]]


Pneumothorax (Option B) shows a region of lucency (darkness) along the lung margin, typically more pronounced on an erect chest X-ray. In this case, symptoms of pleural effusion and x-ray findings suggest fluid rather than air, making pneumothorax unlikely.

[[figure-5]]


Hydropneumothorax (Option D) indicates the presence of both air and fluid in the pleural space, typically seen as an air-fluid level on an upright chest X-ray, which distinguishes it from a simple pleural effusion.

[[figure-6]]



Reference:

question: A 65-year-old male with a history of COPD presents with a 2-week history of increasing shortness of breath and a persistent cough. On examination, decreased breath sounds are noted on the left, and a chest X-ray is taken, which is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: B. It may be mistaken for a lung mass due to its appearance.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Chest X-ray reveals a well-defined homogeneous mass occupying the transverse fissure in the right middle lung field in a patient with heart failure, suggesting a diagnosis of a phantom tumor, which may be mistaken for a lung mass due to its mass-like radiologic appearance.


Phantom Tumor/ Vanishing Tumor:

  • A phantom tumor is a well-demarcated opacity resulting from pleural effusion.
  • It is commonly associated with congestive heart failure.
  • The effusion is typically transudative in nature. (Option D)
  • The most commonly described appearance is a well-defined homogeneous mass, occupying the transverse fissure or sometimes the oblique interlobar fissures. (Option A)
  • It may be mistaken for a lung mass or consolidation because of its radiologic appearance as a mass-like configuration in the lung. (Option B)
  • It vanishes following mobilization of the fluid and effective diuresis. (Option C)

[[figure-1]]

  • Mostly seen in the geriatric population who have a higher incidence of congestive heart failure.
  • Pathophysiology:
    • In congestive heart failure, increased hydrostatic pressure on the right side of the lung interferes with venous and lymphatic drainage.
    • This leads to a predominance of effusion on the right side.
    • Pleuritis can cause obliteration of the pleural space, preventing the spread of fluid.
  • Treatment: Diuretics


Reference:
  1. www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5410121/
  2. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3014119/
