question: Identify the hemorrhage shown in the following image?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The empty delta sign is a radiological finding seen on contrast-enhanced CT scans or MR venography.
  • It indicates the presence of a thrombus in the dural venous sinus, most commonly the superior sagittal sinus.
  • The thrombus appears as a filling defect surrounded by contrast enhancement, forming a triangular or delta-shaped void.

Central venous sinus thrombosis

  • CVT should be suspected in patients presenting with headaches, seizures, or encephalopathy.
  • Can occur in superficial or deep dural venous sinuses, affecting either isolated veins or as part of broader venous sinus thrombosis.
  • Factors like intracranial infections, trauma, dehydration, pregnancy, oral contraceptives, smoking, and vasculitis (e.g., Behçet disease) can trigger CVT. If absent, a thrombophilia screening is necessary.

CT Findings:

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

  • The empty delta sign, visible in contrast-enhanced CT scans, indicates dural venous sinus thrombosis in the superior sagittal sinus as a triangular filling defect outlined by contrast, representing a thrombus.
  • The dense vein sign, a hyperdense vessel sign indicating hyperattenuating thrombus due to acute venous thrombosis, is found in cortical veins or dural venous sinuses.

MRI Findings:

[[figure-3]]

  • Loss of normal flow void; thrombosed vessels may appear hyperintense on T1 and T2 sequences. Very acute thrombus can be hypointense on T2, mimicking flow voids. Additionally, slow flow can also result in loss of the flow void.
  • MR venography (MRV) shows a loss of flow signal or irregularity, indicating a thrombus.
  • SWI (Susceptibility Weighted Imaging) can highlight thrombosed veins and detect acute hemorrhage.

Subarachnoid hemorrhage (Option A): Typically presents with hyperdense blood in the basal cisterns or sulci on non-contrast CT, not an empty delta sign.

Subdural hemorrhage (Option B): Appears as a crescent-shaped hyperdensity along the brain's surface, unrelated to the venous sinuses.

Intraparenchymal hemorrhage (Option D): Appears as a hyperdense lesion within the brain parenchyma on non-contrast CT and is not associated with the empty delta sign



Reference:
  • Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology 7th Edition Page no.1464
  • https://radiopaedia.org/articles/dense-vein-sign
  • https://radiopaedia.org/articles/empty-delta-sign-dural-venous-sinus-thrombosi
question: Identify the condition that presents with an empty delta sign.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • This is the preferred imaging technique for diagnosing primary hyperparathyroidism, especially when the patient is suspected to have a parathyroid adenoma or hyperplasia. The sestamibi scan uses a radiotracer that is taken up by the parathyroid glands, particularly in the presence of adenomas or hyperplasia. It is highly sensitive and specific for detecting parathyroid pathology. Elevated calcium levels and ALP, along with the clinical symptoms, suggest primary hyperparathyroidism, making a sestamibi scan the most appropriate next step.

Radiological features of Primary Hyperparathyroidism:

Features

Image

Subperiosteal erosions and terminal resorption in the phalanges (usually starts in the middle phalanx of the index finger's radial side) along with bone demineralisation.

[[figure-1]]

The "salt and pepper" appearance, or pepper pot skull (lytic lesions in the skull).

[[figure-2]]

Brown tumour or osteitis fibrosa cystica: Cystic lesions in bone from excessive osteoclastic resorption appear as low-density, multiloculated cysts that can lead to bone expansion, accompanied by bleeding and granulation tissue.

[[figure-3]]

Sestamibi scan (Tc-99): Localize the tumour.

[[figure-4]]

MRI (option A): This is not typically used for the initial diagnosis of primary hyperparathyroidism. MRI may be used for further evaluation if other imaging modalities are inconclusive.

FDG PET (option B): This is primarily used for oncology, such as detecting malignancies or metastases, and is not routinely used for diagnosing primary hyperparathyroidism.

CT (option C): CT can be used in some cases to localize parathyroid adenomas, but it is less sensitive than a sestamibi scan and is not the first-line imaging modality for primary hyperparathyroidism.



Reference:
  • Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Volume I, Page 3176-3178.
  • Davidson’s Principles and Practice of Medicine, 24th Edition, Page 663, 664
question: Which imaging technique is preferred for diagnosing primary hyperparathyroidism in a woman who presented with confusion, constipation, and headache, and has elevated serum calcium (13.1 mg/dL) and ALP levels?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The radiological findings and MR spectroscopy results are consistent with neurocysticercosis (NCC), which is caused by Taenia solium.

  • Radiological Features:
    • Cystic lesions with or without ring enhancement
    • Scolex (dot sign) seen within the cyst in vesicular stage
    • Perilesional edema due to inflammatory response
    • Calcifications in the nodular-calcified stage
  • MR Spectroscopy Findings:
    • Lipid lactate peak - degeneration of the parasite
    • Decreased NAA - Neuronal injury
    • Absence of alanine peak - differentiates NCC from tuberculoma

These findings strongly indicate neurocysticercosis as the probable diagnosis.

Neurocysticercosis

  • NCC is the most common parasitic CNS infection worldwide, caused by the ingestion of Taenia solium eggs.

Feature

Details

Clinical Presentation

Seizures, headaches, focal neurological deficits

Stages

Vesicular, Colloidal, Granular, Nodular-calcified

Radiology

Cystic lesions with "dot sign," ring enhancement, or calcifications

MR Spectroscopy

Lipid lactate peak, decreased NAA, no alanine peak

Management

Albendazole + Steroids ± Antiepileptics

[[figure-1]]

Stages of Neurocystericosis

[[figure-2]]

[[figure-3]]

Incorrect Options:

Cerebral toxoplasmosis (Option A): Incorrect because toxoplasmosis does not show the "dot sign" and has different spectroscopy findings (elevated lipids but not alanine).

Cryptococcosis (Option C): Incorrect because cryptococcosis presents as gelatinous pseudocysts in the basal ganglia with low choline and high lipid peaks on MR spectroscopy.

Multiple tuberculomas (Option D): Incorrect because tuberculomas usually present with solid ring-enhancing granulomas and restricted diffusion rather than well-defined cystic lesions with scolex.



Reference:
  1. Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 20th Edition • Page nos. 1642 and 1643
  2. CNS Cryptococcosis
  3. Intracranial Tuberculous Granuloma
  4. Neurotoxoplasmosis
question: A young woman, aged 18, has come forward with seizures. Her radiological image is provided below. MR spectroscopy shows prominent lipid–lactate peaks with decreased N-acetyl aspartate (NAA), what is the probable medical condition she is facing?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Huntington’s disease presents with chorea, personality changes, and dementia due to autosomal dominant CAG repeat expansion, causing caudate nucleus atrophy.

  • It is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by a CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the huntingtin (HTT) gene on chromosome 4.
  • Pathophysiology: The mutation causes toxic gain-of-function protein aggregation, leading to profound atrophy of the caudate nucleus and putamen (striatum).
  • Neurotransmitters: Results in a severe loss of GABAergic and cholinergic neurons in the basal ganglia.
  • Clinical Presentation: Characterized by the classic triad of chorea (involuntary, jerky movements), psychiatric disturbances (irritability, depression, personality changes), and progressive dementia.
  • MRI: Atrophy of the caudate head removes the normal lateral indentation on the lateral ventricles, creating compensatory enlargement known as the "boxcar ventricle" sign.

Tardive Dyskinesia (Option A): Conventional structural brain MRI (T1, T2, FLAIR) typically reveals completely normal brain parenchymal architecture. No pathognomonic macrostructural defects, focal lesions, or localized mass effects are seen, as the underlying pathology is entirely neurochemical (dopamine receptor hypersensitivity).

[[figure-1]]

Sydenham’s chorea (Option C): The brain MRI is normal in the majority of patients. However, during the acute inflammatory phase, it can demonstrate reversible bilateral T2/FLAIR hyperintensity and structural swelling of the striatum (specifically the caudate nuclei and putamen) due to transient autoimmune cross-reactivity and localized neuroinflammation.

[[figure-2]]

Tourette syndrome (Option D): Standard clinical brain MRI sequences are completely normal and demonstrate no focal lesions, signal abnormalities, or structural pathology. Subtle microstructural volumetric reductions in the caudate or frontostriatal pathways are sometimes observed in advanced research settings, but conventional clinical imaging reveals completely healthy anatomy.

[[figure-3]]



Reference:

Harrison’s principles of internal medicine, 21st Edition, Pages 3404, 3405.
question: A 28-year-old man presents with involuntary, jerky movements of the face and limbs that have gradually worsened over the past year. His family reports personality changes, irritability and progressive forgetfulness. On examination, he has choreiform movements involving both upper and lower limbs and an unsteady gait. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: A. No need for any radiological investigation
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In a 12-year-old child presenting with a standard uncomplicated Upper Respiratory Infection (URI) (common cold), routine radiological imaging is not required.

  • .A URI is a self-limiting viral infection affecting the upper airways (nasal passages, sinuses, pharynx, and larynx). The diagnosis is entirely clinical, based on typical symptoms like a runny nose, cough, sore throat, and low-grade fever.
  • The standard of care for an uncomplicated pediatric URI is supportive care (rest, hydration, and antipyretics if needed), not imaging.

HRCT (Option B) and CECT following CT (Option C): These modalities deliver high doses of ionizing radiation. They are reserved for complex, chronic lung diseases (like bronchiectasis or interstitial lung disease) or severe complications (like a lung abscess or empyema), none of which are present in a standard URI.

Chest radiograph (X-ray) (Option D): This is only indicated if a lower respiratory tract infection (like pneumonia) is suspected, signalled by respiratory distress or abnormal lung sounds. It is useless for a standard cold.



Reference:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10814200/

options.text: No need for any radiological investigation

question: Which of the following investigations is approved in a child aged 12 with an upper respiratory infection?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The presentation of fever, headache, confusion, and altered behavior (altered sensorium) is highly suggestive of encephalitis (inflammation of the brain parenchyma), which is more severe than meningitis.
  • The CSF findings of lymphocytic pleocytosis and normal glucose are typical for a viral process.
  • The classic radiological finding of bilateral temporal lobe hyperintensities on MRI is the most distinguishing feature, which is pathognomonic for Herpes Simplex Virus Type 1 (HSV-1) encephalitis. HSV-1 is the most common cause of fatal sporadic encephalitis worldwide and exhibits this characteristic temporal lobe tropism.

Incorrect Options:

  • Viral meningitis (Option A) would present with fever and headache but typically without confusion or altered behavior (normal sensorium), which indicates a process confined to the meninges.
  • Bacterial meningoencephalitis (Option B) is characterized by CSF findings of markedly elevated WBC, very high protein, and low CSF glucose.
  • Mollaret’s meningitis (Option D) is a rare, recurrent, benign form of aseptic meningitis, not the severe, focal, and often fatal encephalitis seen here.



Reference:
  • https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK557643/
question: A 12-year-old presents with 3 days of fever, headache, confusion, and altered behavior. CSF analysis shows WBC 150/µL (lymphocytic), protein 80 mg/dL, and glucose normal. MRI brain: hyperintensities in the temporal lobes. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Answer: B. Sliding Hiatal Hernia (Type I)

Explanation:

Hiatal Hernia:

  • Herniation of abdominal organs through the esophageal hiatus into the thoracic cavity. Commonly herniated organs include the stomach and esophagus.
  • Types of Hiatal Hernias:
    • Type I (Sliding Hiatal Hernia):
      • Most common (80-90% of cases).
      • The gastroesophageal junction (GEJ) and part of the stomach slide above the diaphragm.
      • On barium swallow, gastric rugae or the esophageal B ring (squamo-columnar junction) is seen above the diaphragm.
      • Present as gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD).
    • Type II (Paraesophageal Hernia):
      • The gastric fundus herniates above the diaphragm, but the GEJ remains below it.
      • Can progress to gastric volvulus, with risks of obstruction or infarction.
      • Best visualized on fluoroscopy or CT.
    • Type III: A combination of both sliding and paraesophageal elements, with both the GEJ and a portion of the stomach herniating above the diaphragm.
    • Type IV: Involves mixed type along with the herniation of other abdominal organs.

[[figure-1]]

  • Radiological Findings:
    • Plain radiographs: Hiatal hernias may appear as retrocardiac soft tissue opacities with or without air-fluid levels.
    • Barium swallow: Shows superior displacement of the GEJ in sliding hernias and the gastric fundus herniating through the hiatus in paraesophageal hernias.

Sliding Hiatal Hernia

[[figure-2]]

Paraesophageal Hernia

[[figure-3]]

  • High-resolution manometry: Gold standard for diagnosing small (<2cm) hiatal hernias.
  • CT: To detect larger hernias or complex cases involving multiple organs.
  • Endoscopy: Can reveal displacement of the GEJ and herniation of the stomach, confirming the diagnosis in larger hernias.



Reference:
  1. Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, A Textbook of Medical Imaging, 7th Edition, Page. 492, 493.
  2. Textbook of Radiology & Imaging by David Sutton, 8th Edition, Chapter 28, Mechanical Esophageal Disorders - Hernias.
question: A 55-year-old woman presents with complaints of chronic heartburn, regurgitation, and chest discomfort, especially after meals. A barium swallow study is performed, and the following radiograph is obtained. What is the most likely diagnosis based on the image findings?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Hirschsprung disease: Characterized by aganglionosis of the distal colon, typically presenting in neonates with failure to pass meconium. Radiographic findings show a narrow aganglionic segment with proximal dilatation.


Hirschsprung Disease

  • Hirschsprung disease is characterized by the absence of ganglion cells (aganglionosis) in the distal colon and rectum.
  • This condition may result from a failure of neural crest neuroblasts to migrate into bowel segments or the degeneration of already migrated neuroblasts. It impacts both the myenteric and submucosal plexuses.
  • Hirschsprung disease typically presents in term neonates with failure to pass meconium within 1-2 days after birth. About 75% of cases present within the first 6 weeks, and over 90% present by age 5, though rare adult cases occur.
  • In delayed cases with constipation, manometry can help differentiate short/ultrashort segment Hirschsprung from other causes.
  • Definitive diagnosis is made via full-thickness rectal biopsy (taken 2 cm above the dentate line).


Radiologic Findings for Hirschsprung Disease:

  • Plain Radiograph:
    • Findings resemble bowel obstruction with a smaller caliber affected bowel and varying degrees of colonic distension.
    • Severe cases may lead to dilatation, enterocolitis, and perforation.
  • Fluoroscopy (Contrast Enema):
    • Essential for diagnosis and determining bowel involvement.
    • Shows a narrow aganglionic segment with proximal dilatation and a saw-tooth pattern.
    • Delayed evacuation of contrast and the transition zone is depicted but not accurate for ganglion cell presence.
  • Ultrasound:
    • Can reveal fetal colonic dilatation in some cases.



Toxic Megacolon (Option B ruled out):

  • Acute complications associated with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and less commonly with infectious colitis and other colitides; characterized by severe colonic dilatation and risk of perforation due to loss of neurogenic tone.
  • Radiographic Features:
    • Plain Radiograph: Transverse colon dilated to at least 6 cm (3-6-9 rule); signs of pneumoperitoneum may indicate perforation.
    • CT Scan: Shows loss of haustral markings, pseudopolyps, thumbprinting, and pericolic fat stranding due to mucosal edema.
    • Barium studies and colonoscopy are contraindicated due to perforation risk.


Crohn's disease (Option C): A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any gastrointestinal tract area. It usually presents in older children and adults with abdominal pain and diarrhea, not typically causing meconium passage issues in neonates.


Ulcerative colitis (Option D): Primarily affects the colon, leading to symptoms like bloody diarrhea and abdominal pain. It generally occurs in older children and adults and does not present with the specific failure to pass meconium seen in Hirschsprung disease.



Reference:
  1. radiopaedia.org/articles/hirschsprung-disease
  2. radiopaedia.org/articles/toxic-megacolon
question: A term neonate presents with failure to pass meconium within the first 48 hours of life. Imaging shows a narrow distal bowel segment with proximal colonic dilatation. The Barium Enema image of the neonate is given below. What is the most likely condition affecting this neonate?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical scenario describes skip lesions, cobblestone appearance, and asymmetric mural thickening with deep ulcers, which are hallmark features of Crohn’s disease.
  • The string sign of Kantor is seen in Crohn’s disease and refers to the beaded, string-like appearance of the bowel due to multifocal narrowing from strictures.

Crohn’s Disease

Ulcerative Colitis
  • Skip lesions; ileum and caecum involved; rectum relatively spared.
  • Transmural; leads to ulceration, fissures, abscesses.
  • Bowel wall may be affected asymmetrically with sacculations.
  • Continuous colonic involvement; rectal in 95% of cases.
  • Mucosal and submucosal; less severe.
  • Fissure and abscess are not common.
  • Circumferential bowel wall symmetry is usually maintained.

1. Fluoroscopy (Barium Studies)

  • Mucosal abnormalities: Thickened, nodular folds and a "cobblestone" pattern due to a combination of longitudinal and transverse ulcers.
  • Aphthous ulcers: Appear as areas of barium collection within the swollen mucosa.
  • Shows deep ulcers, fistulae (e.g., enteroenteric, enterocolonic), and sinus tracts.
  • Chronic disease features: Strictures, stenosis, and wall sacculations.
  • String sign of Kantor: A beaded string-like appearance due to multifocal bowel narrowing from strictures.

2. Ultrasonography

  • Concentric mural thickening of the bowel wall.
  • Hyperemia within the inflamed segments.
  • Increased echogenicity of surrounding fat.

3. CT and MRI Enterography

  • Asymmetric Mural thickening
  • Ulcerations: Seen as air or contrast extending into the bowel wall.
  • Strictures
  • Mesenteric changes:
    • Comb sign: Engorgement of the vasa recta.
    • Mesenteric fat stranding, edema, and reactive adenopathy.
  • MRI-specific findings:
    • T2 hyperintense signal: Indicates mural edema, best seen with fat-saturated sequences.
    • Diffusion restriction: Suggestive of active inflammation.
    • Active inflammation shows hyperenhancement in arterial and post-contrast phases.

1. Radiographs

  • Bowel perforation and toxic megacolon: Radiographs (upright and supine) help screen for these conditions.
    • Toxic megacolon: Detected by colonic distension >6 cm, typically in the transverse colon.

Fig. Toxic megacolon in Ulcerative colitis

  • Other findings: Air-fluid levels, loss of colonic haustrations, mucosal islands, and absence of formed stool.

2. Fluoroscopy (Barium Enema)

  • Mucosal abnormalities: Granular and stippled mucosa, with superficial erosions and ulcers.
    • Collar button ulcers: Deeper ulcers extending into the submucosa. (Option B ruled out)
    • Pseudopolyps
  • Chronic disease features:
    • Lead pipe colon: Luminal narrowing and loss of haustrations in the colon. (Option A & C ruled out)
    • Patulous ileocecal valve (IC valve): With granular terminal ileum, indicative of backwash ileitis.

3. CT and MRI Enterography

  • Active phase:
    • Mural hyperenhancement:
    • Concentric mural thickening with stratification.
    • Submucosal edema: Seen as T2 hyperintensity on MRI.
    • Pseudopolyps
  • Chronic phase:
    • Lead pipe colon: Concentric mural thickening with luminal narrowing and loss of haustrations.
    • Submucosal fat deposition
    • Presacral space widening due to perirectal fat.
    • Post Inflammatory pseudopolyps

Comb Sign in active Crohn’s disease

Leadpipe appearance in Ulcerative colitis

String sign of Kantor and rectovaginal fistula

Inflammatory Pseudopolyps



Reference:

David Sutton Textbook of Radiology and Imaging, Volume 1, 8th edition, Page 2226- 2247
question: A 40-year-old male presents with abdominal pain, weight loss, and chronic diarrhea. Radiologic studies reveal skip lesions in the ileum and cecum with a cobblestone appearance and deep ulcers. Which of the following radiologic signs is most consistent with this patient's diagnosis?

correctAnswer: B. Uniform thickening of the entire colon
explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B) Uniform thickening of the entire colon

Explanation:

  • The patient's features including chronic abdominal pain, fever, and weight loss, with a history of exposure to tuberculosis and the small bowel follow-through image showing a circumferential mass effect at the ileocecal valve are characteristic of ileocecal tuberculosis.
  • In ileocecal tuberculosis, there is typically localized thickening (circumferential) rather than uniform thickening of the entire colon.

Ileocecal Tuberculosis:

  • Tubercular bacilli enter the GI tract via infected sputum or milk, leading to mucosal invasion and formation of tubercles in lymphoid tissue.
  • The ileocecal region is most commonly affected due to its abundant lymphoid tissue, with isolated colonic involvement in about 10% of cases, particularly in immunocompromised individuals.
  • Symptoms include chronic abdominal pain, fever, weight loss, and altered bowel habits.
  • Common complications are bowel obstruction and perforation.
  • Differential Diagnosis includes Crohn’s disease, lymphoma, amoebiasis, and cecal malignancy.

Imaging Features of Ileocecal Tuberculosis:

  • Radiographs: May show enteroliths, bowel obstruction with air-fluid levels, and signs of pneumoperitoneum in cases of perforation.
  • Small bowel follow-through:
    • Spasm and edema at the ileocecal valve and terminal ileum, leading to thickening and ulceration. (Option A)
    • Stierlin Sign: Rapid barium emptying in inflamed segments with normal barium column in adjacent segments. (Option D)
    • Features like hypersegmentation (chicken intestine), flocculation, and precipitation may be seen.
    • The inflammation and involvement of the cecum can lead to structural changes, resulting in retraction or elevation of the cecum, which is known as “Pulled up cecum”

[[figure-1]]

  • Contrast-enhanced CT:
    • Circumferential thickening of the terminal ileum and cecum and asymmetric thickening of the ileocecal valve.
    • Pathognomonic associated mesenteric adenopathy (Option C) with characteristic central low attenuation due to caseous necrosis.
    • Chronic stages may present multifocal strictures and diffuse narrowing, with signs like the Fleischner or inverted umbrella sign (thickened ileocecal valve lips with narrowed terminal ileum).






Reference:
  1. David Sutton Textbook of Radiology and Imaging, Volume 1, 8th edition, Page 2254- 2258
  2. Ileocecal tuberculosis | Radiology Reference Article | Radiopaedia.org

options.text: Spasm and edema at the ileocecal valve
Uniform thickening of the entire colon
Stierlin Sign with rapid barium emptying

question: A 35-year-old male presents to the emergency department with chronic abdominal pain, fever, and unintentional weight loss over the past month. He reports altered bowel habits and has a history of exposure to individuals with tuberculosis. A small bowel follow-through imaging is provided below. Based on the clinical presentation and the attached imaging, which of the following features is not typically seen in the patient?

correctAnswer: B. Maintains a colonic haustral pattern
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Sigmoid volvulus is characterized by a twisting of the sigmoid colon, leading to obstruction of the distal large bowel and resulting in a distended abdomen.
  • The "coffee-bean sign" is an X-ray feature that shows a distended sigmoid loop with an inverted U shape, indicative of the condition.
  • Sigmoid volvulus typically has an ahaustral appearance, whereas maintaining a colonic haustral pattern is a feature of cecal volvulus.

Sigmoid Volvulus

Caecal Volvulus
  • Sigmoid volvulus arises in the pelvis, specifically the left lower quadrant. (Option A ruled out)
  • It extends towards the right upper quadrant.
  • It has an ahaustral appearance (lack of haustra).
  • Causes obstruction of the distal large bowel, leading to dilation of the ascending, transverse, and descending colon.
  • A few gas-fluid levels may be seen.
  • Coffee-Bean Sign: The condition is characterized by a distended sigmoid loop with an inverted U shape, known as the coffee-bean sign (or kidney bean sign). (Option D ruled out)
  • Whirlpool Sign: The whirl, or whirlpool sign is observed when the bowel rotates around its mesentery, resulting in whirls of the mesenteric vessels. (Option C ruled out)
  • The torsion is located in the ascending colon above the ileocecal valve.
  • Caecal volvulus arises in the right lower quadrant.
  • It extends towards the epigastrium or left upper quadrant.
  • The colonic haustral pattern is maintained.
  • The distal colon is usually collapsed, and the small bowel is distended.
  • One gas-fluid level may be seen.
  • Definitive Sign: Upward displacement of the appendix and obstruction of the large bowel is a definitive sign of cecal volvulus.
  • May show a U-shaped distended bowel segment and signs of ischemia, including mural thickening, infiltration of the mesenteric fat, and pneumatosis intestinalis.
  • Whirlpool Sign: A whirl sign may be apparent due to tight torsion of the mesentery from a twist between the afferent and efferent loops.
  • Coffee Bean Appearance: A "coffee bean" appearance may be seen in a loop of transverse colon.
  • Bird's Beak Sign: Abrupt cut-off with “bird's beak” tapering at the distal cecum is characteristic.
  • Central appendix sign: Abnormal appendix position near midline.
[[figure-1]] [[figure-2]]




Reference:
  1. radiopaedia.org/articles/sigmoid-volvulus-vs-caecal-volvulus-1
  2. emedicine.medscape.com/article/373585-overview
  3. emedicine.medscape.com/article/364967-overview#a1

options.text: Arises in the pelvis, specifically the left lower quadrant

question: A 60-year-old female presents to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain, bloating, and vomiting. On examination, her abdomen is distended, and bowel sounds are decreased. A radiograph abdomen of the patient is given below. Which of the following is not a feature of the patient’s condition?

correctAnswer: B. Maintains a colonic haustral pattern
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The abdominal radiograph demonstrates a sigmoid volvulus, characterised by a massively dilated loop of sigmoid colon forming the classic coffee-bean sign.

  • The loop typically arises from the left lower quadrant, extends toward the right upper quadrant, and has an ahaustral appearance due to marked colonic distension.
  • On CT, twisting of the sigmoid mesentery produces the characteristic whirl sign, representing rotation of the bowel and mesenteric vessels.

Sigmoid Volvulus

Caecal Volvulus
  • Originates in the left lower quadrant (Option A) (pelvis)
  • Markedly dilated ahaustral sigmoid loop
  • Coffee-bean (kidney-bean) sign (Option D) on plain radiography
  • Bird's beak sign at the site of torsion on contrast studies or CT
  • Whirl sign (Option C) on CT due to twisting of the mesentery and mesenteric vessels
  • Arises from the right lower quadrant
  • Dilated cecum is displaced toward the left upper quadrant or epigastrium
  • Haustral folds are often preserved
[[figure-1]] [[figure-2]]




Reference:
  1. http://radiopaedia.org/articles/sigmoid-volvulus-vs-caecal-volvulus-1
  2. http://emedicine.medscape.com/article/373585-overview
  3. http://emedicine.medscape.com/article/364967-overview#a1

options.text: Arises in the pelvis, specifically the left lower quadrant

question: A 60-year-old woman presents with severe abdominal pain, abdominal distension, and vomiting. Examination reveals a distended abdomen with decreased bowel sounds. The abdominal radiograph is shown above. Which of the following is not a feature of this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Intussusception occurs when one segment of the bowel telescopes into another, often due to a lead point, such as a lymphoma in this case.
  • The ultrasound findings showing a target sign are classic for intussusception.
  • The patient's symptoms of severe abdominal pain, vomiting, and currant jelly stools further support this diagnosis.


Plain Radiograph:

  • Elongated soft tissue mass in the upper right quadrant.
  • Bowel obstruction with air-fluid levels and proximal bowel dilation.
  • Possible absence of gas in the distal collapsed bowel.


Fluoroscopy:

  • Gold standard is the contrast enema, showing the intussusception as an occluding mass.
  • Characteristic "coiled spring sign."

[[figure-1]]

Fig. Coiled spring sign


Ultrasound:

  • Target sign (doughnut sign)- Concentric alternating echogenic and hypoechoic bands are observed, where the echogenic bands represent the serosa and submucosa, flanking the hypoechoic muscularis propria.

[[figure-2]]

  • Pseudokidney sign- Longitudinal ultrasound appearance of the intussuscepted segment of bowel which mimics a kidney

[[figure-3]]

  • Crescent in a doughnut sign.
  • Absence of blood flow in the intussusceptum (contraindication for enema).
  • Features favoring ileocolic intussusception: hyperechoic core, thicker outer hypoechoic wall, larger anteroposterior diameter, and presence of lymph nodes.
  • CT Scan:
    • Characteristic "bowel-within-bowel" configuration.
    • Concentric rings of bowel on axial images, and sausage-shaped mass on longitudinal images.
    • Visualization of the lead point if present, with surrounding mesenteric fat and vessels.


Acute Appendicitis (Option A): Typically presents with right lower quadrant pain, nausea, and fever. It wouldn't show a target sign on imaging, and currant jelly stools are not associated with this condition.


Sigmoid Volvulus (Option C): Involves twisting of the sigmoid colon, presenting with abdominal distension and constipation. It would show a "coffee bean" sign rather than a target sign.


Cecal Volvulus (Option D): Similar to sigmoid volvulus, but involves the cecum. It typically shows signs of obstruction like “bird beak sign” but not the target sign on ultrasound.



Reference:

radiopaedia.org/articles/intussusception
question: A 7-year-old girl with a known H/o lymphoma is brought to the ER for evaluation of severe abdominal pain and intermittent vomiting. Her parents report that she has recently passed currant jelly stools. O/E, a palpable abdominal mass is noted in the RUQ. An abdominal ultrasound is given below. Based on the clinical presentation and the ultrasound findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Small bowel obstruction is characterized by the accumulation of gas and fluid in the intestine due to a blockage. The string of pearls sign, which appears as a row of small gas bubbles along the bowel wall, is virtually diagnostic of this condition, particularly in the context of the patient's symptoms.

String of Pearls Sign:

  • The string of pearls sign consists of a row of small gas bubbles in the abdomen, typically seen obliquely or horizontally.
  • These gas bubbles are trapped along the superior wall of the small bowel, between the valvulae conniventes.
  • The inferior margins of the bubbles have an ovoid appearance due to the meniscal effect of intraluminal fluid.
  • It can be observed on upright or decubitus abdominal radiographs and on CT scans.
  • Clinical Significance: When present in the appropriate clinical context, it is virtually diagnostic of small bowel obstruction.
  • Other Conditions: It may also be seen very rarely in adynamic ileus, acute gastroenteritis, and saline catharsis. (Options A, C & D ruled out)
  • Adynamic ileus:
    • Unlike a mechanical obstruction, where there is a physical blockage in the intestines, adynamic ileus results from impaired neural or muscular activity of the gut.
    • Abdominal X-rays or CT scans show diffuse bowel dilation without specific air-fluid levels or a transition point, which distinguishes ileus from mechanical bowel obstruction.
  • Fibromuscular Dysplasia (FMD): This non-atherosclerotic, non-inflammatory disease of blood vessels (often affecting renal or carotid arteries) produces alternating stenotic and aneurysmal segments, leading to a classic "string of beads" appearance on angiography.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Mesenteric ischemia (Option A): This condition presents with severe abdominal pain and distension due to reduced blood flow to the intestines. However, it usually does not show the characteristic air-fluid levels seen in small bowel obstruction and may include signs of ischemia.

Acute gastroenteritis (Option C): Unlikely, as it often presents with hyperactive bowel sounds, diarrhea, and cramping rather than the severe pain and diminished bowel sounds seen here.

Saline catharsis (Option D): Unlikely, as it typically causes loose stools and abdominal cramping but not severe abdominal pain or radiographic findings of distension.




Reference:
  1. String of pearls sign (gastrointestinal) | Radiology Reference Article
  2. David Sutton Textbook of Radiology and Imaging, Volume 1, 8th edition, Page 2268
question: A 45-year-old male presents to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain, vomiting, and a distended abdomen. On examination, his bowel sounds are diminished. An abdominal radiograph is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient based on the given findings?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • This patient’s symptoms of colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, distension, and the presence of high-pitched bowel sounds are characteristic of a mechanical obstruction.
  • The radiographic findings show dilated loops of the bowel with valculae conniventes, suggestive of small bowel obstruction.
  • The small bowel loops are identified by their location in the central abdomen and their smaller diameter (3–5 cm).
  • Additionally, the presence of previous abdominal surgery is a risk factor for adhesions, which are the most common cause of small bowel obstruction.

Large bowel obstruction (Option B): Typically shows more peripheral bowel dilatation, with larger loop diameters (usually >6 cm), and haustral folds that do not completely extend across the bowel lumen.

Sigmoid volvulus (Option C): This presents with the "coffee bean" sign on abdominal X-ray and is associated with large bowel obstruction, often seen in elderly patients. The absence of such a sign and the presence of small bowel dilatation make this unlikely.

Fig. Coffee bean with Coffee bean sign

Paralytic ileus (Option D): In paralytic ileus, the X-ray typically shows diffuse bowel dilatation without clear air-fluid levels. The high-pitched bowel sounds and specific dilated loops of the small bowel point toward a mechanical obstruction rather than a functional one.

question:
A 65-year-old male presents with colicky abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, and absolute constipation for the past 48 hours. He has a history of prior abdominal surgery. On physical examination, his abdomen is distended with high-pitched bowel sounds. An abdominal X-ray is obtained and shows the following features.

What is the most likely diagnosis based on the clinical presentation and radiographic findings?

explanationHtml:
Answer: C. Jejunal Atresia

Explanation:

Jejunal atresia is characterized by a "triple bubble" sign on an abdominal X-ray.

  • This appearance results from gas trapped in three distended proximal bowel loops: the stomach, duodenum, and proximal jejunum, with no distal gas beyond the atresia.
  • This condition is caused by intrauterine vascular insult leading to segmental bowel absence or occlusion.

Various Bubble signs of the abdomen:

Condition

Radiological Sign

Explanation

Normal Abdomen

Single bubble in the stomach

A single air bubble seen in the left upper quadrant corresponds to the fundus of the stomach. A large single bubble is seen in cases of pyloric atresia, GOO.

Pyloric Atresia (Option A)

"Single bubble" sign

A single distended stomach with no air in the small bowel or beyond, caused by obstruction at the pylorus.

Duodenal Atresia

(Option B)

"Double bubble" sign

Distended stomach and proximal duodenum; no distal bowel gas due to obstruction at the duodenum.

Jejunal Atresia

(Option C)

"Triple bubble" sign

Three distended loops of bowel (stomach, duodenum, proximal jejunum) with no distal gas.

Ileal Atresia

(Option D)

Multiple air-fluid levels

Dilated small bowel loops with air-fluid levels and no gas in the large intestine, more distal than jejunal atresia.

question:
A 1-day-old neonate presents with bilious vomiting and abdominal distension. An abdominal X-ray is performed and is given below.

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Answer: A. Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia (Bochdalek type)

Explanation:

The given chest x-ray shows loops of bowel in the right thoracic cavity, mediastinal shift to the left, and decreased right lung aeration, which is consistent with Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia.

[[figure-1]]

Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia (CDH):

  1. CDH is the intrathoracic herniation of abdominal contents due to congenital defects in the diaphragm.
  2. Types of CDH:
    • Bochdalek Hernia: Occurs through the posterolateral pleuroperitoneal canal, most commonly on the left side.
    • Morgagni Hernia: Anterior hernia located at the right cardiophrenic angle.

[[figure-2]]

Fig. Schematic representation of CDH

  1. Radiologic Features:
    • Chest Radiograph (CXR):
      • Bochdalek hernia: Dome-shaped soft tissue opacity in the posterolateral thorax, often left-sided.
      • May show gas-filled bowel loops or fat content in the thoracic cavity.
      • Mediastinal shift away from the herniation due to mass effect.
      • On the lateral view, hernias appear above the posterior costophrenic recess.
    • CT/MRI:
      • Visualizes herniation of fat, bowel, spleen, or kidney through a diaphragmatic defect.
      • Important for distinguishing from other masses like cystic adenomatoid malformation or pericardial cyst.
      • CT provides clearer differentiation of soft-tissue or fatty mass protruding through the diaphragm.
  2. Complications:
    • Associated with hypoplasia of the ipsilateral lung, leading to respiratory distress, especially in neonates.
    • Neonates may present with respiratory distress and mediastinal deviation.

Esophageal atresia with tracheoesophageal fistula (Option B):

  • The primary abnormality may show air in the esophagus or stomach (if a fistula is present) and sometimes an absence of gas in the abdomen if there is no fistula.
  • This condition doesn't present with bowel loops in the thorax or a large diaphragmatic defect.

Pulmonary sequestration (Option C):

  • It presents as a mass in the lower lobe of the lung, often with an abnormal vascular supply seen on advanced imaging like CT angiography.
  • No bowel loops or significant mediastinal shift would be seen.

Congenital pulmonary airway malformation (CPAM) (Option D) appears as cystic masses within the lung, but the cysts are within the lung parenchyma, not abdominal contents in the thorax.



Reference:
  1. Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, A Textbook of Medical Imaging, 7th Edition, Page. 62, 63.
  2. Textbook of Radiology & Imaging by David Sutton, 8th Edition, Chapter 14: Pleura, Diaphragm, and Chest Wall - The Diaphragm - Hernias of the Diaphragm.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The radiological finding shown is a thin, smooth, circumferential narrowing at the distal esophagus, which is characteristic of a Schatzki ring. It causes intermittent dysphagia and is often seen in older adults.

[[figure-1]]

Esophageal Rings:

Types:

A Rings

B Rings

C Rings
  • Muscular rings formed due to hypertrophy of smooth muscle in the distal esophagus.
  • Covered in squamous epithelium.
  • Transient and result from active muscle contraction.
  • Asymptomatic and incidentally noted during esophagography.
  • Lower esophageal rings - fixed, mucosal rings located at the squamocolumnar junction.
  • Commonly found just above a hiatal hernia.
  • Symptomatic B rings - Schatzki Rings (diameter <13 mm) may cause dysphagia, especially when food passes through the narrowed area.
  • Located distal to the squamocolumnar junction.
  • Covered by squamous epithelium.
  • Least common and asymptomatic.
  • Represent diaphragmatic indentation of the esophagus

Imaging Features:

  • Best visualized on esophagography (barium swallow) with full barium distension of the esophagus.
  • A rings appear superior to B rings.
  • B rings present as concentric, fixed narrowing, seen during a barium swallow in the right anterior oblique position.

[[figure-2]]

Fig. Esophageal rings

Plummer-Vinson syndrome (Option B):

  • It is associated with esophageal webs in the upper esophagus, not lower, along with iron deficiency anemia.
  • The barium swallow in this condition usually shows a web-like filling defect in the cervical esophagus rather than a ring at the gastroesophageal junction.

Diffuse esophageal spasm (Option C):

  • It is characterized by uncoordinated, simultaneous contractions of the esophagus.
  • On a barium swallow, this typically produces a "corkscrew" appearance rather than a circumferential ring-like narrowing.

Achalasia (Option D):

  • It involves failure of the lower esophageal sphincter to relax, leading to progressive dysphagia for both solids and liquids.
  • Radiologically, a barium swallow shows a "bird-beak" appearance in the distal esophagus and dilatation of the proximal esophagus.

  • Wall thickening ranges from 5 to 15 mm

question: A 55-year-old patient presents with progressive dysphagia, initially for solids and later for liquids. A barium swallow study is performed, and two different radiographic findings are shown below. Which of the following statements correctly differentiates between these images?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The radiological image shows a diverticulum arising from the midline of the posterior wall of the distal pharynx. This is the characteristic radiological finding of a Zenker's diverticulum on a barium swallow examination.


Zenker’s Diverticulum- Radiological Findings:

Imaging Modality

Key Findings

Barium Swallow (Fluoroscopy)
  • Diverticulum arising from the midline of the posterior wall of the distal pharynx
  • Located near the pharyngoesophageal junction
  • Best identified during swallowing
  • Best seen on lateral view
  • Typically noted at the C5-6 level
  • May be transient (referred to as a "pharyngeal pouch")

Additional Findings
  • ~90% of patients also show a hiatal hernia and gastro-esophageal reflux
  • The distended sac may compress the cervical esophagus

question: A 58-year-old man presents to the emergency department with acute onset of severe abdominal pain and distension. An abdominal X-ray is performed, showing free air in the peritoneal cavity. Which of the following signs represents free air outlining the lateral umbilical ligaments?

question:
A 72-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of severe abdominal pain and distension. An upright chest X-ray is performed, showing the following finding:

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis based on this radiographic finding?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • In this clinical scenario, the presence of free air under the right hemidiaphragm on an erect chest X-ray suggests pneumoperitoneum, which commonly indicates a perforated viscus, such as a peptic ulcer.
  • The cupola sign and Rigler’s sign further support the diagnosis, as they reveal free gas and an outline of the bowel wall.
  • Chilaiditi sign represents a pseudo-pneumoperitoneum where the intestine (usually colon) is interposed between the liver and diaphragm, mimicking free air but not representing true pneumoperitoneum. Therefore, it must not be present in this scenario.

[[figure-1]]

Fig. Chailaiditi sign

Pneumoperitoneum

  • Pneumoperitoneum refers to the presence of free gas in the peritoneal cavity, typically indicating a perforated viscus (e.g., perforated peptic ulcer).
  • Causes:
    • Common: Perforated peptic ulcers, bowel obstruction, inflammatory conditions, ischemia, injury during colonoscopy.
    • Other causes without peritonitis: Postoperative (up to 7 days), peritoneal dialysis, sealed perforation, and tracking from pneumomediastinum.
  • Diagnosis on Imaging:
    • Erect CXR: Free gas seen under the right hemidiaphragm (cupola sign), difficult to differentiate on the left due to gastric or colonic gas. (Option A & C ruled out)
    • Supine AXR: Right upper quadrant gas in the perihepatic, subhepatic space, Morrison’s pouch, and ligament visualization (e.g., falciform ligament).
    • Rigler’s Sign: Visualization of both sides of the bowel wall due to surrounding gas. (Option B ruled out)
    • CT Scan: Most sensitive; small volumes of gas seen in the liver or peritoneal recesses, often using broad window settings.
  • Pseudo-pneumoperitoneum: Conditions mimicking free gas such as Chilaiditi syndrome (intestine between liver and diaphragm), subphrenic abscess, or subdiaphragmatic fat.
  • Pneumoperitoneum may be clinically silent, especially in elderly, steroid-treated, unconscious, or critically ill patients.




Reference:

Grainger and Allison’s Textbook of Diagnostic Radiology, 7th edition, Page 463-465

question: A 65-year-old man presents with sudden, severe abdominal pain and a rigid abdomen. He has a history of peptic ulcer disease. An erect chest X-ray is given below. Which of the following radiological signs is NOT expected in this case?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The invertogram is crucial for assessing the most distal level of the bowel in male patients with imperforate anus, particularly when meconium is present on the perineum without an apparent perineal fistula. Proper positioning is essential for accurate evaluation.


Invertogram

  • Used to classify anal atresia in neonates by visualizing the distance between the gas bubble in the terminal colon and the perineal skin.
  • Typically performed 24 hours after birth to allow for small fistulas to become apparent.
  • The newborn is inverted from the lower limbs, with careful positioning to avoid hip and shoulder rotation.
  • Remove any radiopaque items and ensure the X-ray is taken during full inspiration.
  • Can cause discomfort and crying, which may lead to misleading results; a prone cross-table lateral view can be a more comfortable alternative.

[[figure-1]]

Invertogram image showing anal atresia


Plain abdominal X-ray (Option A): While useful for ruling out esophageal atresia and other anomalies, it does not provide specific information about the anatomy or level of the anorectal malformation.


Abdominal ultrasound (Option C): This is important for evaluating hydrocolpos and hydronephrosis in females with cloacal anomalies but does not assess the anorectal malformation itself.


Distal colostogram (Option D): This test can evaluate the distal bowel but is typically performed after a colostomy has been created, making it less relevant for initial assessment in a newborn with an imperforate anus.

question: A newborn is diagnosed with an anorectal malformation (imperforate anus) on physical examination. Given the high association with VACTERL anomalies, the medical team decides to conduct a series of radiographic studies to assess for potential associated conditions. Which of the following is a key imaging modality in the evaluation of a neonate with imperforate anus?

correctAnswer: A. Large bowel obstruction due to sigmoid volvulus
explanationHtml:
The Omega sign, coffee bean sign, or bent tube sign on a plain abdominal X-ray is classic for sigmoid volvulus. It results from twisting of the sigmoid colon, leading to a large, dilated, U-shaped loop with an apex pointing toward the diaphragm.

Sigmoid volvulus is common in elderly patients, especially those with a history of chronic constipation or conditions like scoliosis, which may cause colonic redundancy or altered anatomy.

Sigmoid Volvulus

Caecal Volvulus
  • Sigmoid volvulus arises in the pelvis, specifically the left lower quadrant.
  • It extends towards the right upper quadrant.
  • It has an ahaustral appearance (lack of haustra).
  • Causes obstruction of the distal large bowel, leading to dilation of the ascending, transverse, and descending colon.
  • A few gas-fluid levels may be seen.
  • Coffee-Bean Sign: The condition is characterized by a distended sigmoid loop with an inverted U shape, known as the coffee-bean sign (or kidney bean sign).
  • Whirlpool Sign: The whirl, or whirlpool sign is observed when the bowel rotates around its mesentery, resulting in whirls of the mesenteric vessels.
  • The torsion is located in the ascending colon above the ileocecal valve.
  • Caecal volvulus arises in the right lower quadrant.
  • It extends towards the epigastrium or left upper quadrant.
  • The colonic haustral pattern is maintained.
  • The distal colon is usually collapsed, and the small bowel is distended.
  • One gas-fluid level may be seen.
  • Definitive Sign: Upward displacement of the appendix and obstruction of the large bowel is a definitive sign of cecal volvulus.
  • May show a U-shaped distended bowel segment and signs of ischemia, including mural thickening, infiltration of the mesenteric fat, and pneumatosis intestinalis.
  • Whirlpool Sign: A whirl sign may be apparent due to tight torsion of the mesentery from a twist between the afferent and efferent loops.
  • Coffee Bean Appearance: A "coffee bean" appearance may be seen in a loop of transverse colon.
  • Bird's Beak Sign: Abrupt cut-off with “bird's beak” tapering at the distal cecum is characteristic.
  • Central appendix sign: Abnormal appendix position near midline.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Large bowel obstruction due to faecolith (Option B): This is incorrect because faecoliths are typically seen as radio-opaque masses in the colon and do not produce the characteristic "coffee bean sign."

Cecal volvulus (Option C): This is incorrect because cecal volvulus shows a dilated cecum displaced to the midline or left upper quadrant, not the classic U-shaped appearance of sigmoid volvulus.

Small bowel obstruction due to bowel perforation (Option D): This is incorrect because small bowel obstruction typically shows multiple air-fluid levels and dilated loops of the small intestine. A perforation would present with free air under the diaphragm on an upright X-ray, not a coffee bean sign.



Reference:
  1. Sigmoid volvulus vs cecal volvulus | Radiology Reference Article | Radiopaedia.org
  2. Sigmoid Volvulus Imaging
  3. Cecal Volvulus Imaging and Diagnosis: Practice Essentials, Radiography, Computed Tomography

Large bowel obstruction due to faecolith

Intestinal obstruction (Option B):

  • Typically presents with dilated bowel loops confined to the abdominal cavity.
  • Does not involve bowel loops appearing in the chest on imaging.

Pleural effusion (Option C):

  • Characterized by fluid collection in the pleural space.
  • May show blunting of the costophrenic angle or fluid layering but no bowel loops.

Pneumonia (Option D):

  • Presents as patchy or lobar opacities in the lung parenchyma.
  • Does not involve bowel loops in the thoracic cavity.

question: Which of the following images accurately represents the medical condition described in the given scenario?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Intussusception is a medical condition in which one segment of the intestine telescopes into another segment, causing an obstruction.
  • In a barium enema procedure (as shown in the image), intussusception may appear as a characteristic ‘claw sign’ appearance, where the affected segment of the intestine invaginates into the adjacent segment. This is due to the filling defect it creates for the enema.

Intussusception

  • Intussusception occurs when one segment of the bowel is pulled into another, often leading to bowel obstruction and ischemia.
  • It is a common cause of acute abdomen in children, while in adults, it is typically associated with a focal lesion acting as a lead point.
  • The classic clinical presentation of intussusception in children may include intermittent abdominal pain, vomiting, and a palpable "sausage-like" mass in the right upper quadrant, although these symptoms occur in less than 20% of cases.
  • Parents may also report "currant jelly" stools, indicating bowel ischemia, and approximately 15% of patients may present without abdominal pain.
  • Plain Radiograph:
    • Elongated soft tissue mass in the upper right quadrant.
    • Bowel obstruction with air-fluid levels and proximal bowel dilation.
    • Possible absence of gas in the distal collapsed bowel.
  • Fluoroscopy:
    • Gold standard is the contrast enema, showing the intussusception as an occluding mass.
    • Characteristic "coiled spring sign."

[[figure-1]]

Fig. Coiled spring sign

  • Ultrasound:
    • Target sign (doughnut sign)- Concentric alternating echogenic and hypoechoic bands are observed, where the echogenic bands represent the serosa and submucosa, flanking the hypoechoic muscularis propria.

[[figure-2]]

  • Pseudokidney sign- Longitudinal ultrasound appearance of the intussuscepted segment of bowel which mimics a kidney

[[figure-3]]

  • Crescent in a doughnut sign.
  • Absence of blood flow in the intussusceptum (contraindication for enema).
  • Features favoring ileocolic intussusception: hyperechoic core, thicker outer hypoechoic wall, larger anteroposterior diameter, and presence of lymph nodes.
  • CT Scan:
    • Characteristic "bowel-within-bowel" configuration.
    • Concentric rings of bowel on axial images, and sausage-shaped mass on longitudinal images.
    • Visualization of the lead point if present, with surrounding mesenteric fat and vessels.

Volvulus (Option B) refers to the twisting or rotation of a portion of the intestine, leading to obstruction of the blood supply and potential bowel strangulation. In a barium enema, volvulus may appear as a characteristic "bird's beak" or "corkscrew" appearance.

Diverticulitis (Option C) is the inflammation or infection of small pouches called diverticula that can develop in the colon. During a barium enema, diverticulitis may present as localized outpouching or sac-like structures filled with barium. Inflammation and thickening of the bowel wall may be visible, and in severe cases, abscesses or fistulas may be observed.

Ulcerative Colitis (Option D) is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease that primarily affects the colon and rectum. In a barium enema, ulcerative colitis may show diffuse inflammation and ulceration of the colonic mucosa. The bowel wall may appear thickened, with loss of haustral markings (the characteristic folds of the colon) and a coarse or granular appearance. The extent and severity of the disease can be evaluated using barium enema imaging.



Reference:

Grainger and Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page no: 678

question: Which of the options below represents a characteristic observed in cases of large bowel obstruction?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical scenario and the X-ray findings of dilated bowel loops with visible valvulae conniventes suggest small bowel obstruction involving the jejunum.

question: A patient presents with abdominal pain and distension. An X-ray was taken which showed dilated bowel loops as given in the image below. Identify the segment involved.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • In the given scenario, the best investigation to be used in the emergency room is FAST (Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma).
  • FAST is a rapid bedside ultrasound examination that is commonly used in the emergency setting to evaluate patients with suspected abdominal or thoracic trauma.
  • It is a non-invasive and relatively quick procedure that can provide valuable information about potential injuries and guide further management.

FAST (Focused Abdominal Sonography for Trauma) and eFAST (Extended FAST):

  • Purpose: Assess for free fluid in the abdominal cavity, thoracic cavities, and pericardium.
  • Nature of Injury: Not used to determine the specific nature or extent of injury.
  • Advantages:
    • Rapid, reproducible, portable, and non-invasive bedside test.
    • Can be performed simultaneously with resuscitation.
    • Accurate at detecting >100 mL of free blood.
  • Limitations:
    • Operator-dependent and may be unreliable in obese patients or when the bowel is full of gas.
    • Low sensitivity (29–35%) for detecting hollow viscus or solid organ injuries without haemoperitoneum.
    • Unreliable for excluding injuries in penetrating trauma.
    • Requires repeat or supplementary investigations if needed.
    • Unreliable for assessing retroperitoneum.

[[figure-1]]

Diagnostic Peritoneal Lavage (DPL): (Option C)

  • Purpose: Assess for the presence of blood or contaminants in the abdomen, valuable in resource-limited settings.
  • Procedure:
    • Nasogastric tube and urinary catheter placement.
    • Cannula insertion below the umbilicus for aspiration and fluid infusion.
    • The positive result is if
      • Frank blood or contaminants are present, or
      • If laboratory results show >100,000 red cells/µL or >500 white cells/µL or
      • Amylase levels in the fluid of more than 175 IU/dl.
    • Drainage of lavage fluid via a chest drain indicates diaphragm penetration.
  • Limitations: Largely replaced by eFAST but remains the standard in some settings where eFAST is unavailable or unreliable.
  • Contraindications:
    • When laparotomy is indicated
    • Previous laparotomy
    • Pregnancy
    • Obesity

[[figure-2]]

X-ray (Option B): are less sensitive in detecting injuries to internal organs. Therefore, it may not be the best initial investigation for this patient.

CT scan (Option B): Gold standard for detailed assessment but requires a stable patient. This patient is hypotensive, making CT less ideal initially.



Reference:

  2. SRB’s Manual of Surgery (6th Edition) page 139, 140

explanationHtml:
A Morgagni hernia is a rare type of diaphragmatic hernia where abdominal contents herniate into the thoracic cavity through the foramen of Morgagni (anterior defect of the diaphragm).

Clinical features: Often presents with mild, intermittent abdominal pain, respiratory symptoms, or may be asymptomatic.

X-ray findings: On a chest X-ray, the herniated bowel loops may appear as air-filled structures in the anterior mediastinum, often on the right side near the heart.

Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia (CDH):

  1. CDH is the intrathoracic herniation of abdominal contents due to congenital defects in the diaphragm.
  2. Types of CDH:
    • Bochdalek Hernia: Occurs through the posterolateral pleuroperitoneal canal, most commonly on the left side.
    • Morgagni Hernia: Anterior hernia located at the right cardiophrenic angle.

[[figure-1]]

Fig. Schematic representation of CDH

  1. Radiologic Features:
    • Chest Radiograph (CXR):
      • Bochdalek hernia: Dome-shaped soft tissue opacity in the posterolateral thorax, often left-sided.
      • May show gas-filled bowel loops or fat content in the thoracic cavity.
      • Mediastinal shift away from the herniation due to mass effect.
      • On the lateral view, hernias appear above the posterior costophrenic recess.
    • CT/MRI:
      • Visualizes herniation of fat, bowel, spleen, or kidney through a diaphragmatic defect.
      • Important for distinguishing from other masses like cystic adenomatoid malformation or pericardial cyst.
      • CT provides clearer differentiation of soft-tissue or fatty mass protruding through the diaphragm.
  2. Complications:
    • Associated with hypoplasia of the ipsilateral lung, leading to respiratory distress, especially in neonates.
    • Neonates may present with respiratory distress and mediastinal deviation.

Bochdalek hernia (option A): Incorrect because a Bochdalek hernia is a posterior diaphragmatic hernia, typically found on the left side. It is more common in neonates and is not located anteriorly.

Gastric volvulus (option C): Incorrect because gastric volvulus involves twisting of the stomach, often leading to acute severe pain and vomiting, which does not match the mild, intermittent pain described here. X-ray would show a "double bubble" or distended stomach with air-fluid levels.


Eventration of diaphragm (option D): Incorrect because eventration refers to abnormal elevation of the diaphragm, often involving one hemidiaphragm, but does not involve herniation of bowel loops into the thoracic cavity.

Angiomyolipoma is a benign renal tumour composed of fat, blood vessels, and smooth muscle. On CT, it is characterised by fat density (-10 to -100 Hounsfield units) within the lesion, which is a hallmark feature.

It is most commonly seen in middle-aged individuals and is associated with tuberous sclerosis in some cases.

[[figure-1]]

Angiomyolipoma in both kidneys (arrows) in computer tomography. The tumours are hypodense (dark) due to fat content.

RCC (Renal Cell Carcinoma) (option A): RCC typically presents as an enhancing mass on CT without significant fat density. It may show irregular enhancement due to necrosis but does not have fat as a primary feature.

Renal Oncocytoma (option B): Renal oncocytoma is a benign tumour and appears as a homogeneously enhancing mass on CT but does not exhibit fat density.

Renal Cyst (option D): Renal cysts appear as well-defined, non-enhancing lesions with water density (0-20 Hounsfield units) on CT, without fat.

question: The following radiological image was taken to assess the urinary tract. Identify the investigation shown below.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Emphysematous Pyelonephritis:

  • This is a severe, necrotizing infection of the kidney, typically caused by gas-producing organisms (e.g., E. coli, Klebsiella).
  • The hallmark imaging feature in CT scan would be the presence of gas in the renal parenchyma or renal collecting system.
  • Symptoms typically include flank pain, fever, chills, and rigors, and it is commonly seen in diabetic patients or those with immunocompromised states.
  • The radiological finding of gas within the renal parenchyma on the CT scan supports this diagnosis.

Acute Pyelonephritis

Xanthogranulomatous Pyelonephritis

Emphysematous Pyelonephritis

Ultrasound (USG): This may show kidney enlargement, reduced echogenicity, and dilated collecting systems.

[[figure-1]]

Ultrasound (USG): Shows an enlarged kidney with echogenic staghorn calculi and hypoechoic masses replacing renal parenchyma.

[[figure-2]]

Plain Abdominal X-ray: Detects gas in the kidney region in about 70% of cases.

[[figure-3]]

Contrast-enhanced CT: Most sensitive, showing wedge-shaped hypodense areas, striated nephrograms, and pelvic wall thickening.

[[figure-4]]

CT Scan reveals a non-functioning kidney, staghorn calculus, expanded calyces, and inflammatory changes. A characteristic bear paw sign is noted.

[[figure-5]]

CT: Gold standard, reveals gas within the kidney, renal enlargement, perinephric stranding and abscesses. Helps classify into Type 1 (gas without fluid) or Type 2 (gas with fluid).

[[figure-6]]

Acute infection of the kidney involving the renal parenchyma and collecting system is usually caused by ascending bacteria.
  • It is a chronic granulomatous response to recurrent renal infection - that leads to the destruction of renal parenchyma and its replacement by lipid-laden foamy macrophages.
  • Destruction spreads from the renal pelvis→medulla→ cortex.
  • Usually, staghorn calculus is present in the pelvis.

Severe necrotizing infection with gas accumulation in and around the kidney, primarily in diabetic patients.

Cholecystitis (option A): Incorrect because cholecystitis is an inflammation of the gallbladder, typically presenting with right upper quadrant pain, fever, and nausea. The imaging would show gallstones and a thickened gallbladder wall rather than gas in the renal system.

Small bowel obstruction (option C): Incorrect because small bowel obstruction presents with symptoms of vomiting, abdominal distension, and failure to pass flatus or stool. Imaging would typically show dilated loops of bowel and air-fluid levels, not gas in the kidney or renal system.

Volvulus (option D): Incorrect because volvulus refers to the twisting of the bowel, leading to bowel obstruction. It would cause abdominal distension, pain, and vomiting, with imaging showing distended loops of bowel and sometimes a twisted mesenteric root. There would be no gas in the kidney or renal parenchyma.

question: A 55-year-old female patient presents to the emergency department with chills and rigors. She has acute pain in the right flank region. The imaging is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The jejunum is the second part of the small intestine, following the duodenum and preceding the ileum. It is typically characterized by:

  • A thicker, more vascular wall compared to the ileum.
  • Plicae circulares (circular folds) are prominent in the jejunum, and the mucosal surface appears folded in the barium study.
  • The barium study would show coarse, dense mucosal folds which is a distinctive feature of the jejunum.

Various Bubble signs of the abdomen:

Condition

Radiological Sign

Explanation

Normal Abdomen

Single bubble in the stomach

A single air bubble seen in the left upper quadrant corresponds to the fundus of the stomach. A large single bubble is seen in cases of pyloric atresia, GOO.

[[figure-1]]

Pyloric Atresia

"Single bubble" sign

A single distended stomach with no air in the small bowel or beyond, caused by obstruction at the pylorus.

[[figure-2]]

Duodenal Atresia

"Double bubble" sign

Distended stomach and proximal duodenum; no distal bowel gas due to obstruction at the duodenum.

[[figure-3]]

Jejunal Atresia

"Triple bubble" sign

Three distended loops of bowel (stomach, duodenum, proximal jejunum) with no distal gas.

[[figure-4]]

Ileal Atresia

Multiple air-fluid levels

Dilated small bowel loops with air-fluid levels and no gas in the large intestine, more distal than jejunal atresia.

Ileum (option A): Incorrect because the ileum is the third and longest part of the small intestine. It is often characterized by fewer, less prominent folds compared to the jejunum and a thinner wall. In a barium study, it would show less dense mucosal folds than the jejunum.

Transverse colon (option B): Incorrect because the transverse colon is part of the large intestine, which would appear with a wider lumen and less defined folds compared to the small intestine. The characteristic features of the transverse colon would not match the dense folds of the jejunum seen in the barium study.

Splenic flexure (option D): Incorrect because the splenic flexure is the bend between the ascending colon and the descending colon, located near the spleen. It has a much larger and less folded appearance compared to the jejunum in a barium study.

question: Identify the condition in the image shown below:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The X-ray given above shows the presence of air under the diaphragm without any visible bowel markings, which is indicative of pneumoperitoneum.

Pneumoperitoneum

  • Pneumoperitoneum refers to the presence of free gas in the peritoneal cavity, typically indicating a perforated viscus (e.g., perforated peptic ulcer).
  • Causes:
    • Common: Perforated peptic ulcers, bowel obstruction, inflammatory conditions, ischemia, injury during colonoscopy.
    • Other causes without peritonitis: Postoperative (up to 7 days), peritoneal dialysis, sealed perforation, and tracking from pneumomediastinum.
  • Diagnosis on Imaging:
    • Erect CXR: Free gas seen under the right hemidiaphragm (cupola sign), difficult to differentiate on the left due to gastric or colonic gas.
    • Supine AXR: Right upper quadrant gas in the perihepatic, subhepatic space, Morrison’s pouch, and ligament visualization (e.g., falciform ligament).
    • Rigler’s Sign: Visualization of both sides of the bowel wall due to surrounding gas.
    • CT Scan: Most sensitive; small volumes of gas seen in the liver or peritoneal recesses, often using broad window settings.
  • Pseudo-pneumoperitoneum: Conditions mimicking free gas such as Chilaiditi syndrome (intestine between liver and diaphragm), subphrenic abscess, or subdiaphragmatic fat.
  • Pneumoperitoneum may be clinically silent, especially in elderly, steroid-treated, unconscious, or critically ill patients.

Small bowel obstruction (SBO) (Option B): typically presents with dilated bowel loops, air-fluid levels, and no free air under the diaphragm.

[[figure-1]]

Esophageal perforation (Option C): While it can lead to air escaping into surrounding areas, it more commonly results in pneumomediastinum or subcutaneous emphysema rather than free air under the diaphragm.

Pneumomediastinum (Option D): Air in the mediastinum is seen along the heart border and mediastinal structures, not under the diaphragm.

[[figure-2]]



Reference:

Grainger and Allison’s Textbook of Diagnostic Radiology, 7th edition, Page 463-465

question: A 6-week-old child is brought to the emergency department with recurrent projectile, non-bilious vomiting. Based on the radiograph provided, what is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Dysphagia that is more pronounced for liquids than solids suggests achalasia, a motility disorder of the esophagus.
  • Achalasia is characterized by failure of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) to relax, leading to progressive dilation of the esophagus with tapering at the gastroesophageal junction.
  • On barium swallow, achalasia classically shows a "Rat-tail sign"—a smooth, gradual narrowing at the distal esophagus due to the non-relaxing LES.

    [[figure-1]]

  • Radiological Signs in Esophageal Disorders

    Radiological Sign

    Associated Condition

    Appearance

    Rat-tail sign (Correct Answer)

    Achalasia

    Smooth tapering of the esophagus at the LES

    Filling defect

    Esophageal tumors, strictures

    Irregular defect in the barium column

    Corkscrew esophagus

    Diffuse esophageal spasm (DES)

    Multiple non-peristaltic contractions creating a "corkscrew" pattern

    Apple-core lesion

    Esophageal or colonic cancer

    Constricted lumen with irregular edges, resembling an apple core

    Filling defect (Option B) is incorrect because a filling defect is a non-specific radiological finding seen in conditions like oesophageal tumours, varices, or strictures. It does not typically present with dysphagia that is worse for liquids.

    Corkscrew oesophagus (Option C) is incorrect because it is seen in diffuse oesophageal spasm (DES), which presents with intermittent chest pain and dysphagia for both solids and liquids, rather than a progressive pattern.

    Apple-core lesion (Option D) is incorrect because it is a characteristic finding in colorectal cancer, not an oesophageal disorder.


Reference:

Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics, 21st edition, Page 1947

Grainger and Allison’s Textbook of Diagnostic Radiology, 7th edition, Page 463-465
question: A patient presents with a history of dysphagia, which is more pronounced for liquids than solids. Which radiological sign is most likely to be seen?

explanationHtml:
• X-ray shows a characteristic "coffee bean sign"- a large, dilated loop of bowel with an inverted U-shape, which is highly suggestive of sigmoid volvulus.
  • Clinical presentation of absolute constipation and abdominal distension is typical of large bowel obstruction.
  • Sigmoid volvulus is common in elderly patients, especially those with chronic constipation, neurological disorders, or bed-ridden status.
  • The transition point is usually at the sigmoid colon, without gas in the rectum.

Sigmoid Volvulus

Feature

Sigmoid Volvulus

Etiology

Chronic constipation, long redundant sigmoid colon

Radiological Sign

Coffee bean sign on X-ray, bird’s beak sign on contrast enema

Symptoms

Abdominal distension, pain, absolute constipation, vomiting

Treatment

Endoscopic detorsion (if no gangrene), surgery for recurrent cases

[[figure-1]]

Caecal Volvulus (Option A): Incorrect because caecal volvulus shows a kidney-shaped distended caecum displaced to the upper abdomen, often with small bowel dilatation.

Intestinal Obstruction (Option C): Incorrect because intestinal obstruction is a broad term that includes various causes, whereas the X-ray here is specific for sigmoid volvulus.

Small Bowel Volvulus (Option D): Incorrect because small bowel volvulus presents with central dilated loops with air-fluid levels rather than the classical coffee bean sign.

explanationHtml:
• Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) is a high-resolution imaging modality that combines endoscopy with ultrasonography to provide detailed images of the gastrointestinal (GI) wall and adjacent structures.
  • It is primarily used for staging esophageal cancer, allowing assessment of:
    • Depth of tumor invasion (T stage)
    • Involvement of regional lymph nodes (N stage)
    • Adjacent mediastinal structures

Applications of Endoscopic Ultrasound (EUS)

Application

Primary Use

Staging of esophageal cancer (Correct Answer)

Evaluates tumor depth and lymph node involvement

Pancreatic lesions

Subepithelial GI tumors

Differentiates between leiomyomas, GISTs, and neuroendocrine tumors

Detects choledocholithiasis and bile duct strictures

Determines depth of invasion and lymph node involvement

Evaluation of GERD (Option B): Incorrect because GERD is typically assessed with pH monitoring, manometry, or upper endoscopy, not EUS.

Identifying the cause of dysphagia (Option C): Incorrect because barium swallow or esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) are first-line tests; EUS is used mainly for cancer staging or assessing submucosal lesions.

Assessing cardiac and aortic pathology (Option D): Incorrect because transesophageal echocardiography (TEE), not EUS, is preferred for cardiac/aortic evaluation.

question: Which of the following is a primary use of this imaging modality?

explanationHtml:
Option A - Ulcerative Colitis (UC) - Symptoms:

  • Lower abdominal pain: Common in UC, often colicky or cramping.
  • Passage of blood mixed with stools: A cardinal symptom of UC, as the inflammation primarily affects the superficial mucosal lining, leading to friability and bleeding.
  • 3 months duration: Fits the chronic, relapsing-remitting nature of IBD.
  • 26-year-old male: UC commonly presents in young adults.

Ulcerative Colitis (UC) - Xrays

  • Loss of haustral markings ("lead pipe" or "garden hose" appearance): This is a classic sign of chronic UC due to continuous inflammation and fibrosis.

Incorrect Options:

Option B - Pseudomembranous Colitis (PMC) - X-rays:

  • Often non-specific in early or mild cases.
  • Colonic dilatation: Can be diffuse or segmental.
  • Nodular haustral thickening / "Thumbprinting": This is a relatively classic finding, representing prominent edema and thickening of the haustral folds, and is often more pronounced than in UC. It can also be seen in ischemic colitis.

Option C - Crohn's Disease - X-rays:

  • Often normal.
  • Dilated loops of small bowel with air-fluid levels: Suggestive of small bowel obstruction, a common complication due to strictures.
  • "String sign": Severe narrowing of a segment of bowel, often the terminal ileum, appearing as a thin, continuous string of barium. This indicates a stricture.
  • "Skip lesions": Inflamed areas separated by normal bowel, a characteristic feature. Difficult to see on plain X-ray, more apparent on barium studies.

Option D - Intestinal Tuberculosis (TB) - X-rays:

  • Often non-specific.
  • Ascites: Can be present, especially in peritoneal TB.
  • Absence of gas shadows in the right iliac fossa: Due to thickened, matted bowel loops in the ileocecal region.


Reference:

David Sutton Textbook of Radiology and Imaging, Volume 1, 8th edition, Page 2226- 2247

He also reports occasional headaches and mouth breathing but denies any facial pain or fever.
