correctAnswer: C. Non-contrast CT abdomen followed by CECT
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The gold standard investigation for diagnosing urinary tract calculi (kidney stones) is a non-contrast computed tomography (NCCT) scan of the kidneys, ureters, and bladder (NCCT KUB).

  • It has a sensitivity and specificity of over 95%.
  • It detects radiolucent stones (like uric acid stones) that are completely invisible on standard X-rays, as well as stones as small as 1–2 mm.
  • It measures the exact size, precise location, and hardness (Hounsfield units) of the stone. This tells if the stone can pass on its own or needs surgery.
  • It instantly shows if the stone is causing a dangerous blockage, marked by hydronephrosis (kidney swelling) or perinephric stranding.
  • A contrast-enhanced CT (CECT) is only used afterward if the NCCT is negative and we suspects a different emergency, like a torn blood vessel or a tumor.

Plain radiograph followed by CT (Option A): Misses up to 20% of stones because radiolucent stones don't show up, and small stones are easily hidden by overlying bowel gas or fecal matter.

Ultrasonography followed by CT (Option B): While excellent for checking hydronephrosis, ultrasound is notoriously bad at finding stones in the mid-ureter because bowel gas blocks the view. It is only used as a first-line test for pregnant women and children to avoid radiation.

Intravenous pyelography (IVP) (Option D): This historical test is obsolete. It requires injecting contrast dye and taking multiple X-rays over an hour. It is dangerous if the patient already has kidney damage from the blockage.



Reference:

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Pages 728, 730

question: A patient presents with acute left flank pain. What is the most appropriate imaging investigation?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The comet-tail artefact on ultrasound is a characteristic finding of gallbladder adenomyomatosis, caused by reverberation from cholesterol crystals trapped within Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses. These sinuses represent cystic invaginations of the mucosa into a thickened gallbladder wall.

Gallbladder adenomyomatosis:

  • Also known as adenomyomatous hyperplasia or cholecystitis glandularis proliferans, is a benign condition characterised by epithelial and smooth muscle hyperplasia.
  • Sites: It most commonly involves the fundus of the gallbladder and is often an incidental finding, though patients may present with biliary-type pain.
  • Benign condition; does not require surgery unless symptomatic.

Porcelain gallbladder (Option A): Characterised by calcification of the gallbladder wall. Appears as a hyperechoic rim with shadowing.

Acute calculous cholecystitis (Option C): Characterised by gallbladder distension, wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid, and a positive sonographic Murphy sign, rather than ring-down artefacts.

Gallbladder carcinoma (Option D): Shows an irregular mass, asymmetric wall thickening, and possible liver invasion.



Reference:

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Pages 662, 664.
question: A 54-year-old man complains of episodic right upper quadrant discomfort without fever or jaundice. Ultrasound examination of the gallbladder shows localised mural thickening with intramural echogenic foci producing a comet-tail artefact. No gallstones are seen. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The hallmark "sausage-shaped" pancreas on imaging is a key finding in autoimmune pancreatitis, along with long segmental ductal strictures. The pancreas may appear diffusely enlarged, and ductal strictures without significant calcification or atrophy help differentiate this from chronic pancreatitis.

Imaging Modality

Chronic pancreatitis

Autoimmune Pancreatitis

CT scan

• Calcifications within the pancreas.

• Pancreatic atrophy with dilated ductal system.

• Irregularities or strictures of the pancreatic duct.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

• Diffuse pancreatic enlargement ("sausage-shaped" appearance).

• Homogeneous delayed enhancement of the pancreas.

• Capsule-like rim of low density, suggesting peripancreatic inflammation or fibrosis.

• Ductal narrowing or strictures

[[figure-3]]

MRCP

• Characteristic "chain of lakes" appearance due to alternating strictures and dilatation of the pancreatic duct.

[[figure-4]]

Chronic pancreatitis (Option A) typically shows ductal dilations and calcifications, but the "sausage-shaped" pancreas is more specific for autoimmune pancreatitis.

Necrotising pancreatitis (Option C) is usually associated with severe acute inflammation, necrosis, and fluid collections, not strictures.

Pancreatic pseudocyst (Option D) refers to a fluid collection following pancreatitis but does not cause "sausage-shaped" pancreatic enlargement or strictures.



Reference:
  1. Grainger and Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 690,692,694,698
  2. Textbook of Radiology and Imaging, David Sutton, 8th Edition, Volume 1, Page 2735-2742
question: A 60 y/o man presents with recurrent abdominal pain and jaundice. A CT abdomen reveals a "sausage-shaped" pancreas and long segmental pancreatic duct strictures. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: B. Double duct sign - Carcinoma of the head of pancreas
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Double duct sign is classic for pancreatic head carcinoma and involves simultaneous dilation of both the common bile duct and the pancreatic duct.
  • The presence of a hypoattenuating ill-defined mass in the pancreatic head, with Courvoisier sign (palpable gallbladder + painless jaundice) supports this.
  • Most characteristic imaging modality: CECT.

Radiological Features: Carcinoma of Pancreatic Head vs Periampullary Carcinoma vs Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma:

Feature

Carcinoma of Pancreatic Head

Periampullary Carcinoma

Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma (PDAC)

Imaging Modality

CECT, MRI/MRCP

CECT, MRI/MRCP, EUS

CECT, MRI, EUS

Typical CT/MRI Look

Hypoattenuating, ill-defined; T1/T2 hypointense; double duct, inverted 3 sign

Variable: hypoattenuating mass, ductal dilatation if ampullary

Ill-defined hypoattenuating mass; double duct sign if head

Distinctive Signs

Double duct, inverted 3 sign, Courvoisier sign, duct cutoff, distal atrophy

Double duct sign, duct dilatation (if ampullary/head)

Double duct sign, duct cutoff, distal atrophy

Vessel Involvement

Frequent; SMA, SMV, portal vein invasion assessed

Considered if head or ampulla involved

Frequent; SMA, SMV, portal vein involvement assessed

EUS Utility

Detects small lesions, guides biopsy, evaluates nodes

Same as left column

Same as left column

Common Metastases

Liver, peritoneum, lung

Liver, peritoneum, lung (if invasive)

Liver, peritoneum, lung

Imaging Highlights and Features by Tumor Type

Carcinoma of the Head of Pancreas

  • Double duct sign: Simultaneous dilation of bile and pancreatic ducts.
  • Inverted "3" sign: Duodenal wall indentation seen on barium study.
  • Courvoisier sign: Enlarged, painless gallbladder with jaundice.
  • CT/MRI findings: Poorly defined hypoattenuating lesion; low T1/T2 signal.
  • Other signs: Abrupt duct cutoff, distal gland atrophy.

Periampullary Carcinoma

  • Anatomic range: Tumors at ampulla, distal CBD, duodenum, and sometimes pancreatic head.
  • Imaging variability: May resemble pancreatic head tumors if arising nearby.
  • Important findings: Double duct sign (ampullary/head), duct dilatation depending on site.
  • EUS role: Especially useful for ampullary and small tumors.

Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma (PDAC)

  • Location: Anywhere in the pancreas (commonly head).
  • Imaging: Hypoattenuating mass with duct obstruction and atrophy.
  • MRI: Ill-defined, low T1/T2 signal, poor enhancement.
  • Signs (if in head): Double duct, abrupt cutoff, distal atrophy.
  • Metastatic spread: Liver, peritoneum, lung.

Corkscrew sign - Cholangiocarcinoma (Option A): Incorrect because corkscrew appearance refers to twisted bile ducts, seen in sclerosing cholangitis, not associated with double duct sign or pancreatic head mass.

Apple core lesion - Duodenal carcinoma (Option C): Incorrect because apple core lesions indicate constrictive colonic or duodenal growth, not ductal dilatation.

Inverted umbrella sign- Ampullary carcinoma (Option D): Incorrect as this is not a recognized or standard radiological sign for ampullary carcinoma. Ampullary carcinoma may cause double duct sign but is less commonly associated with a palpable gallbladder.

  3. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10887967/

• Imaging Features: Multiple small cysts, sometimes with central scar calcification.Honeycomb pattern, possible stellate scar.

• Benign: Rarely malignant.

• Common in: Older women in their 6-s-70s - hence called grandmother tumour.

Mucinous Cystic Neoplasm (MCN)

[[figure-3]]

• Common Site: Tail of the pancreas.

• Imaging Features: Large, multilocular, thick septations, peripheral calcifications, and sometimes solid components.

• Risk: Malignant transformation

• Common in: Perimenopausal women (40-60 years-Mother tumour.)

Intraductal Papillary Mucinous Neoplasm (IPMN)

[[figure-4]]

• Types: Main duct, branch duct, mixed.

• Common Site: Ductal origin—main duct or branch duct.

• Risk: Higher malignancy risk in main duct type.

• Main duct IPMNs: Show cystic dilatation of the main duct, enhancing mural nodules, and viscid mucus causing obstruction.

• Protruding ampulla of Vater-Fish mouth appearance

Solid Pseudopapillary Tumor (SPT):

[[figure-5]]

• Imaging Features: Large, encapsulated, solid and cystic mass, often with haemorrhage &necrosis.

• Demographics: Young women (Daughter tumour), particularly in Asian and African-American populations.

question: A 55 y/o perimenopausal woman presents with vague abdominal pain. A CT scan of the abdomen reveals a large, multilocular cystic lesion in the tail of the pancreas with thick septations and peripheral calcifications. Lab results show elevated CEA levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient’s presentation, gas in the gallbladder wall, and pneumoperitoneum on CT are hallmark findings of emphysematous cholecystitis, especially in a diabetic patient with high sepsis risk.


Emphysematous Cholecystitis

  • Definition: A rare, severe form of acute cholecystitis with gallbladder wall necrosis causing gas formation within the lumen or wall; surgical emergency due to high risk of gangrene and perforation.
  • Radiographic Diagnosis: Air detected in the gallbladder wall or bile ducts without any abnormal communication to the GI tract.
  • Ultrasound Features:
    • Highly echogenic reflectors with low-level posterior shadowing and reverberation artefact (dirty shadowing and ring-down artefact).
    • Champagne Sign: Pathognomonic sign showing non-shadowing echogenic foci rising from the dependent portion of the gallbladder, resembling bubbles in champagne.
  • CT Imaging:
    • The most sensitive and specific modality for detecting gas within the gallbladder wall or lumen.
    • Pneumoperitoneum on CT suggests gallbladder perforation.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]


Chronic cholecystitis (Option A) and Acute calculous Cholecystitis (Option B) are less likely as they do not usually feature gas in the gallbladder wall or pneumoperitoneum.


Gallbladder Adenocarcinoma (Option D) is unlikely since gallbladder adenocarcinoma rarely presents with intramural gas or signs of acute infection.



Reference:

radiopaedia.org/articles/emphysematous-cholecystitis
question: A 65 y/o diabetic male presents with severe right upper quadrant pain, fever, and signs of sepsis. A USG reveals highly echogenic reflectors with dirty shadowing and ring-down artefacts in the gallbladder. Subsequent CT imaging demonstrates gas within the gallbladder wall and pneumoperitoneum. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
MRCP is correct because it non-invasively identifies the worm as a hypointense structure in the hyperintense CBD, with the distinctive "three-line sign" on 3T MRI.

Biliary Ascariasis

  • Common helminthic infection from Ascaris lumbricoides affects about 1 billion people worldwide.
  • Fluoroscopy: The worm appears as a longitudinal or curved filling defect in the intestinal lumen during contrast studies.
  • Ultrasonography: Shows a long, hyperechoic structure with a central hypoechoic line within the liver.
  • CT Imaging: Dilated CBD with a curved, hyperdense structure (worm) showing central hypodensity; appears as a filling defect in the contrast-filled intestinal lumen.
  • MRCP: Preferred non-invasive method; worm appears hypointense within hyperintense CBD. "Three line sign" on 3T MRI confirms the diagnosis.
  • ERCP: Gold standard but invasive; used both for diagnosis and CBD worm extraction.

[[figure-1]]

USG showing ascaris in gallbladder

[[figure-2]]

MRCP shows a “three-line” appearance in the dilated common bile duct (arrows), filing defect in the dilated cystic duct (arrow) and ascites (arrowheads).

Fluoroscopy (Option A): While it can identify the worm as a filling defect in the intestine, it is less commonly used for biliary ascariasis specifically.

CT (Option B) may show a dilated CBD with the worm as a hyperdense structure but lacks the non-invasive specificity of MRCP for biliary duct visualization.

ERCP (Option D) is the gold standard for both diagnosis and treatment but is invasive and usually reserved for therapeutic intervention.



Reference:

Biliary ascariasis
question: A 35 y/o woman from a rural area presents with severe right upper quadrant pain, fever, and jaundice. She reports intermittent episodes of abdominal discomfort. Laboratory tests reveal an elevated bilirubin level, and an ultrasound shows a long, echogenic structure within the common bile duct with a hypoechoic centre. What imaging modality is preferred for non-invasively confirming the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The imaging findings of a hypervascular liver lesion with mosaic enhancement, washout on delayed phases, and characteristic "nodule-in-nodule" appearance are strongly indicative of HCC.

Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC) Radiographic Features

Ultrasound (USG)

CT

MRI

• Heterogeneous mass appearance.

• May display a "nodule-in-nodule" pattern.

[[figure-1]]

• Hypervascular with mosaic enhancement.

• Washout of contrast observed in the portal venous or delayed phases.

[[figure-2]]

• T1: Decreased signal intensity.

• T2: Increased signal intensity.

• Contrast Phases:

◦ Late arterial phase: Hyperenhancement.

◦ Portal venous/delayed phase: Washout, indicating malignancy.

[[figure-3]]

Focal Nodular Hyperplasia (FNH) (Option A): FNH typically shows a central scar and does not exhibit the washout pattern seen in HCC, distinguishing it from the described imaging findings.

Hepatic Adenoma (Option C): Hepatic adenomas usually appear as hypervascular lesions but lack the mosaic pattern and washout phases distinctive of HCC.

Metastatic Liver Disease (Option D): Liver metastases commonly show peripheral rim enhancement rather than the described central hyperenhancement and washout pattern, which is more typical of HCC.



Reference:

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 628, 629
question: A 55-year-old male with a history of chronic hepatitis presents with abdominal discomfort. Ultrasound shows a heterogeneous liver mass with a "nodule-in-nodule" appearance. CT reveals a hypervascular lesion with mosaic enhancement and washout on delayed phases. MRI demonstrates decreased T1 and increased T2 signal intensities with late arterial enhancement. Based on the imaging findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The presence of air within the gallbladder wall on CT is diagnostic of emphysematous cholecystitis, a rare but life-threatening variant of acute cholecystitis.

Etiology: It occurs due to ischemia and necrosis of the gallbladder wall, followed by infection with gas-forming organisms such as Clostridium perfringens and E. coli.

Risk factors: This condition is classically seen in elderly patients and diabetics

Complications: High risk of gangrene, perforation, and sepsis

Treatment: Emergency cholecystectomy with broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics.

Acute pancreatitis (Option A): CT shows pancreatic enlargement, peripancreatic fat stranding, and fluid collections. Gas in the gallbladder wall is not a feature.

Choledocholithiasis (Option C): Characterised by stones in the common bile duct with biliary dilatation. Intramural gallbladder gas is absent.

Calculous cholecystitis (Option D): Results from cystic duct obstruction by gallstones. Imaging may show gallstones and wall thickening, but air in the gallbladder wall is not seen.



Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK448099/
question: A patient presents with acute right upper quadrant pain and systemic toxicity. CT abdomen shows air within the gallbladder wall without evidence of biliary-enteric communication. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The ultrasound finding described represents the triangular cord sign, which corresponds to a fibrous remnant of the obliterated extrahepatic bile duct. This sign is highly suggestive of biliary atresia, a progressive obliterative cholangiopathy affecting both intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts.
  • Biliary atresia commonly presents with persistent neonatal jaundice, clay-colored stools, and hepatomegaly. If left untreated, it rapidly progresses to biliary cirrhosis, portal hypertension, and liver failure. Ultrasound may show an absent or hypoplastic gallbladder along with the triangular cord sign. Early diagnosis is critical, as timely Kasai portoenterostomy improves survival.

[[figure-1]]

Galactosemia (Option A): A metabolic disorder presenting with jaundice, hepatomegaly, and hypoglycemia. Imaging does not show biliary ductal abnormalities or the triangular cord sign.

Hemangioma (Option B): A vascular liver lesion that appears as a well-defined hyperechoic mass on ultrasound. It does not cause biliary obstruction or fibrotic changes at the porta hepatis.

Caroli’s disease (Option D): A congenital disorder characterised by segmental dilatation of intrahepatic bile ducts, producing the central dot sign on imaging, not the triangular cord sign.



Reference:

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Pages 1838, 1839
question: A neonate presents with persistent jaundice and pale stools since birth. Ultrasound abdomen shows an echogenic triangular structure anterior to the right portal vein at the porta hepatis. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The presence of gas bubbles in a thick-walled collection indicates necrotic material, suggesting walled-off necrosis.(Option B)

Feature

Pseudocyst (Option A)

Walled-off Necrosis (Option B)

Definition

Encapsulated fluid collection that develops more than 4 weeks after acute pancreatitis.

Encapsulated collection of necrotic material, which develops after 4 weeks in necrotising pancreatitis

Gas Presence

No gas (Option A ruled out)

Gas bubbles may indicate infection

Location

Peripancreatic space (may extend to mediastinum)

Pancreatic and/or peripancreatic tissues

Imaging findings

Homogeneous low-attenuation fluid with capsule

[[figure-1]]

CT showing pseudocyst

Thick-walled collection may show gas on CT

[[figure-2]]

CT Showing “walled off necrosis”

Resolution

Most resolve spontaneously.

If more than 5 cm or recurrent, cystogastrostomy is done

Often requires drainage or necrosectomy if infected

Abscess (Option C): While an abscess may also contain gas, it is generally associated with infection and may not specifically relate to pancreatitis.

Interstitial edematous pancreatitis (Option D): This diagnosis involves swelling of the pancreas without a necrotic collection and would not explain the thick-walled fluid collection observed on the CT scan

question: A 45 y/o woman with a history of acute pancreatitis presents with persistent abdominal pain and weight loss. A CT scan performed 5 weeks after her initial episode shows a thick-walled fluid collection containing gas bubbles. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The above clinical features and an erect abdominal X-ray showing a colon cut-off sign in a patient with an acute abdomen are suggestive of acute pancreatitis.

  • The colon cut-off sign refers to the sudden cessation of gas in the colon, typically at the splenic flexure.
  • In acute pancreatitis, inflammation spreads from the pancreas to the transverse mesocolon and phrenicocolic ligament, leading to functional spasm of the splenic flexure, producing this characteristic radiographic appearance.
  • Although initially described on plain radiographs, this sign can also be seen on contrast studies and CT.

Acute pancreatitis: Acute inflammatory condition of the pancreas due to premature activation of pancreatic enzymes.

  • Most common causes: Gallstones and alcohol.

Clinical Features

  • Sudden, severe epigastric pain radiating to the back.
  • Associated with nausea and vomiting.
  • Pain is relieved by sitting forward.

Pathophysiology

  • Inflammation spreads to adjacent tissues.
  • Causes localised paralytic ileus of the transverse colon near the splenic flexure.

Large bowel obstruction (Option A): Shows generalised colonic dilatation with multiple air-fluid levels extending up to the site of obstruction, rather than abrupt gas cut-off at the splenic flexure.

[[figure-1]]

Sigmoid volvulus (Option C): Characterised by a massively dilated sigmoid colon with a classic coffee-bean or inverted U sign, usually arising from the pelvis.

[[figure-2]]

Diverticulitis (Option D): Primarily a CT diagnosis; plain X-ray findings are nonspecific and do not show a colon cut-off sign.



Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1272.
question: A 48-year-old man presents with a sudden onset of severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, associated with repeated vomiting. The pain worsens after meals and is partially relieved by leaning forward. X-ray findings are shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The investigation of choice for prognostic assessment in acute pancreatitis is contrast-enhanced CT (CECT), as it allows evaluation of pancreatic necrosis, peripancreatic collections, and complications that directly influence outcome.
  • CECT is used to calculate the Modified CT Severity Index (MCTSI), which incorporates the extent of pancreatic inflammation, necrosis, and extrapancreatic complications. It is the most reliable imaging modality for risk stratification and prognosis, rather than initial diagnosis.
  • The optimal timing for CECT is after 72 hours from symptom onset, as imaging done earlier may underestimate the degree of necrosis. CECT is particularly indicated in patients with severe acute pancreatitis, organ failure, sepsis, or clinical deterioration despite treatment.
  • Plain abdominal radiographs and an erect chest X-ray have no prognostic role and are used only to exclude differentials such as perforation or obstruction.

Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) (Option A): Useful for detecting gallstones and microlithiasis, but does not assess severity or prognosis in acute pancreatitis.

MRCP (Option C): Helpful for evaluating biliary and pancreatic ductal anatomy, especially in suspected biliary pancreatitis, but not used for prognostic scoring.

ERCP (Option D): Primarily a therapeutic procedure indicated in gallstone pancreatitis with cholangitis or persistent obstruction; it has no role in prognostic assessment.



Reference:

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Pages 686-688
question: A patient diagnosed with acute pancreatitis is being evaluated for disease severity and prognosis after initial stabilisation. Which imaging modality is most appropriate to assess pancreatic necrosis and predict outcome in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The given clinical presentation with MRCP demonstrating simultaneous dilatation of the common bile duct and pancreatic duct (double duct sign) is most suggestive of carcinoma of the head of the pancreas.
  • The double duct sign refers to the concurrent dilatation of the common bile duct and the pancreatic duct, indicating an obstructing lesion at or near the pancreatic head or ampulla. On MRCP, additional findings such as dilatation of pancreatic duct side branches further support a malignant obstructive process, commonly pancreatic head carcinoma.
  • Pancreatic head carcinoma typically presents with painless obstructive jaundice, anorexia, weight loss, and pruritus. As an anatomical sign, the double duct sign can be visualised on ultrasound, CT, MRI, MRCP, and ERCP, but MRCP provides excellent non-invasive ductal delineation.

Choledocholithiasis (Option A): An impacted distal CBD stone can occasionally cause a double duct appearance due to oedema, but pancreatic duct side-branch dilatation and progressive painless jaundice favour malignancy.

Chronic cholecystitis (Option B): Primarily a gallbladder disease associated with wall thickening and gallstones; it does not cause pancreatic duct dilatation or a double duct sign.

Primary sclerosing cholangitis (Option D): Characterised by multifocal strictures and a beaded appearance of intra- and extrahepatic bile ducts, not by isolated double duct dilatation.



Reference:

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 666
question: A patient presents with progressive painless jaundice, anorexia, and weight loss. The MRCP performed for biliary evaluation is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: D. Carcinoma head of the pancreas
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical features of anorexia and weight loss, combined with a barium study showing widening of the duodenal loop with the inverted “3 sign” (Frostberg sign), are characteristic of carcinoma of the head of the pancreas.
  • Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma most commonly arises from the head of the pancreas. On barium examination, a pancreatic head mass causes external compression and oedema of the medial wall of the second part of the duodenum, leading to effacement of mucosal folds and the classic Frostberg’s inverted “3” sign. This may also be associated with widening of the duodenal C-loop.
  • Clinically, pancreatic head carcinoma often presents with weight loss, anorexia, abdominal pain, and early biliary obstruction with jaundice due to proximity to the common bile duct.

Malignant duodenal ulcer (Option A): Typically shows an irregular ulcer crater with mucosal destruction on barium study rather than smooth extrinsic compression or C-loop widening.

Crohn’s disease (Option B): Involves skip lesions, string sign, and mucosal ulceration, commonly affecting the terminal ileum rather than producing an inverted “3” sign in the duodenum.

Carcinoma of the pylorus (Option C): Causes gastric outlet obstruction with pyloric narrowing and delayed gastric emptying, not medial duodenal wall compression.



Reference:

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 714
question: A middle-aged man presents with progressive weight loss, anorexia, and upper abdominal discomfort. A barium meal study of the patient is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: A. Serous cystadenoma of the pancreas
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The presence of a spongy or microcystic pancreatic mass with a central sunburst (stellate) calcification on CT is characteristic of a serous cystadenoma of the pancreas, a benign cystic neoplasm.
  • Serous cystadenoma typically appears on CT as a multicystic, lobulated lesion, often described as a “bunch of grapes”, most commonly involving the pancreatic head.
  • A central fibrous scar may be present, which can show stellate or sunburst calcification in approximately 20% of cases.
  • The lesion enhances due to its vascular septae, helping differentiate it from other cystic pancreatic tumours.
  • These tumours are usually benign, slow-growing, and often incidentally detected.

Pancreatic adenocarcinoma (Option B): Typically presents as a solid hypodense mass with pancreatic ductal dilatation and vascular encasement; cystic spongy appearance and central calcification are not features.

Adenosquamous carcinoma (Option C): An aggressive variant of pancreatic carcinoma presenting as a solid infiltrative mass without a microcystic or sunburst calcification pattern.

Mucinous cystadenocarcinoma (Option D): Usually a unilocular or macrocystic lesion with thick walls and peripheral calcification, most commonly in the pancreatic body or tail, not central stellate calcification.



Reference:

https://radiopaedia.org/articles/serous-cystadenoma-of-the-pancreas-1
question: A contrast-enhanced CT abdomen of a patient is given below. Which diagnosis best fits this imaging description?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The above clinical scenario with CT imaging demonstrating the central dot sign is characteristic of Caroli’s disease.
  • The central dot sign represents an enhancing fibrovascular bundle containing portal vein radicles, seen centrally within a focally dilated intrahepatic bile duct, producing a dot-in-cyst appearance on contrast CT.
  • Caroli’s disease is a congenital disorder of intrahepatic bile ducts, leading to non-obstructive saccular or fusiform dilatation. Patients typically present in childhood with recurrent abdominal pain, jaundice, and cholangitis. CT and MRCP are key imaging modalities for diagnosis.

Hepatoma (Option B): Usually appears as a solid enhancing hepatic mass with arterial hyperenhancement and washout, not cystic bile duct dilatation.

Hydatid cyst (Option C): Shows well-defined cysts with daughter cysts, calcified walls, or water-lily sign; does not show a central enhancing dot.

Hepatic hemangioma (Option D): Classically demonstrates peripheral nodular enhancement with centripetal fill-in on contrast imaging, without bile duct involvement.



Reference:

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 673
question: A child presents with jaundice and intermittent right upper quadrant abdominal pain. Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen of the patient is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The above clinical scenario with imaging findings points towards the diagnosis of hepatic adenoma.
  • Hepatic adenoma is a benign liver tumour strongly associated with oral contraceptive use, particularly in young women of reproductive age. Estrogen exposure plays a key role in its pathogenesis, leading to hepatocellular proliferation.
  • On imaging, hepatic adenomas typically appear as well-circumscribed lesions, often solitary, and may show heterogeneous attenuation or signal intensity due to intralesional fat, haemorrhage, or necrosis.
  • They are usually hypervascular in the arterial phase and may show washout on delayed phases. These lesions carry a risk of spontaneous haemorrhage and malignant transformation, especially when large.
  • Discontinuation of oral contraceptives can lead to regression of smaller adenomas, while larger or symptomatic lesions often require surgical resection.

Hepatic hemangioma (Option A): This is the most common benign liver tumour, typically unrelated to oral contraceptive use. Imaging classically shows peripheral nodular enhancement with centripetal fill-in on delayed phases.

Metastatic liver deposits (Option C): Usually present as multiple lesions in patients with a known primary malignancy. Imaging often shows variable enhancement patterns rather than a solitary, well-defined lesion.

Hepatocellular carcinoma (Option D): Commonly arises in the background of chronic liver disease or cirrhosis and is associated with risk factors such as hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and alcoholism, rather than oral contraceptive use.



Reference:

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 618
question: A young female patient with a history of long-term oral contraceptive use undergoes abdominal imaging that is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The above clinical context relates to suspected splenic rupture, most commonly seen after blunt abdominal trauma.
  • On plain radiographs, indirect signs of splenic injury may be present due to associated hemoperitoneum and local inflammatory changes.
  • Kehr’s sign, however, is not a radiographic sign. It is a clinical finding, referring to referred pain at the tip of the left shoulder caused by diaphragmatic irritation from intraperitoneal blood accumulating beneath the left hemidiaphragm. It may also be elicited by elevating the left leg.
  • Radiographic findings that support splenic rupture are indirect and include displacement or obscuration of normal anatomical shadows.
  • Definitive diagnosis and grading of splenic injury are performed using contrast-enhanced CT (CECT), which demonstrates splenic lacerations as linear low-attenuation defects, usually accompanied by hemoperitoneum.

[[figure-1]]

Elevation of the left hemidiaphragm (Option A): Seen due to subphrenic blood collection or splenic enlargement following rupture.

Obliteration of the splenic outline (Option B): Occurs because of adjacent hemoperitoneum and loss of normal soft-tissue planes.

Loss of the left psoas shadow (Option D): Results from retroperitoneal or intraperitoneal bleeding obscuring the psoas margin.



Reference:

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 2140

question: Following blunt abdominal trauma, a patient is suspected to have splenic injury. Which of the following findings is least likely to be identified on a plain abdominal or chest radiograph?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The absence of pericholecystic fluid is more indicative of chronic cholecystitis, as acute cholecystitis often shows pericholecystic fluid due to active inflammation.

Radiological Differentiation of Acute and Chronic Cholecystitis:

Acute Cholecystitis:

Ultrasound (US):

  • Gallstones + sonographic Murphy sign (tenderness) (Option A ruled out)
  • Gallbladder wall thickness > 3 mm
  • Gallbladder distension (> 5 cm)
  • Pericholecystic fluid

CT Scan:

  • Gallbladder wall thickening
  • Subserosal oedema
  • Gallbladder distension (Option D ruled out)
  • High-density bile (Option C ruled out)
  • Pericholecystic fluid
  • Inflammatory fat stranding

[[figure-1]]

Chronic Cholecystitis:

Ultrasound (US):

  • Gallbladder wall thickening (without gallstones in many cases)
  • Consider other causes of wall thickening

[[figure-2]]

Key Distinguishing Features:

Feature

Acute Cholecystitis

Chronic Cholecystitis

Gallstones

Present

Absent

Gallbladder Wall Thickening

Pronounced

Mild

Pericholecystic Fluid/Inflammation

Common

Rare (Option B)

Functional Imaging (CCK-Cholescintigraphy)

Not commonly used

Impaired contractility (<35% EF) is diagnostic.


Reference:

Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 660, 661
question: A 45 y/o woman presents with right upper quadrant pain and fever. Ultrasound shows gallbladder wall thickening, gallstones, and pericholecystic fluid. Which of the following findings would most likely suggest chronic cholecystitis rather than acute cholecystitis?

correctAnswer: D. T-tube cholangiography assesses stone clearance post-CBD exploration.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

T-tube cholangiography is specifically performed after exploring the common bile duct (CBD) during cholecystectomy. It evaluates whether stones have been cleared and ensures that the contrast medium passes freely into the duodenum, confirming the procedure’s effectiveness.

Imaging Modalities for Gallbladder

Ultrasound

• Transabdominal US is the first choice for hepatobiliary issues, outperforming CT for acute biliary disease (Option C ruled out), and useful for detecting stones, and polyps, and assessing vascularity with Doppler.

• CEUS enhances detail in cases like cholecystitis perforation and cholangiocarcinoma.

[[figure-1]]

Normal gallbladder and common bile duct as seen on abdominal USG

Computed Tomographic Cholangiography (CT-IVC)

• CT-IVC with iodinated contrast provides high-resolution images of bile duct obstructions and leaks but is ineffective in jaundiced patients due to its dependence on normal liver function. (Option A ruled out)

[[figure-2]]

Magnetic Resonance Cholangiopancreatography (MRCP)

• MRCP, using T2-weighted sequences, is preferred over ERCP and PTC for imaging bile ducts in jaundiced patients.

• Contrast-enhanced MR adds functional imaging, though with lower spatial resolution than CT-IVC.

[[figure-3]]

Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP)

• ERCP offers direct bile duct imaging and interventions like stone removal, with a high success rate (92%–97%) but carries a risk of complications, primarily pancreatitis. (Option B ruled out)

[[figure-4]]

T- Tube Cholangiography

• Performed after CBD exploration to check for residual stones by confirming contrast passage into the duodenum; careful injection prevents air bubbles..

[[figure-5]]

Percutaneous Transhepatic Cholangiography (PTC)

• Primarily for biliary interventions as its diagnostic role is now largely replaced by ERCP and MRCP; requires a 22-G needle for intrahepatic duct access and coagulation correction.

[[figure-6]]

Hepatobiliary Scintigraphy (HIDA)

• HIDA with technetium-99m evaluates bile duct function and gallbladder patency, effective only with near-normal bilirubin, though some agents can work with mild elevations.

[[figure-7]]

Endoscopic Ultrasound (EUS)

• EUS provides detailed imaging and Doppler assessment of the biliary tree and pancreas, enabling both diagnostic and therapeutic interventions like fine-needle aspiration and biliary drainage.

[[figure-8]]

Porcelain Gallbladder on EUS


Reference:
  1. Grainger and Allison’s Textbook of Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Pages 657-659
  2. David Sutton Textbook of Radiology and Imaging, Volume 1, 8th Edition, Page 2587-2605

question: Which of the following statements about imaging modalities for the gallbladder is TRUE?

explanationHtml:
Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is the most appropriate choice in this scenario because it allows for direct visualization of the bile ducts and allows for simultaneous treatment of obstructions, such as stone removal.

Feature

Magnetic Resonance Cholangiopancreatography (MRCP)

Endoscopic Retrograde

Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP)

Indications

• Indications include suspected bile duct calculus, cholestasis, pre-surgical biliary evaluation, biliary leak, unknown aetiology sclerosing cholangitis, and unsuccessful or contraindicated ERCP.

• Not typically used for interventions. (Option A ruled out)

• It allows for visual assessment of the duodenum and ampulla of Vater.

• Allows biopsies, stone extraction, and other Interventional procedures like sphincterotomy, biliary stenting, and biliary stricture dilation.

More Suitable for jaundiced patients

Less suitable for jaundiced patients as it is invasive

Substantially replaces PTC and ERCP

Success rates of 92%–97%

Lower complications; no specified rates

Complication rates of 0.9% to 2.3% (severe)

High spatial resolution for detailed imaging

Image

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Ultrasound (Option C) can help identify biliary obstruction and is a good first-line imaging tool, but it does not provide therapeutic options.


Computed Tomography (Option D) can show obstructions and related complications but does not allow for therapeutic interventions. It may be used as a supplementary tool, but ERCP is the preferred option when immediate treatment of a suspected obstruction is necessary.

question: From the CT abdomen given below identify the labeled structures.

correctAnswer: B. Typically asymptomatic and often found incidentally.
explanationHtml:
The MRI findings suggest Von Meyenberg complexes (VMCs), which are small, typically asymptomatic lesions in the liver resulting from ductal plate malformations. They are often discovered incidentally during imaging and can be associated with conditions like autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease.

Von Meyenberg complex (Bile Duct Microhamartomas)

  • Small (<1.5 cm), usually multiple greyish nodular lesions in the liver due to ductal plate malformations.
  • Associated with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, Caroli's disease, and congenital hepatic fibrosis. (Option D ruled out)
  • Histology: Cystically dilated bile ducts lined by a single layer of cuboidal epithelium in a collagenous stroma.
  • Clinical Presentation
    • Generally asymptomatic; Incidental findings during laparoscopic procedures or autopsies.
    • Can present with non-specific abdominal discomfort or episodes of cholangitis.
  • Imaging Modalities and Findings
    • Ultrasound: Multiple hyper- or hypoechoic areas with comet tail echoes.
    • CT Scan: Multiple irregular small low-attenuated areas, typically without enhancement on contrast injection. (Option C ruled out)
    • MRI/MRCP: Multiple irregularly delineated hyper-intense cystic nodules, not communicating with the biliary tree. Gadolinium contrast enhances differentiation from Caroli's disease.
  • Rare malignant transformation to cholangiocarcinoma. (Option A ruled out)
  • VMCs are rare liver findings with distinct MRI features. They typically cause no symptoms but can occasionally lead to abdominal discomfort or liver infections.

[[figure-1]]

  2. Von Meyenberg complex

explanationHtml:
The Mercedes-Benz sign is a radiological finding that appears in some gallstones. It is characterised by a triradiate pattern created by gas fissures within the gallstones, which resemble the three-pointed star logo of the Mercedes-Benz automobile.

Ultrasound Findings of Gallstones:

  • Appearance: Bright (echogenic) foci with acoustic shadowing.
  • False Negatives: Common due to small stones or poor acoustic access.
  • Differentiation from Polyps: Mobility or acoustic shadowing helps.
  • Double-Arc Shadow Sign: Seen with a gallbladder full of stones, showing two echogenic lines and dense shadowing.

[[figure-1]]

Mercedes-Benz Sign in Gallstones:

  • A star-shaped pattern of gas-fissuring within gallstones.
  • It is observed in about 50% of gallstones; often fluid-filled, with some containing nitrogen gas.
  • Indicates potential complications such as cholecystitis, emphasising the need for detailed imaging.

[[figure-2]]

Comprises various minerals: calcium oxalate, uric acid, struvite, and cystine.

Gallstones are better visualised on USG.

Renal stones are better seen on CT

Cholesterol stones may be hard to see on X-rays but are identifiable via ultrasound due to acoustic shadows. (Option A ruled out)

correctAnswer: B. T1-weighted images show a normal liver as hypointense compared to the spleen and kidney.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Normal liver parenchyma appears hyperintense on T1-weighted images compared to the spleen, kidney, and pancreas.

Imaging Techniques of Liver

Ultrasonography

• First-line investigation for hepatic disorders. (Option A ruled out)

• Cost-effective and useful for repeated follow-up.

• Elastography quantifies liver stiffness.

• Contrast-enhanced USG evaluates vascularity without radiation exposure.

• Colour Doppler assesses hepatic vessel flow and patency.

[[figure-1]]

Computed Tomography

• Investigation of choice for vascular anatomical assessment.

• It is less expensive and more accessible than MRI.

• Excellent for volumetry and surgical feasibility evaluation.

• Allows Triple-phase examinations, including:

◦ Arterial Phase

◦ Portal Phase

◦ Delayed Phase (Option C ruled out)

• If the lesion is enhanced in the arterial phase, it is hepatocellular carcinoma.

[[figure-2]]

Magnetic Resonance Imaging

• Best for assessing liver parenchyma and biliary system.

• Excellent soft tissue resolution.

• Effective in evaluating diffuse liver conditions like steatosis and fibrosis.

• Uses gadolinium-based contrast agents (e.g., Gd-DTPA, Gd-DOTA) for T1 enhancement.

• Breath-hold 3D T1 weighted sequences allow multiphasic examinations similar to CT.

• Hepatobiliary-specific agents target the reticulo-endothelial system (RES) or hepatocytes.

• T1-Weighted Images

◦ Normal Liver Parenchyma: Hyperintense compared to muscle, spleen, and kidney.

◦ Pathological Lesions: Typically T1 hypointense due to higher water or cellular density.

• T2-Weighted Images

◦ Normal Liver Signal: Hypointense compared to spleen, kidney, and pancreas.

◦ Lesions: Usually hyperintense, aiding in detection.

[[figure-3]]

MRI revealed multiple metastatic liver tumours

A- T1 MRI, B- T2 MRI

Digital Subtraction Angiography

• Largely reserved for therapeutic purposes. (Option D ruled out)

• Has been superseded by CT and MR angiographies for diagnostics.

[[figure-4]]

explanationHtml:
MRCP is a non-invasive imaging method that provides a detailed view of the biliary system and is particularly effective for diagnosing bile duct obstructions. It also does not rely on the excretion of contrast agents. It is the preferred next step when further non-invasive evaluation is needed after ultrasound, as it can detect stones, strictures, or masses causing the bile duct dilation.

[[figure-1]]

MRCP showing common bile duct dilation

[[figure-2]]

USG showing double barrel sign

Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) (Option B): While ERCP is highly effective for diagnosing and treating bile duct obstructions, it is an invasive procedure. It involves the insertion of an endoscope and contrast injection into the bile ducts, which carries risks like pancreatitis and infection. Though very useful when intervention is required, ERCP is not considered a non-invasive technique, making it less appropriate.

[[figure-3]]

ERCP showing dilation of the common bile duct (white arrow)

Ultrasound with colour Doppler (Option C): Although a repeat ultrasound with colour Doppler can help distinguish bile ducts from blood vessels by detecting blood flow, it does not provide detailed information on the cause of the dilation.

Plain radiography (Option D): Plain X-rays provide minimal information about the biliary system. They may show calcifications, but they cannot assess soft tissues or provide detailed views of the bile ducts



Reference:
  1. Grainger and Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 658, 666
  2. Textbook of Radiology and Imaging, David Sutton, 8th Edition, Volume 1, Page 2596
question: A 60 y/o jaundiced patient presents with upper abdominal pain. Ultrasound reveals a dilated bile duct, but the cause of obstruction is unclear. What would be the next best non-invasive imaging technique to evaluate this condition?

correctAnswer: B. Beaded appearance due to alternating strictures and dilations
explanationHtml:
• Beaded appearance due to alternating strictures and dilations is the hallmark finding of PSC on MRCP
  • The alternating areas of narrowing and dilation give the bile ducts a characteristic "beaded" or string-of-pearls appearance
  • This pattern reflects the chronic, patchy inflammation and fibrosis that affects both intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts in PSC, making it a key diagnostic feature for this condition.
  • There is also obliteration of the peripheral portions of the ducts, giving it the “pruned tree” appearance.

[[figure-1]]

MRCP showing a beaded appearance of dilated intrahepatic bile ducts in PSC

[[figure-2]]

ERCP showing: A) Beaded appearance, B) Pruned tree appearance, C) Band-like strictures


Diffuse dilation of bile ducts (Option A): PSC does not cause uniform dilation throughout the bile ducts. Instead, the disease leads to segmental areas of narrowing (strictures) and dilations, which result from progressive inflammation and fibrosis of the bile ducts.


A single long stricture in the common bile duct (Option C): A single long stricture would be more indicative of cholangiocarcinoma or a malignant obstruction, rather than PSC.


Multiple large masses in the liver (Option D): The presence of large masses in the liver would suggest a different pathology, such as metastatic liver disease or advanced hepatocellular carcinoma, rather than PSC.



Reference:
  1. Grainger and Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 670
  2. Textbook of Radiology and Imaging, David Sutton, 8th Edition, Volume 1, Page 2662, 2663

question: Which of the following is the hallmark radiological feature of primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) on MRCP?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The "triangular cord sign" is a hallmark finding on ultrasound in biliary atresia. This sign represents a fibrotic remnant of the bile ducts near the porta hepatis. Other ultrasound findings include an absent/abnormal gallbladder and a wide hepatic artery. Biliary atresia also presents with persistent jaundice and pale stools in infancy, which further supports this diagnosis.

[[figure-1]]

Triangular cord sign on USG

Other Investigations:

  • HIDA Scan: Lack of tracer in the duodenum after 24 hours suggests biliary atresia.
  • Radioisotope Studies: Highly sensitive to biliary atresia but poor specificity due to other conditions affecting bile excretion (e.g., infections, metabolic diseases).
  • Preoperative percutaneous transhepatic cholecysto-cholangiography combined with liver biopsy has 100% sensitivity
  • Definitive diagnosis: Intraoperative cholangiography


Choledochal Cyst (Option A): They are characterized by abnormal dilation of the bile ducts, which is absent in this case. Ultrasound in choledochal cysts typically shows prominent bile ducts and potential cystic formations, thus making it an unlikely diagnosis.


Neonatal Hepatitis (Option C):

Feature Biliary Atresia Neonatal Hepatitis
Nature Extrahepatic obstruction Hepatocellular inflammation
Onset Persistent jaundice >2 weeks Similar presentation
Stool color Acholic (clay-colored) Usually pigmented (may be pale sometimes)
GGT Markedly elevated Mild/moderate elevation
Ultrasound Absent/small GB, triangular cord sign Normal GB
HIDA Scan No excretion into intestine Delayed but present excretion
Liver biopsy Bile duct proliferation, fibrosis Giant cell transformation, hepatocyte injury
Treatment Kasai surgery Supportive, nutritional therapy


Caroli’s Disease (Option D): This is a rare condition associated with segmental dilation of the intrahepatic bile ducts, leading to bile duct cyst formation. The absence of bile duct dilation in this case makes Caroli’s disease an unlikely diagnosis.

question: A 2-month-old infant presents with persistent jaundice and pale stools. An ultrasound reveals no biliary dilation but shows the "triangular cord sign." Which condition is most likely suggested by this finding?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

A Hepatobiliary Iminodiacetic Acid (HIDA) scan is nearly 100% sensitive, for detecting bile leaks. It works by injecting a radioactive tracer that travels through the biliary system, highlighting any bile leakage. However, it cannot precisely identify the origin of the leak, making it less useful for surgical planning or pinpointing the exact location.


HIDA scan:

  • Most sensitive for bile leak (gold standard is ERCP)
  • Most accurate for acute cholecystitis (IOC- USG)
  • Best investigation to rule out EHBA (gold standard - PTC)

[[figure-1]]


CECT (Option B): CECT is the initial imaging study used in patients with suspected postoperative complications. It is useful for identifying localized fluid collections such as bilomas (encapsulated bile) or abscesses. While it can indicate the presence of fluid that might suggest a bile leak, it is less sensitive than HIDA for confirming the leak itself and may miss smaller leaks.

[[figure-2]]


MRI with Hepatobiliary Contrast (Option C): MRI with hepatobiliary-specific contrast agents, like gadoxetate disodium, effectively visualises the anatomy of the biliary system and can identify the exact location of a leak by showing contrast extravasation, but it is not sensitive in detecting leaks as compared to HIDA scan.

[[figure-3]]


Percutaneous Transhepatic Cholangiography (Option D): PTC is a specialized imaging technique where a contrast dye is injected directly into the bile ducts through a needle inserted into the liver. While it can provide details of the biliary anatomy, it is not typically the first choice for detecting leaks and is used more often when ductal injury is suspected.

explanationHtml:
The patient’s clinical presentation of severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and elevated lipase levels strongly suggests acute pancreatitis. Sentinel loop sign is a classic X-ray finding in acute pancreatitis, showing a dilated loop of the small intestine near the pancreas due to localized ileus caused by the inflammation.

Acute Pancreatitis

Clinical Diagnosis (Requires 2 of 3):

  1. Abdominal pain is strongly suggestive of acute pancreatitis.
  2. Serum amylase and/or lipase level at least 3 times the upper limit of normal.
  3. Imaging findings characteristic of acute pancreatitis.

X-ray Features

• Sentinel loop sign (Option C):

◦ Dilated loop of small intestine near the inflamed pancreas due to localized ileus.

◦ Significance: Early indicator of acute pancreatitis on X-ray.

[[figure-1]]

Sentinel loop sign

• Colon cut-off sign:

◦ Abrupt termination of gas in the colon at the splenic flexure, with collapsed distal colon loops.

◦ Significance: Suggests localized pancreatic inflammation, causing colonic spasm as an indirect sign of acute pancreatitis

[[figure-2]]

Investigations of Choice:

  • Contrast-enhanced CT (CECT): Primary tool for assessing pancreatic necrosis, peripancreatic inflammation, fluid collections, and complications.
    • Most reliable for staging and detecting complications.
    • May underestimate necrosis if done in the first 24 hours.

Morphological Types (Revised Atlanta Classification 2008):

  1. Interstitial oedematous pancreatitis:: Mild form with pancreatic oedema and swelling but no necrosis.
  2. Necrotising pancreatitis: Severe form involving pancreatic parenchymal necrosis, associated with higher morbidity and mortality.

Colon cut-off sign (Option A): Seen in acute pancreatitis, it indicates abrupt gas cut-off in the colon at the splenic flexure but doesn't explain small intestine dilation abdominal X-ray findings.

Pneumoperitoneum (Option B): Refers to free air under the diaphragm, often due to bowel perforation, and is not linked to acute pancreatitis.

Ground-glass opacity (Option D): Typically seen in lung imaging (e.g., pneumonia, ARDS), not related to pancreatitis or abdominal X-ray findings.



Reference:
  1. Grainger and Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 680,684,685
  2. Textbook of Radiology and Imaging, David Sutton, 8th Edition, Volume 1, Page 2022,2023,2725

question: A 50-year-old male presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to his back, ongoing for four days. Serum lipase is elevated. A contrast-enhanced CT scan reveals over 30% pancreatic necrosis, multiple peripancreatic fluid collections, and bilateral pleural effusions. Based on the Modified CT Severity Index (MCTSI) for acute pancreatitis, how would you grade this patient’s condition?

correctAnswer: C. Non-enhancing areas in the pancreatic body and tail
explanationHtml:
By day 3 of necrotizing pancreatitis, areas of non-enhancement are observed on imaging due to tissue necrosis.

Features of Acute Pancreatitis

  • Interstitial edematous pancreatitis: Swollen pancreas with intact microcirculation, showing homogeneous contrast enhancement, often with mild peripancreatic fat stranding and fluid.
  • Necrotizing pancreatitis: Disruption of microcirculation leads to nonenhancement of necrotic pancreatic tissue, with time-dependent pancreatic and peripancreatic inflammatory changes.

Imaging Findings in Acute Pancreatitis

Bulky Pancreas

• Enlarged pancreas with heterogeneous enhancement.

• Mild thickening of pancreatic tissue.

• Indicative of oedema in acute interstitial edematous pancreatitis.

[[figure-1]]

CECT revealing bulky pancreas

Renal halo sign:

• The "renal halo" sign presents as a high-density outline around the kidney indicating the inflammatory process in acute pancreatitis extending toward the left pancreatic tail and left pararenal space

[[figure-2]]

CECT revealing Renal halo sign

CT Findings

Day 1:

• Normally enhancing pancreas

[[figure-3]]

Day 3:

• Significant necrosis observed.

• The greater part of the pancreatic body and tail shows no enhancement.

[[figure-4]]

Post 2 weeks:

• Gas bubbles in the peripancreatic collection are consistent with an infected acute necrotic collection.

[[figure-5]]

Features of chronic pancreatitis

  • Parenchymal calcifications
  • Ductal dilatation
  • Parenchymal atrophy due to fibrosis and chronic damage.
  • Cystic lesions

Bulky pancreas with mild thickening (Option A): This finding is characteristic of interstitial edematous pancreatitis, not necrotizing pancreatitis.

Parenchymal calcifications (Option B) indicate chronic changes and are not typically seen in acute necrotizing pancreatitis.

Homogeneous enhancement of the pancreas (Option D): This finding suggests intact microcirculation and is typical of early interstitial edematous pancreatitis, not necrotizing pancreatitis.

  2. Bulky pancreas
  3. Imaging findings
  4. Grainger and Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page 692

question: A 52 y/o man diagnosed with necrotizing pancreatitis presents with worsening abdominal pain. A CT scan on day 3 of his illness is performed. What is the most likely imaging finding seen on day 3 in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option A - Choledochal cyst:

  • The given MRCP image shows a fusiform dilatation of the common hepatic and common bile ducts.
  • Fusiform dilatation of the extrahepatic biliary ducts on MRCP is the classic hallmark of a Type I choledochal cyst, the most common subtype (≈70–80%).
  • Type I involves smooth, uniform enlargement of the CHD and CBD, and MRCP is the investigation of choice for defining ductal anatomy.
  • It is characterized by the dilatation of bile duct
  • It is a congenital anomaly of the bile duct
  • It is more common in children and females
  • CECT of choledochal cyst: Central dot sign (in Caroli's disease-type V)

Incorrect Options:

question: Identify the condition based on the non-contrast CT scan of a patient given below:

explanationHtml:
Correct Option: A) Portal Vein

Explanation:

In an ultrasound of the liver, the portal vein appears as a tubular structure running through the liver tissue. It can be visualized as a hypoechoic (darker) tube with a characteristic branching pattern.

The portal vein plays a crucial role in delivering nutrients and substances absorbed from the digestive system to the liver for processing and detoxification.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Hepatic Artery (Option B):The hepatic artery is a blood vessel that supplies oxygenated blood to the liver. In an ultrasound of the liver, the hepatic artery may be visualized as a smaller, pulsatile vessel alongside the portal vein. It appears as a hyperechoic (brighter) tube with a pulsating motion. The hepatic artery delivers oxygenated blood to the liver cells for their metabolic needs.

Hepatic Vein (Option C): The hepatic veins are blood vessels that drain deoxygenated blood from the liver and carry it back to the heart via the inferior vena cava. In an ultrasound of the liver, the hepatic veins can be seen as hypoechoic (darker) tubular structures that converge and eventually merge into a single vessel known as the main hepatic vein. The hepatic veins drain blood from the liver and play a role in the liver's excretory function.

Inferior Vena Cava (Option B): The inferior vena cava (IVC) is a large vein that receives deoxygenated blood from the lower body and carries it to the right atrium of the heart. In an ultrasound of the liver, the IVC is typically visualized as a larger, hypoechoic (darker) vessel located posterior to the liver. It can be observed entering the liver at the level of the main hepatic vein. The IVC acts as the final drainage pathway for blood leaving the liver through the hepatic veins.



Reference:

Grainger and Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 7th Edition, Page no: 1456

Imaging Modality

Key Features

Ultrasound (US)

Cystic mass with an echogenic nodule (Rokitansky nodule) projecting into the lumen.
Predominantly echogenic mass with posterior sound attenuation (tip of the iceberg sign) due to sebaceous material and hair.

Fluid-fluid level representing sebaceous material floating on fluid.

Rokitansky nodule/dermoid plug attached to the cyst wall.

explanationHtml:
The clinical scenario and imaging findings showing

  • Enlarged, symmetrical uterus
  • Sub-endometrial linear striations (Venetian blind sign)
  • A "rain shower" appearance

is suggestive of adenomyosis.

Imaging findings in Adenomyosis:

Imaging Modality

Findings in Adenomyosis

Ultrasound (TVUS)
  • Enlarged, globular uterus with asymmetry of the anterior and posterior uterine walls (asymmetrical myometrial thickening)
  • Diffuse echogenic nodules
  • Subendometrial echogenic linear striations (Venetian blind sign)
  • Subendometrial cysts (2-6 mm), seen in 50% of cases
  • Endometrial pseudo widening
  • Poor definition of the endo-myometrial interface
  • Multiple fine areas of attenuation (‘rain shower’ appearance)
  • A speckled pattern of increased vascularity on Color Doppler

MRI (T2-weighted images)

Ill-defined areas of low myometrial signal intensity due to smooth muscle hyperplasia
Diffuse or focal thickening of the junctional zone (JZ)

  • JZ ≥12 mm strongly predicts adenomyosis;
  • JZ ≤8 mm excludes it


High T2 signal intensity foci within low signal myometrium (ectopic endometrial tissue or cystic gland dilatation) (Salt and Pepper appearance)

High T2 signal linear striations (finger-like projections) extending from the endometrium into myometrium

MRI (T1-weighted images)

High T1 signal intensity foci represent small punctate haemorrhages, with a 95% positive predictive value for adenomyosis

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Uterine fibroids (Option A) typically present as well-circumscribed, solid masses on ultrasound, not associated with the "rain shower" appearance or sub-endometrial cysts.

Endometrial polyp (Option B) usually shows a feeder vessel sign (a single feeding artery to the poly that's visible on an USG), but not the sub-endometrial changes seen in adenomyosis.

Endometriosis (Option D) involves ectopic endometrial tissue outside the uterus, often associated with ovarian cysts (endometriomas), and does not cause the specific ultrasound features of adenomyosis.

question: A 30-year-old woman undergoing controlled ovarian hyperstimulation for in vitro fertilization presents with abdominal pain and significant distension. Which of the following is the most likely finding on an ultrasound seen in this patient that helps differentiate it from PCOS?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient most likely has ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS), a complication of controlled ovarian stimulation during assisted reproductive techniques.

  • The presence of ascites on ultrasound is the hallmark imaging finding that distinguishes OHSS from PCOS and reflects increased capillary permeability with third-space fluid accumulation mediated by vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF).

[[figure-1]]


Ultrasound findings in OHSS:

  • Bilaterally enlarged ovaries (often 5-12 cm)
  • Multiple enlarged follicles/theca lutein cysts
  • Ascites (hallmark finding)
  • In severe cases, pleural effusion may also be present

Echogenic ovarian stroma (Option A): Increased stromal echogenicity is a characteristic ultrasound feature of PCOS, resulting from stromal hypertrophy and hyperthecosis.

Ovarian volume >10 mL (Option B): An ovarian volume >10 mL is one of the Rotterdam ultrasound criteria for PCOS. Although ovaries are enlarged in OHSS, ovarian enlargement alone does not distinguish the two conditions.

Multiple cysts measuring 2-9 mm (Option D): Numerous small peripheral follicles measuring 2-9 mm producing the classic "string of pearls" appearance are typical of PCOS. In contrast, OHSS is characterized by multiple enlarged follicles/theca lutein cysts rather than small peripheral follicles.

[[figure-2]]

correctAnswer: B. Increased resistance to blood flow in the placenta, indicating potential placental insufficiency
explanationHtml:
Answer: B) Increased resistance to blood flow in the placenta, indicating potential placental insufficiency

Explanation:

An abnormal S/D ratio indicates increased resistance in placental blood flow, which may affect fetal growth and necessitate closer monitoring.

Obstetric Doppler Applications

  • Fetal Well-Being Assessment
    • Crucial for evaluating blood flow in the fetus and placenta.
    • An abnormal S/D ratio in umbilical artery Doppler indicates possible placental insufficiency and necessitates further evaluation. (Option B)
    • High S/D ratio reflects increased resistance in placental blood flow, potentially affecting fetal growth. (Option A ruled out)
    • S/D ratio>3 beyond 28 weeks is a marker of uteroplacental insufficiency

[[figure-1]]

  • Detection of Fetal Anemia
    • Doppler assessment of middle cerebral artery (MCA) blood flow can indicate fetal anaemia.(Option B ruled out)
    • MCA peak systolic velocity (>1.5 MoM) predicts moderate-to-severe fetal anemia
    • Particularly relevant in blood-group allo-immunization cases, where fetal anemia is a severe risk.

  • MCA Doppler in Growth Restriction
    • While helpful for detecting fetal anaemia, its role in managing fetal growth restriction is unclear.
    • An abnormal cerebroplacental ratio may indicate fetal distress, but its impact on delivery timing is not yet established as standard practice. (Option D ruled out)

[[figure-2]]

  • Ductus Venosus Assessment
    • Like MCA Doppler, ductus venosus evaluation has not shown significant benefits in perinatal outcomes.
    • Offers insights into cardiac dysfunction in severe growth restriction but is not routinely recommended for clinical management.

[[figure-3]]

  • Guiding Prenatal Procedures
    • Doppler is instrumental in guiding prenatal interventions, including procedures like cordocentesis.


Reference:
  1. Williams Obstetrics, 26th Edition, Page 261-263
  2. DC Dutta’s Textbook of Obstetrics, 9th Edition, Page 604

question: A 32-year-old woman presents for a routine ultrasound at 28 weeks of gestation. The obstetrician notes an abnormal S/D ratio in the umbilical artery Doppler assessment. Which of the following implications is most likely associated with this finding?

correctAnswer: B. Increased resistance to blood flow in the placenta, indicating potential placental insufficiency
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The umbilical artery Doppler assesses fetoplacental circulation.

  • An elevated S/D ratio (Option A) indicates increased placental vascular resistance, suggesting placental insufficiency.
  • This finding is associated with fetal growth restriction (FGR), adverse perinatal outcomes, and the need for closer fetal surveillance.
  • As placental insufficiency worsens, Doppler abnormalities may progress from increased resistance to absent and eventually reversed end-diastolic flow, both of which are associated with increasing fetal compromise.

Obstetric Doppler Applications

  • Umbilical artery Doppler:
    • Assesses fetoplacental circulation.
    • An elevated S/D ratio or pulsatility index indicates increased placental vascular resistance and possible placental insufficiency.
  • Middle cerebral artery (MCA) Doppler:
    • Peak systolic velocity >1.5 MoM is highly suggestive of moderate-to-severe fetal anemia (Option C), particularly in red-cell alloimmunization.
    • MCA Doppler also contributes to surveillance of fetal growth restriction as part of the cerebroplacental ratio (CPR).
  • Ductus venosus Doppler:
    • Evaluates fetal cardiac function and is particularly useful in early-onset severe fetal growth restriction to assess fetal deterioration
    • Aid decisions regarding the timing of delivery.
  • Prenatal procedures:
    • Doppler ultrasound guides interventions such as cordocentesis and other fetal procedures.

Indicates fetal distress and warrants immediate delivery (Option D): An elevated umbilical artery S/D ratio alone does not mandate delivery. Management depends on the gestational age, fetal growth, overall fetal surveillance, and the severity of Doppler abnormalities (e.g., absent or reversed end-diastolic flow).

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

[[figure-3]]



Reference:
  1. Williams Obstetrics, 26th Edition, Pages 261-263
  2. DC Dutta’s Textbook of Obstetrics, 9th Edition, Pages 604

question: A 32-year-old woman undergoes a routine obstetric ultrasound at 28 weeks of gestation. Umbilical artery Doppler demonstrates an abnormal systolic/diastolic (S/D) ratio. What is the most likely implication of this finding?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Increased amniotic fluid volume is not typically associated with IUFD; it may be normal or reduced in such cases.


Ultrasound Imaging in Intrauterine Fetal Demise (IUFD)

  • Key Findings:
    • Absent fetal heartbeat (definitive sign of IUFD)
    • Absent fetal movements (strong indicator)
    • Roberts sign: Gas shadow in the heart or great vessels due to postmortem blood degeneration, typically appearing 12–48 hours after death
    • Spalding Sign: Overlapping skull bones suggesting fetal death (Option B ruled out)
    • Maceration: Distortion of fetal anatomy due to decomposition (Option A ruled out)
    • Soft Tissue Edema: Notable when skin thickness exceeds 5 mm (Option D ruled out)
    • Echogenic Amniotic Fluid: Presence of debris in amniotic fluid


MRI Imaging

  • Additional Details: Useful when ultrasound findings are unclear.
  • Key Signs:
    • Constricted heart (poorly defined cardiac chambers, abnormal heart signal)
    • Brain ischemia (global ischemic changes in brain tissue)
    • Abnormal globes and effusions (indicate systemic effects)
    • Cord thrombosis (thrombus in the umbilical cord)

Answer: A) Second-trimester anatomy scan at 20 weeks

Explanation:

Second-trimester anatomy scan (aka TIFFA-Targeted imaging for fetal anomalies) at 20 weeks (anomaly scan) is a comprehensive ultrasound essential for evaluating fetal anatomy and detecting potential structural anomalies, especially in cases with increased NT.

Nuchal Translucency (NT)

  • Definition:
    • NT refers to the fluid-filled space between the fetal skin and soft tissue at the back of the neck.

[[figure-1]]

  • Measurement:
    • Conducted via ultrasound between 11-14 weeks of gestation in a sagittal plane.
    • Accurate measurement follows specific criteria.
  • Significance:
    • Increased NT: Linked to higher risks of:
      • Fetal Aneuploidy (abnormal chromosome number).
        • Trisomy 21(most common) >monosomy X>Trisomy 18 and 13
      • Structural Anomalies (especially fetal heart defects).
  • Screening Role:
    • NT is part of first-trimester aneuploidy screening.
  • Threshold for Concern:
    • NT ≥ 3 mm is abnormal and requires further investigation (detailed fetal anatomy survey/ anomaly scan). (Option A)

[[figure-2]]

  • Outcome: As the fetus develops into the second trimester, nuchal translucency might either:
    • Regress
    • Evolve into:
      • Nuchal edema
      • Cystic hygroma

[[figure-3]]

    • Dual test [free b-hCG and PAPP-A (Pregnancy Associated Plasma Protein-A)] + NT scan

  • Anomaly to detect: Down’s syndrome

Fetal echocardiography (Option B) is a specialized exam for assessing cardiac structure but is usually performed later if there are specific concerns identified during the anatomy scan.

question: A 30-year-old woman undergoes a first-trimester transvaginal ultrasound at 6 weeks' gestation. The scan demonstrates an early twin pregnancy. Which ultrasound sign shown in the image indicates a dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy?

explanationHtml:
Answer: A) Ring of fire appearance

Explanation: The "ring of fire" appearance on Doppler ultrasound refers to the increased peripheral vascularity surrounding an extrauterine mass or gestational sac. The presence of this peripheral vascularity, along with the absence of an intrauterine pregnancy, is a definitive radiologic feature of an ectopic pregnancy.

Ectopic Pregnancy:

  • Empty extrauterine sac with a hyperechoic ring.

[[figure-1]]

  • Extrauterine yolk sac and/or fetal pole with or without cardiac activity.
  • Inhomogeneous adnexal mass or extrauterine halo-like structure - a probable ectopic pregnancy.
  • Colour Doppler imaging: Placental blood flow within the periphery of an ectopic pregnancy - ring of fire appearance. (Option A)

[[figure-2]]

  • In ruptured ectopic, blood is present in the pouch of Douglas, which shows echoes on USG because of the presence of hemoperitoneum.

[[figure-3]]

Lambda sign (Option B): It is seen in dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancies.

Trilaminar appearance (Option C): The trilaminar appearance of the endometrium is normally seen in the late proliferative phase of the menstrual cycle.

Double decidual sac sign (Option D): This sign confirms the presence of an intrauterine pregnancy and is not seen in ectopic pregnancy.

  1. William’s Gynecology, 4th Edition, Page 164-66.
  2. DC Dutta’s Textbook of Obstetrics, 9th Edition, Page 192, 601.
question: A 33-year-old woman with a history of tubal ligation presents with sudden lower abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding. She has a positive serum hCG, and transvaginal ultrasound is shown below. What is the most definitive radiological feature confirming the diagnosis of ectopic pregnancy in this case?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The image demonstrates the ring of fire appearance, which refers to marked peripheral hypervascularity surrounding an adnexal gestational sac or ectopic trophoblastic tissue on color Doppler ultrasound.

  • This vascular pattern reflects increased blood flow around the trophoblastic tissue and is a classic Doppler finding associated with ectopic pregnancy.
  • However, the ring of fire sign is not specific and may also be seen in a corpus luteum cyst.
  • The most definitive sonographic evidence of an ectopic pregnancy is visualisation of an extrauterine gestational sac containing a yolk sac and/or embryo, with or without cardiac activity.
  • Other ultrasound findings suggestive of ectopic pregnancy include:
    • Extrauterine gestational sac with a hyperechoic tubal ring

[[figure-1]]

    • Inhomogeneous adnexal mass ("blob sign")
    • Hemoperitoneum in ruptured ectopic pregnancy

[[figure-2]]

Lambda sign (Option B): The lambda (twin peak) sign is seen in dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancies and indicates the presence of chorionic tissue extending between the intertwin membranes.

Trilaminar appearance (Option C): A trilaminar endometrium is a normal finding during the late proliferative phase of the menstrual cycle and is unrelated to ectopic pregnancy.

Double decidual sac sign (Option D): The double decidual sac sign is highly suggestive of an early intrauterine pregnancy and helps distinguish a true gestational sac from a pseudogestational sac seen in ectopic pregnancy.

An image of the transvaginal ultrasound is shown below. shows a well-defined gestational sac with the double decidual sac sign, but no yolk sac or fetal pole is visible. explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The provided radiological image is from a Hysterosalpingography (HSG), showing a right-side dilated, tortuous right fallopian tube with no contrast spillage into the peritoneal cavity. The contrast remains confined within the tube, indicating distal blockage. The most likely diagnosis is right hydrosalpinx.


Hysterosalpingography

  • It is a radiographic imaging technique
  • Indication:
    • Infertility evaluation to assess the endocervical canal, the endometrial cavity, and the fallopian tube lumina and patency.
  • Procedure:
    • Radiopaque contrast material is injected through the cervical canal
    • It is performed between cycle days 5 and 10
  • Normal findings:
    • The spill of contrast from the tubes into the peritoneal cavity suggests patency of the fallopian tubes.
    • The endometrial cavity is usually triangular and has a smooth contour.
  • Contraindications:
    • Acute pelvic infection
    • Active uterine bleeding
    • Pregnancy
    • Iodine allergy

Images:

[[figure-1]]

Normal uterine cavity with contrast extravasation through a posterior cervical canal (black arrow).

[[figure-2]]

[[figure-3]]

a: Right hydrosalpinx

b: Block at right cornua (No distention of the tube) (Option D ruled out)


[[figure-4]]

Small filling defect: Uterine adhesions (Option C ruled out)


Ovarian cyst (Option B): It is a fluid-filled sac within the ovary. Since the contrast does not enter the cyst, it is not directly visualized in HSG. In this case, a dilated right fallopian tube with contrast accumulation within the fallopian tube and the lack of spillage of contrast is consistent with the hydrosalpinx picture.
